It asks to compute, for January 2025, per subscription: total units used, compare to the plan's included_units, and return only positive overages along with the subscription_id and plan name, ordered by subscription_id. It uses tables: subscriptions, plans, and usage_events.

results.question: Find customers whose open invoices total at least 50 across all subscriptions. Return customer_id, name, open_invoice_count, and open_amount rounded to two decimals, ordered by customer_id. Exclude paid and void invoices.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(i.invoice_id) AS open_invoice_count, ROUND(SUM(i.amount), 2) AS open_amount
FROM customers c
JOIN subscriptions s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN invoices i ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
WHERE i.status NOT IN ('paid','void')
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(i.amount) >= 50
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
results.classification_explanation: Valid read-only database query. The request asks to find customers with open invoices totaling at least 50 across all subscriptions, returning customer_id, name, open_invoice_count, and open_amount rounded to two decimals, ordered by customer_id, excluding paid and void invoices.

results.question: Find subscriptions that have at least one usage event but have never had an invoice of any status. Return subscription_id, customer name, and plan name, ordered by subscription_id.
results.sql:
SELECT s.subscription_id, c.name AS customer_name, p.name AS plan_name
FROM subscriptions s
JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN plans p ON s.plan_id = p.plan_id
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM usage_events ue WHERE ue.subscription_id = s.subscription_id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoices i WHERE i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id)
ORDER BY s.subscription_id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: Valid read-only database question. It asks for subscriptions with at least one usage_event but with no invoices of any status, returning subscription_id, customer name, and plan name ordered by subscription_id. All required tables (usage_events, invoices, subscriptions, customers, plans) exist in the schema, so this is answerable without requiring writes or external data.

results.question: Show each paid invoice together with the running paid revenue for its customer across all subscriptions. Apply invoices in billed_on then invoice_id order within each customer. Return customer_id, invoice_id, billed_on, and running_paid_amount rounded to two decimals. Order by customer_id, billed_on, and invoice_id.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       i.invoice_id,
       i.billed_on,
       ROUND(SUM(i.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY date(i.billed_on), i.invoice_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_paid_amount
FROM invoices i
JOIN subscriptions s ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE i.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.customer_id, date(i.billed_on), i.invoice_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It can be answered by querying invoices joined to subscriptions to obtain customer_id, filtering for paid invoices, and computing a running total per customer ordered by billed_on then invoice_id (using a window SUM).

results.question: Which customers have at least one subscription and have at least one paid invoice for every subscription they have ever held, including cancelled or paused subscriptions? Return customer_id and name, ordered by customer_id.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM subscriptions s WHERE s.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM subscriptions s2
    WHERE s2.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM invoices i
          WHERE i.subscription_id = s2.subscription_id
            AND i.status IS NOT NULL
            AND UPPER(i.status) = 'PAID'
      )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question asking to identify customers who have at least one subscription and, for every subscription they have ever held (including cancelled/paused), at least one paid invoice. It uses only existing tables and requires a read query (no updates).

results.question: Which high-priority tickets currently have status open? Return ticket_id, opened_at, and assigned_agent_id, retaining NULL for unassigned tickets. Sort by opened_at ascending, then ticket_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT ticket_id, opened_at, assigned_agent_id
FROM tickets
WHERE status COLLATE NOCASE = 'open' AND priority COLLATE NOCASE = 'high'
ORDER BY opened_at ASC, ticket_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database query: fetch high-priority tickets with status 'open', return ticket_id, opened_at, and assigned_agent_id (NULL if unassigned), sorted by opened_at and then ticket_id.

results.question: Count closed tickets for each priority that has at least one closed ticket. Return priority and closed_ticket_count, sorted by priority alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT priority, COUNT(*) AS closed_ticket_count
FROM tickets
WHERE closed_at IS NOT NULL AND priority IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY priority ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks to compute the number of closed tickets by priority using the tickets table (considering status/closed_at), grouped by priority, filtering groups with at least one closed ticket, and sorting alphabetically by priority.

results.question: List the agents in team 1. Return agent_id and name, sorted by name alphabetically, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT agent_id, name
FROM agents
WHERE team_id = 1
ORDER BY name ASC, agent_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: Answerable read-only request: retrieve agent_id and name from agents where team_id = 1, ordered by name ascending, then agent_id ascending.

results.question: For every team, count its unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending, including tickets without an assigned agent. Include teams with zero unresolved tickets. Return team_id, team_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT t.team_id,
       t.name AS team_name,
       COUNT(tk.ticket_id) AS unresolved_ticket_count
FROM teams t
LEFT JOIN tickets tk
  ON tk.team_id = t.team_id
  AND tk.status IN ('open', 'pending')
GROUP BY t.team_id, t.name
ORDER BY t.team_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The request asks for a read-only aggregate query over the provided schema: it requires counting unresolved tickets (status in ('open','pending')) per team, including tickets with no assigned agent, and returning team_id, team_name, and the count sorted by team_id. This is a valid read-only data retrieval task using the given tables (teams, tickets) and a left join to include teams with zero unresolved tickets.

results.question: For every customer, report the number of tickets of any status and the number of those tickets with no assigned agent. Include customers without tickets with both counts zero. Return customer_id, customer_name, ticket_count, and unassigned_ticket_count, sorted by customer_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS ticket_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN t.ticket_id IS NULL THEN 0 WHEN t.assigned_agent_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unassigned_ticket_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question: compute, for each customer, the total number of tickets and the number of tickets with no assigned agent, including customers with zero tickets. Returns customer_id, customer_name, ticket_count, and unassigned_ticket_count, sorted by customer_id ascending.

results.question: For each ticket that has received an agent_reply event, find its earliest agent reply and the elapsed hours from opening to that reply. Ignore other event types. Return ticket_id, first_reply_at, and response_hours rounded to two decimal places, sorted by ticket_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH first_replies AS (
  SELECT e.ticket_id, MIN(e.created_at) AS first_reply_at
  FROM ticket_events e
  WHERE lower(e.event_type) = 'agent_reply'
  GROUP BY e.ticket_id
)
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       fr.first_reply_at,
       ROUND((julianday(fr.first_reply_at) - julianday(t.opened_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS response_hours
FROM first_replies fr
JOIN tickets t ON t.ticket_id = fr.ticket_id
WHERE fr.first_reply_at >= t.opened_at
ORDER BY t.ticket_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The request asks for a read-only query over the provided schema to compute, for each ticket with an agent_reply event, the earliest reply time and hours since opening, returning ticket_id, first_reply_at, and response_hours, sorted by ticket_id.
critique_issues: Timestamp handling: fr.first_reply_at and t.opened_at are TEXT. Although julianday can parse ISO-8601-like strings, if timestamps are not consistently formatted, calculation may fail. Consider normalizing timestamps on insert or explicitly casting to a numeric epoch (e.g., julianday(CAST(fr.first_reply_at AS TEXT))) or ensure ISO 8601 format before calculation.

Data integrity guard placement: The query filters out negative durations in a WHERE clause (WHERE fr.first_reply_at >= t.opened_at), which is good. If you prefer to keep the check in SELECT, ensure that any rows with first_reply_at < opened_at are excluded or clearly documented; currently the proposed version relies on the WHERE clause, which is acceptable.

First reply time type: The query returns first_reply_at as TEXT. If downstream code expects a TIMESTAMP/DATE type, consider casting in the SELECT (e.g., CAST(fr.first_reply_at AS TEXT) is already text; for ISO8601 you might CAST to DATETIME or keep as TEXT but document format).

Performance considerations: The query uses a lower() check on event_type which can be slow on large tables unless an index or a functional index exists (e.g., CREATE INDEX idx_agent_reply_lower ON ticket_events(LOWER(event_type));). Consider normalizing event_type to a consistent case at insert time or add an index to support this predicate.

Limit handling: A LIMIT 1000 is present for bounding results. If unlimited results are required, ensure pagination is implemented (e.g., with LIMIT and OFFSET parameters) to support large datasets and consistent paging.

results.question: Which agents are assigned at least two tickets with status closed? Return agent_id, agent_name, and closed_ticket_count. Sort by closed_ticket_count descending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS closed_ticket_count
FROM agents a
JOIN tickets t ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
WHERE t.status = 'closed'
GROUP BY a.agent_id, a.name
HAVING COUNT(t.ticket_id) >= 2
ORDER BY closed_ticket_count DESC, a.agent_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only data question about existing tables (agents, tickets) and can be answered without modifying the schema. It asks for agents with at least two closed tickets and to return agent_id, agent_name, and the count, sorted as specified.

results.question: Find the oldest unresolved ticket, meaning status open or pending, for each team that has one. Exclude tickets without a team. If a team has several tickets opened at the same time, choose the lowest ticket_id. Return team_id, team_name, ticket_id, and opened_at, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH unresolved AS (
  SELECT
    t.ticket_id,
    t.team_id,
    t.opened_at,
    tm.name AS team_name,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY t.team_id
      ORDER BY t.opened_at ASC, t.ticket_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM tickets t
  JOIN teams tm ON t.team_id = tm.team_id
  WHERE t.status IN ('open', 'pending')
)
SELECT
  team_id,
  team_name,
  ticket_id,
  opened_at
FROM unresolved
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY team_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question: it asks for the oldest unresolved ticket (status open or pending) for each team, excluding tickets without a team, and to return team_id, team_name, ticket_id, and opened_at, sorted by team_id. It fits a read-only query against the provided schema; no data modification is requested.

results.question: Build a complete assignment roster showing every ticket of any status with its assigned agent, every unassigned ticket with NULL agent fields, and every agent with no tickets with NULL ticket fields. Return agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, and status. Sort by agent_id ascending with NULL agents last, then ticket_id ascending with NULL tickets last.
results.sql:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT a.agent_id AS agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, t.ticket_id AS ticket_id, t.status AS status
  FROM tickets t
  JOIN agents a ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL AS agent_id, NULL AS agent_name, t.ticket_id AS ticket_id, t.status AS status
  FROM tickets t
  WHERE t.assigned_agent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT a.agent_id AS agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, NULL AS ticket_id, NULL AS status
  FROM agents a
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tickets t WHERE t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id)
) AS x
ORDER BY CASE WHEN agent_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ASC, agent_id, CASE WHEN ticket_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ASC, ticket_id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It can be answered by joining agents with tickets (including unassigned tickets where agent is NULL) and including agents with no tickets (NULL ticket fields), then selecting agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, and status, and sorting by agent_id (NULLs last) and ticket_id (NULLs last).

results.question: For each team, identify all agents tied for the largest number of assigned unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending. Exclude teams where every agent has zero assigned unresolved tickets. Count workload by the agent's team, and ignore unassigned tickets. Return team_id, team_name, agent_id, agent_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH per_agent AS (
  SELECT
    a.team_id,
    t.name AS team_name,
    a.agent_id,
    a.name AS agent_name,
    COUNT(tk.ticket_id) AS unresolved_ticket_count
  FROM agents a
  JOIN teams t ON a.team_id = t.team_id
  LEFT JOIN tickets tk
    ON tk.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
   AND tk.status IN ('open','pending')
  GROUP BY a.team_id, t.name, a.agent_id, a.name
)
SELECT
  team_id,
  team_name,
  agent_id,
  agent_name,
  unresolved_ticket_count
FROM (
  SELECT
    p.*,
    MAX(unresolved_ticket_count) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS max_per_team
  FROM per_agent p
) AS q
WHERE unresolved_ticket_count = max_per_team
  AND max_per_team > 0
ORDER BY team_id ASC, agent_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a valid read-only database question. It asks to compute, per team, the agents who have the largest number of unresolved tickets (tickets with status open or pending and having a non-null assigned_agent_id), and to return team and agent details along with the count. Teams with all zero unresolved tickets are excluded. No data modification or schema changes are required; only a read query is needed.

results.question: Which rooms have a current nightly_rate of 160 or less? Return room_number, room_type, and nightly_rate. Sort by nightly_rate descending, then room_number ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT room_number, room_type, nightly_rate
FROM rooms
WHERE nightly_rate <= 160
ORDER BY nightly_rate DESC, room_number ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It requests room_number, room_type, and nightly_rate from the rooms table where nightly_rate is 160 or less, sorted by nightly_rate in descending order and then by room_number ascending.

results.question: List confirmed bookings whose check-in date falls in February or March 2025. Return booking_id, check_in, and check_out, sorted by check_in ascending, then booking_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT booking_id, check_in, check_out
FROM bookings
WHERE status = 'confirmed'
  AND date(check_in) BETWEEN date('2025-02-01') AND date('2025-03-31')
ORDER BY check_in ASC, booking_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The user asks for a read-only data retrieval: list confirmed bookings with check-in in February or March 2025, returning specific columns and sorting. The schema includes a bookings table with fields status, check_in, and check_out, which supports this query. No write or administrative operation is requested.

results.question: For each checked_out booking, calculate its number of nights and booking value using booked_nightly_rate. Checkout day is excluded. Return booking_id, nights as an integer, and booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  booking_id,
  CAST(julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in) AS INTEGER) AS nights,
  ROUND(booked_nightly_rate * CAST(julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in) AS INTEGER), 2) AS booking_value
FROM bookings
WHERE status = 'checked_out'
ORDER BY booking_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The question asks for per-booking nights and value using check_in, check_out, and booked_nightly_rate from the bookings table, which is a read-only query and all required data exists in the provided schema.

results.question: For every room, count checked_out bookings and their total nights, excluding checkout days. Include rooms without checked_out bookings with both totals zero. Return room_id, room_number, completed_booking_count, and total_nights as an integer, sorted by room_number ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  rooms.room_id,
  rooms.room_number,
  CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN bookings.status = 'checked_out' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS INTEGER) AS completed_booking_count,
  CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN bookings.status = 'checked_out' THEN julianday(bookings.check_out) - julianday(bookings.check_in) ELSE 0 END) AS INTEGER) AS total_nights
FROM rooms
LEFT JOIN bookings ON rooms.room_id = bookings.room_id
GROUP BY rooms.room_id, rooms.room_number
ORDER BY rooms.room_number ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database request. It asks to compute, for every room, the number of bookings with a status indicating checkout (e.g., checked_out) and the total nights for those bookings, excluding the checkout day. It should include rooms with zero completed bookings. The result should include room_id, room_number, completed_booking_count, and total_nights, ordered by room_number. This can be answered from the provided schema using joins between rooms and bookings and aggregations (group by room).

results.question: For every guest, total the booking value of their checked_out stays, using each booking's historical booked_nightly_rate multiplied by nights and excluding checkout days. Include guests with no checked_out stays with a zero total. Return guest_id, guest_name, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT g.guest_id,
       g.name AS guest_name,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN date(b.check_out) <= date('now')
                              THEN b.booked_nightly_rate * (CAST(julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in) AS INTEGER))
                         ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS completed_booking_value
FROM guests g
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON g.guest_id = b.guest_id
GROUP BY g.guest_id, g.name
ORDER BY g.guest_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database query request. It asks to compute, for every guest, the total value of their completed (checked_out) stays by summing booked_nightly_rate * nights for each booking, excluding checkout days, and to include guests with zero total. It requires joining bookings with guests (and optionally rooms for rates) and returning guest_id, guest_name, and the rounded total, sorted by guest_id ascending. No data modification operations are requested.

results.question: How much net cash has been received for checked_out bookings in each room type? Sum signed payments so refunds reduce the total; exclude payments for other booking statuses and unallocated payments. Only include room types with at least one qualifying payment. Return room_type and net_payments rounded to two decimal places, sorted by room_type alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT r.room_type,
       ROUND(SUM(p.amount), 2) AS net_payments
FROM bookings b
JOIN rooms r ON b.room_id = r.room_id
JOIN payments p ON p.booking_id = b.booking_id
WHERE b.status = 'checked_out'
GROUP BY r.room_type
ORDER BY r.room_type ASC;
results.classification_explanation: Valid: This is an answerable read-only query asking to compute net payments by room_type for bookings with status 'checked_out'. It uses the bookings, payments, and rooms tables, requires summing signed payments (refunds reduce total), excludes payments for other statuses and unallocated payments, includes only room types with at least one qualifying payment, and asks for results rounded to two decimals sorted by room_type. No SQL needed here.

results.question: Which checked_out bookings still have a positive outstanding balance? Balance equals nights excluding checkout day times booked_nightly_rate, minus all signed payments for that booking; treat no payments as zero. Return booking_id, guest_name, room_number, and outstanding_balance rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending. Test positivity before rounding.
results.sql:
WITH per_booking AS (
  SELECT
    b.booking_id,
    g.name AS guest_name,
    r.room_number,
    julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in) AS nights_raw,
    b.booked_nightly_rate AS rate_raw,
    COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) AS payments_total
  FROM bookings b
  JOIN guests g ON b.guest_id = g.guest_id
  JOIN rooms r ON b.room_id = r.room_id
  LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.booking_id = b.booking_id
  WHERE date(b.check_out) < date('now')
  GROUP BY b.booking_id, g.name, r.room_number
)
SELECT
  booking_id,
  guest_name,
  room_number,
  ROUND((MAX(nights_raw) * MAX(rate_raw)) - payments_total, 2) AS outstanding_balance
FROM per_booking
GROUP BY booking_id, guest_name, room_number
HAVING (MAX(nights_raw) * MAX(rate_raw)) - payments_total > 0
ORDER BY booking_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: Answerable read-only database question. It asks to compute outstanding balances for bookings that have checked_out, using bookings, payments, guests, and rooms tables, and to return booking_id, guest_name, room_number, and outstanding_balance rounded to two decimals. This is a read-only query requiring joins and aggregations, which is supported by the schema.
critique_issues: LIMIT 100 is present in the final proposal but there was no LIMIT requested; remove it unless a cap is required.

In the inner CTE, nights_raw (julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in)) and rate_raw (booked_nightly_rate) are selected and grouped by booking_id, name, room_number without aggregation. This can yield indeterminate values if there are multiple joined rows for a single booking. Action: aggregate these values in the inner query (e.g., MAX(nights_raw) AS nights, MAX(rate_raw) AS rate) or include them in the GROUP BY to guarantee a single value per booking.

results.question: Find overlapping pairs of bookings for the same room, considering only confirmed and checked_out bookings. A booking occupies [check_in, check_out), so a checkout on another booking's check-in date is not an overlap. Return each pair once, with the lower booking_id first. Return room_number, first_booking_id, and second_booking_id, sorted by room_number, first_booking_id, then second_booking_id, all ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.room_number, b1.booking_id AS first_booking_id, b2.booking_id AS second_booking_id
FROM bookings b1
JOIN bookings b2 ON b1.room_id = b2.room_id
JOIN rooms r ON b1.room_id = r.room_id
WHERE b1.booking_id < b2.booking_id
  AND b1.status IN ('confirmed','checked_out')
  AND b2.status IN ('confirmed','checked_out')
  AND b1.check_in < b2.check_out
  AND b2.check_in < b1.check_out
ORDER BY r.room_number, b1.booking_id, b2.booking_id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question that can be answered using the provided schema. It asks to find overlapping booking pairs for the same room, considering only bookings with status 'confirmed' and 'checked_out', using the check_in/check_out intervals [check_in, check_out). It will involve self-joining bookings on the same room and filtering by the status and interval overlap, and returning room_number, first_booking_id, and second_booking_id (ordered as specified). No SQL generation is required here.

results.question: Within each room type, find every room tied for the highest total booking value from checked_out stays. Use historical booked_nightly_rate times nights excluding checkout days, and assign zero to rooms without checked_out stays; if every room in a type has zero, return all of them. Return room_type, room_number, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places. Rank using unrounded totals and sort by room_type alphabetically, then room_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH per_room AS (
  SELECT r.room_type,
         r.room_number,
         COALESCE(SUM(b.booked_nightly_rate * (JULIANDAY(b.check_out) - JULIANDAY(b.check_in))), 0) AS completed_booking_value_unrounded
  FROM rooms r
  LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.room_id = r.room_id
                          AND b.status = 'checked_out'
                          AND JULIANDAY(b.check_out) > JULIANDAY(b.check_in)
  GROUP BY r.room_type, r.room_number
), max_per_type AS (
  SELECT room_type,
         MAX(completed_booking_value_unrounded) AS max_total
  FROM per_room
  GROUP BY room_type
)
SELECT p.room_type,
       p.room_number,
       ROUND(p.completed_booking_value_unrounded, 2) AS completed_booking_value
FROM per_room p
JOIN max_per_type m ON p.room_type = m.room_type AND p.completed_booking_value_unrounded = m.max_total
ORDER BY p.room_type ASC, p.room_number ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only analytical request over the provided schema (bookings, guests, payments, rooms). It asks to compute, per room_type, the rooms tied for the highest total booking value from stays that have checked_out, using booked_nightly_rate * nights (excluding checkout day), with zero for rooms without checked_out stays, and to rank by room_type then room_number. It is answerable using the existing tables without writes.

results.question: Which guests have at least two checked_out stays and an average stay length strictly above the average length across all checked_out bookings? Compute nights excluding checkout day, and compare the unrounded averages; the overall average is per booking, not per guest. Return guest_id, guest_name, and average_nights rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH
  overall AS (
    SELECT AVG(julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in)) AS avg_nights_all
    FROM bookings
    WHERE status = 'checked_out'
  ),
  guest_stats AS (
    SELECT
      g.guest_id,
      g.name AS guest_name,
      AVG(julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in)) AS avg_nights,
      COUNT(*) AS checked_out_count
    FROM guests g
    JOIN bookings b ON b.guest_id = g.guest_id
    WHERE b.status = 'checked_out'
    GROUP BY g.guest_id, g.name
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
  )

results.question: For every part classified as assembly, count its distinct direct component parts and sum their direct quantities per one assembly unit. Use zero for both values when the assembly has no components. Return part_id, name, component_count, component_quantity, ordered by part_id ascending.

results.question: For each part with at least one completed work order, show the total completed quantity and the number of distinct direct component parts in its bill of materials. results.question: For each completed work order, show the previous completed work order date for the same part and the integer calendar-day gap from it. results.sql:
WITH w AS (

results.question: Calculate the leaf-material requirements for building three Desk lamps (part_id 1). A leaf material is a descendant with no components of its own. Multiply quantities along each path, add quantities when a leaf appears along multiple paths, and price the resulting quantity at the leaf part's unit_cost. Return leaf_part_id, name, required_quantity, material_cost rounded to two decimal places, ordered by leaf_part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE
  path(leaf, qty, depth) AS (
    -- start from root's direct components (root_id = 1)
    SELECT b.component_part_id AS leaf,
           b.quantity AS qty,
           1 AS depth
    FROM bom b
    WHERE b.parent_part_id = 1

    UNION ALL
    -- extend paths with a depth guard to guarantee termination
    SELECT b.component_part_id AS leaf,
           p.qty * b.quantity AS qty,
           p.depth + 1 AS depth
    FROM path p
    JOIN bom b ON b.parent_part_id = p.leaf
    WHERE p.depth + 1 <= 1000
  )
SELECT
  path.leaf AS leaf_part_id,
  p_leaf.name,
  SUM(path.qty) AS required_quantity,
  ROUND(SUM(path.qty) * p_leaf.unit_cost, 2) AS material_cost
FROM path
JOIN parts p_leaf ON p_leaf.id = path.leaf
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bom b3 WHERE b3.parent_part_id = path.leaf)
GROUP BY path.leaf, p_leaf.name, p_leaf.unit_cost
ORDER BY path.leaf ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only question that asks to compute leaf materials for a BOM rooted at part_id 1, summing quantities along paths and pricing by leaf unit_cost. It can be answered from the schema (bom and parts) without altering data; no SQL generation is requested.
critique_issues: LIMIT 1000 is present in the final query but the user asked for complete results (no paging). Remove the LIMIT clause or make it a configurable parameter if paging is desired.

Root handling is hard-coded to 1 instead of parameterized :root_id. The original critique recommended parameterization to support other roots without rewriting the query. If you intend to keep parameterization, replace 1 with :root_id and ensure a binding value is supplied.

The recursive path includes a depth limit (p.depth + 1 <= 1000) to prevent infinite recursion. While acceptable, consider also explicitly guarding against cycles with a visited-set approach or a deterministic traversal strategy to avoid potential overcounting in cyclic BOM graphs. If you keep only depth, document the max_depth and consider an explicit cycle check.

Leaf detection uses NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bom b3 WHERE b3.parent_part_id = path.leaf). This is generally robust, but ensure there are no NULL parent_part_id values and that the schema enforces NOT NULL for parent_part_id to avoid edge cases. Since your schema defines NOT NULL, this is likely fine, but include a note about data integrity.
No explicit indexing guidance was included. For performance on large BOMs, add an index on bom(parent_part_id, component_part_id) to speed up the recursive joins and leaf checks.

results.question: For every ancestor part that has components, list all its direct and indirect descendant parts. For one unit of the ancestor, multiply quantities along each path and add the quantities across all paths to the same descendant. Exclude the ancestor itself. Return ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, required_quantity, ordered by ancestor_part_id and then descendant_part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE
  descendants(ancestor, descendant, qty, depth) AS (
    SELECT bom.parent_part_id, bom.component_part_id, bom.quantity, 1
    FROM bom
    UNION ALL
    SELECT d.ancestor, b.component_part_id, d.qty * b.quantity, d.depth + 1
    FROM descendants d
    JOIN bom b ON b.parent_part_id = d.descendant
  )
SELECT
  d.ancestor AS ancestor_part_id,
  d.descendant AS descendant_part_id,
  SUM(d.qty) AS required_quantity
FROM descendants d
WHERE d.ancestor != d.descendant
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bom b2 WHERE b2.parent_part_id = d.ancestor)
GROUP BY d.ancestor, d.descendant
ORDER BY d.ancestor, d.descendant
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks to compute, for every ancestor part that has components, all direct and indirect descendant parts, multiplying quantities along each path and summing across paths, excluding the ancestor itself. This is a recursive aggregation over the bom table (transitive closure) and can be answered using a read-only query against the provided schema. No SQL is provided here.

results.question: For every product, show total current on-hand units across warehouses and the net sum of all quantity changes recorded during January 2025. Compute the two totals independently, using zero when a product has no stock or no January movements. Return product_id, name, total_on_hand, january_net_change, ordered by product_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH stock_totals AS (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(on_hand) AS total_on_hand
  FROM stock
  GROUP BY product_id
), january_movements AS (
  -- ISO-8601 dates to guarantee correct string comparisons in SQLite
  SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity_change) AS january_net_change
  FROM movements
  WHERE movement_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-31'
  GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT
  p.id AS product_id,
  p.name,
  COALESCE(st.total_on_hand, 0) AS total_on_hand,
  COALESCE(jm.january_net_change, 0) AS january_net_change
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN stock_totals st ON p.id = st.product_id
LEFT JOIN january_movements jm ON p.id = jm.product_id
ORDER BY p.id ASC;

results.question: For every movement at warehouse 1, calculate the running net quantity change for that product, beginning at zero before its first recorded movement. Sequence each product's movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, running_net_change, ordered by product_id, movement_date, movement_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT
    id AS movement_id,
    product_id,
    movement_date,
    quantity_change,
    SUM(quantity_change) OVER (
      PARTITION BY product_id
      ORDER BY movement_date, id
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_net_change
  FROM movements
  WHERE warehouse_id = 1
)
SELECT movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, running_net_change
FROM ordered
ORDER BY product_id, movement_date, movement_id
LIMIT 1000;

results.question: Rank existing stock records within each warehouse by on_hand descending. Equal quantities share a rank and the next different quantity receives the next consecutive rank with no gaps. Return warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, stock_rank, ordered by warehouse_id, stock_rank, product_id ascending.

SELECT

results.question: For each movement whose reason is outbound, show the date of the immediately following recorded movement for the same warehouse and product, considering all reasons when finding that following movement. Sequence movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, next_movement_date, gap_days as an integer calendar-day difference; use NULL for the final two columns if there is no later movement. Order by movement_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT
    m.id AS movement_id,
    m.warehouse_id,
    m.product_id,
    m.movement_date,
    m.reason,
    LEAD(m.movement_date) OVER (
      PARTITION BY m.warehouse_id, m.product_id
      ORDER BY m.movement_date, m.id
    ) AS next_movement_date
  FROM movements m
)
SELECT
  movement_id,
  warehouse_id,
  product_id,
  movement_date,
  next_movement_date,
  CAST((julianday(next_movement_date) - julianday(movement_date)) AS INTEGER) AS gap_days
FROM t
WHERE reason = 'outbound'
ORDER BY movement_id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks, for each movement with reason='outbound', to find the immediately following movement for the same warehouse and product (based on movement_date then movement_id), and to return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, next_movement_date, and the gap in days. critique_issues: Unrequested LIMIT: The proposal adds LIMIT 100, which changes the result set size and violates the user's instruction to return all matching readings. Remove LIMIT or clarify intent.

Date/time parsing risk: The query uses datetime(reading_at) >= datetime('2025-01-02 00:00:00') AND datetime(reading_at) < datetime('2025-01-03 00:00:00'). This relies on reading_at being in a format datetime() can parse reliably. If reading_at is stored as ISO8601 with a 'Z' suffix (e.g., 2025-01-02T00:00:00Z) or in a different format, this may fail or yield incorrect results. Action: either compare against literal strings using the exact stored format (e.g., reading_at >= '2025-01-02T00:00:00Z' AND reading_at < '2025-01-03T00:00:00Z') or normalize using a canonical format (e.g., store in ISO-8601 UTC consistently) and use appropriate comparisons.

Boundary handling clarification: The exclusive upper bound excludes readings exactly at 2025-01-03 00:00:00 in the chosen format. If you want to include readings up to and including that boundary, adjust to <= with a suitable upper bound. Decide and document the intended inclusivity.

Indexing suggestion: For large tables, a performance issue is possible since the query filters on reading_at and reading_kwh. Recommend creating an index on readings(reading_at) (and potentially readings(reading_kwh)) to speed range scans.

NULL handling consistency: The query filters on reading_kwh IS NOT NULL and reading_at IS NOT NULL, which is appropriate for nonmissing energy readings. If there are additional NULL-sensitive columns in related queries, ensure consistent NULL filtering across queries to avoid unexpected omissions.

Column naming consistency: The query returns reading_id as id from readings. This matches the requested alias, but verify that the user expects reading_id to map to readings.id and meter_id to readings.meter_id. If the user expects the original column names, consider aliasing only as needed.

       MIN(r.reading_kwh) AS minimum_kwh,
       MAX(r.reading_kwh) AS maximum_kwh,
       ROUND(MAX(r.reading_kwh) - MIN(r.reading_kwh), 2) AS observed_range_kwh
FROM meters m
JOIN readings r ON r.meter_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id
HAVING COUNT(r.reading_kwh) >= 2
ORDER BY site_id ASC, meter_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question that can be answered using the provided schema. It asks for aggregations (min, max, range) on readings per meter (with at least two non-missing readings) joined to meters and sites, and requires rounding and ordering. No write operations are involved.

results.question: For each nonmissing reading with a matching regional tariff, show the tariff effective on that reading's UTC calendar date. The valid_from date is inclusive, valid_to is exclusive, and NULL valid_to has no upper limit. Return reading_id, meter_id, reading_date formatted YYYY-MM-DD, price_per_kwh, ordered by reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH active AS (
  SELECT r.id AS reading_id,
         r.meter_id,
         strftime('%Y-%m-%d', r.reading_at, 'utc') AS reading_date,
         t.price_per_kwh,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY r.id
           ORDER BY date(t.valid_from) DESC, t.id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM readings r
  JOIN meters m ON r.meter_id = m.id
  JOIN sites s ON m.site_id = s.id
  JOIN tariffs t ON t.region = s.region
  WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
    AND date(r.reading_at, 'utc') >= date(t.valid_from)
    AND (t.valid_to IS NULL OR date(r.reading_at, 'utc') < date(t.valid_to))
)
SELECT reading_id,
       meter_id,
       reading_date,
       price_per_kwh
FROM active
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY reading_id ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question. It requires joining readings to meters to sites to tariffs, filtering nonmissing reading_kwh, and selecting the tariff where reading_at (interpreted as UTC date) falls within [valid_from, valid_to) for the matching regional tariff (with NULL valid_to meaning no upper bound). It returns reading_id, meter_id, reading_date (YYYY-MM-DD), and price_per_kwh, ordered by reading_id ascending. No write or schema changes needed.
critique_issues: Unnecessary LIMIT: The proposal adds LIMIT 1000, which truncates results and violates the requirement to return all readings with a matching tariff. Remove LIMIT 1000 to produce the full result set.

Inconsistent UTC handling for validity bounds: The query compares date(r.reading_at, 'utc') to date(t.valid_from) without applying 'utc' to valid_from. To ensure correct UTC-based comparison, use date(t.valid_from, 'utc') (and similarly date(t.valid_to, 'utc') if used) to align time zones across both sides.

Deterministic tie-breaker already addressed in ROW_NUMBER, but ensure the added tie-breaker is explicit: include a secondary order by t.id DESC (as currently done) to resolve identical valid_from values; this is correct, but confirm in final code.

Assuming tariffs are region-wide is fine if that is true; if tariffs can vary by additional attributes (e.g., site or meter), ensure the join condition (t.region = s.region) correctly reflects the intended scope for tariff applicability.

results.question: Within each meter, sequence nonmissing readings by reading_at and then reading_id ascending and form intervals between consecutive nonmissing readings. Omit the first reading. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, elapsed_hours rounded to two decimals, consumed_kwh as current minus previous reading rounded to two decimals, average_kw as consumed_kwh divided by elapsed hours rounded to three decimals. Use NULL average_kw for zero elapsed hours. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH nonnull AS (
  SELECT id AS reading_id, meter_id, reading_at, reading_kwh
  FROM readings
  WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
), with_prev AS (
  SELECT
    meter_id,
    reading_id,
    reading_at,
    reading_kwh AS current_kwh,
    LAG(reading_kwh) OVER (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY reading_at, reading_id) AS prev_kwh,
    LAG(reading_at) OVER (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY reading_at, reading_id) AS prev_at
  FROM nonnull
)
SELECT
  meter_id,
  reading_id,
  reading_at,
  ROUND((julianday(reading_at) - julianday(prev_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS elapsed_hours,
  ROUND((current_kwh - prev_kwh), 2) AS consumed_kwh,
  CASE
    WHEN (ROUND((julianday(reading_at) - julianday(prev_at)) * 24.0, 2)) > 0 THEN
      ROUND((current_kwh - prev_kwh) / ROUND((julianday(reading_at) - julianday(prev_at)) * 24.0, 2), 3)
    ELSE NULL
  END AS average_kw
FROM with_prev
WHERE prev_at IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id
results.classification_explanation: The request describes a read-only data operation over the provided schema: for each meter, sequence nonmissing readings by reading_at and reading_id, form intervals between consecutive readings, omit the first, and return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, elapsed_hours (rounded to 2 decimals), consumed_kwh (current minus previous, rounded to 2 decimals), and average_kw (consumed_kwh divided by elapsed_hours, rounded to 3 decimals, with NULL if elapsed_hours is 0). It specifies ordering and calculations but does not ask for data modification. This is answerable as a read-only query over the readings (and related) tables.

results.question: For each meter, derive consumed kWh between consecutive nonmissing readings, sequencing by reading_at and then reading_id ascending. Omit the first reading because it has no preceding interval. For every remaining interval, calculate the arithmetic mean of its consumption and up to two preceding interval consumptions for that meter; divide by the number of available intervals, without time weighting. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, consumed_kwh, trailing_mean_kwh, with both kWh outputs rounded to two decimals. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH nonnull AS (
  SELECT
    m.id AS meter_id,
    r.id AS reading_id,
    r.reading_at,
    r.reading_kwh,
    LAG(r.reading_kwh) OVER (PARTITION BY m.id ORDER BY r.reading_at, r.id) AS prev_kwh
  FROM meters m
  JOIN readings r ON r.meter_id = m.id
  WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
),
intervals AS (
  SELECT
    meter_id,
    reading_id,
    reading_at,
    (reading_kwh - prev_kwh) AS consumed_kwh
  FROM nonnull
  WHERE prev_kwh IS NOT NULL
),
final AS (
  SELECT
    i.meter_id,
    i.reading_id,
    i.reading_at,
    ROUND(i.consumed_kwh, 2) AS consumed_kwh,
    ROUND(AVG(i.consumed_kwh) OVER (
      PARTITION BY i.meter_id
      ORDER BY i.reading_at, i.reading_id
      ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ), 2) AS trailing_mean_kwh
  FROM intervals i
)
SELECT
  meter_id,
  reading_id,
  reading_at,
  consumed_kwh,
  trailing_mean_kwh
FROM final
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question requesting a computed result over the readings and meters tables (no writes or schema changes). It describes deriving consumed kWh between consecutive non-missing readings, calculating trailing means, and returning specific columns in a defined order. No unsupported operations required; just a data query.

results.question: Rank meters having at least two nonmissing readings by observed consumption, defined as maximum minus minimum reading, in descending order. Equal unrounded consumption values share a rank, and the next rank skips the number of tied positions. Return meter_id, label, observed_consumption_kwh rounded to two decimals, consumption_rank, ordered by consumption_rank and then meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH meter_consumption AS (
  SELECT m.id AS meter_id,
         m.label,
         (MAX(r.reading_kwh) - MIN(r.reading_kwh)) AS consumption,
         COUNT(r.reading_kwh) AS n_readings
  FROM meters m
  JOIN readings r ON r.meter_id = m.id
  WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY m.id, m.label
  HAVING COUNT(r.reading_kwh) >= 2
)
SELECT meter_id,
       label,
       ROUND(consumption, 2) AS observed_consumption_kwh,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY consumption DESC) AS consumption_rank
FROM meter_consumption
ORDER BY consumption_rank, meter_id
LIMIT 200;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question that can be answered using the provided schema (meters, readings). It asks to compute, per meter, the observed consumption as max(reading_kwh) - min(reading_kwh) over non-missing readings, only for meters with at least two readings, then assign ranks with ties sharing a rank and skipping subsequent ranks (standard competition ranking), and return meter_id, label, the rounded consumption, and the rank in the specified order. No SQL execution is needed here, just classification as answerable.

results.question: List active routes. Return route_id, name, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS route_id, name FROM routes WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks to list active routes from the routes table, returning route_id (id), name, and ordering by route_id ascending (no writes or schema changes required).

results.question: List stops in the Central zone. Return stop_id, name, ordered by stop_id ascending.

results.question: Count trips in each status occurring from service date 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-03, both dates inclusive. Return status, trip_count, ordered by status alphabetically.
results.sql:

results.question: For every route, report its number of listed stop positions and highest stop sequence. A route with no listed stops has stop_count zero and last_stop_sequence NULL. Return route_id, name, stop_count, last_stop_sequence, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS route_id, r.name, COUNT(rs.stop_id) AS stop_count, MAX(rs.stop_sequence) AS last_stop_sequence
FROM routes AS r
LEFT JOIN route_stops AS rs ON rs.route_id = r.id
GROUP BY r.id
ORDER BY r.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a valid read-only database question. It asks for per-route statistics using the existing tables routes and route_stops: stop_count as the number of listed stop positions per route and last_stop_sequence as the maximum stop_sequence (or NULL if there are no stops). The schema supports these expressions via an aggregate over route_stops and a left join from routes, returning route_id, name, stop_count, and last_stop_sequence ordered by route_id.

results.question: For each completed trip with an actual departure recorded, calculate departure delay in minutes as actual departure minus scheduled departure, allowing negative values for early departures. Return trip_id, route_name, delay_minutes rounded to two decimals, ordered by trip_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  t.id AS trip_id,
  r.name AS route_name,
  ROUND((julianday(t.actual_departure) - julianday(t.scheduled_departure)) * 1440.0, 2) AS delay_minutes
FROM trips t
JOIN routes r ON t.route_id = r.id
WHERE t.status = 'completed' AND t.actual_departure IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY t.id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only SQL query over the provided schema. It selects completed trips with an actual_departure, joins trips to routes to get route_name, computes delay_minutes as (actual_departure - scheduled_departure) in minutes (allowing negatives), rounds to two decimals, and orders by trip_id ascending.

results.question: For every route, report its number of completed trips and number of listed stop positions, counting each trip and each position once. Use zero for missing counts. Return route_id, name, completed_trip_count, stop_count, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS route_id,
       r.name,
       COALESCE(ct.completed_trip_count, 0) AS completed_trip_count,
       COALESCE(rs.stop_count, 0) AS stop_count
FROM routes r
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS completed_trip_count
    FROM trips
    WHERE lower(status) = 'completed'
    GROUP BY route_id
) ct ON ct.route_id = r.id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS stop_count
    FROM route_stops
    GROUP BY route_id
) rs ON rs.route_id = r.id
ORDER BY r.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is a valid read-only database request. It asks to aggregate data from routes, trips, and related route_stops to report, for every route, the count of completed trips and the count of listed stop positions (with missing counts treated as zero), returning route_id, name, completed_trip_count, stop_count, ordered by route_id ascending. No write or schema changes needed.

results.question: Show every pair of adjacent stop positions on the same route, where the destination sequence is exactly one greater than the origin sequence. Return route_id, origin_sequence, origin_stop, destination_stop, segment_minutes using the destination position's travel_minutes_from_previous. Order by route_id and then origin_sequence ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT a.route_id,
       a.stop_sequence AS origin_sequence,
       origin_stop.name AS origin_stop,
       destination_stop.name AS destination_stop,
       b.travel_minutes_from_previous AS segment_minutes
FROM route_stops a
JOIN route_stops b ON b.route_id = a.route_id AND b.stop_sequence = a.stop_sequence + 1
JOIN stops origin_stop ON origin_stop.id = a.stop_id
JOIN stops destination_stop ON destination_stop.id = b.stop_id
ORDER BY a.route_id, a.stop_sequence
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: Valid read-only database question. It asks for a data retrieval over the provided schema (route_stops, stops, routes) to identify adjacent stop pairs on the same route with consecutive stop_sequence, returning specified fields. No writes or unsupported tables are required.

results.question: For every listed route stop, calculate planned elapsed travel minutes from the first stop through that position, treating a missing segment time as zero. Return route_id, stop_sequence, stop_name, elapsed_minutes, ordered by route_id and then stop_sequence ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT rs.route_id,
       rs.stop_sequence,
       s.name AS stop_name,
       SUM(COALESCE(rs.travel_minutes_from_previous, 0)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY rs.route_id
           ORDER BY rs.stop_sequence
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS elapsed_minutes
FROM route_stops AS rs
JOIN stops AS s ON rs.stop_id = s.id
ORDER BY rs.route_id, rs.stop_sequence;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks to compute a cumulative elapsed_minutes per route_stop by summing travel_minutes_from_previous (treat NULL as zero) across stops for each route, returning route_id, stop_sequence, stop_name, and elapsed_minutes ordered by route_id then stop_sequence. It uses only existing tables (route_stops and stops) and requires no data modification.

results.question: For every route with a completed trip, return exactly its latest completed trip, choosing by service_date descending, then scheduled_departure descending, then trip_id descending. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.route_id, t.id AS trip_id, t.service_date, t.actual_departure,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY t.route_id ORDER BY t.service_date DESC, t.scheduled_departure DESC, t.id DESC) AS rn
  FROM trips t
  WHERE t.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY route_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks for, per route that has a completed trip, the latest completed trip by service_date (then scheduled_departure, then trip_id) and to return route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure ordered by route_id. It uses the trips table (status = completed), joined by route_id via routes, and does not require writing data.

results.question: Within each route, divide completed trips in chronological order into two batches of sizes differing by at most one. Order trips by service_date, scheduled_departure, and trip_id ascending; batch 1 contains the earlier trips and gets the extra trip when the count is odd. A route with one completed trip uses only batch 1. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, batch_number, ordered by route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    t.route_id,
    t.id AS trip_id,
    t.service_date,
    t.scheduled_departure,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY t.route_id
      ORDER BY t.service_date, t.scheduled_departure, t.id
    ) AS rn,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY t.route_id) AS cnt
  FROM trips t
  WHERE t.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT
  route_id,
  trip_id,
  service_date,
  CASE WHEN rn <= ((cnt + 1) / 2) THEN 1 ELSE 2 END AS batch_number
FROM ranked
ORDER BY route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request. You want to partition completed trips per route into two batches (sizes differ by at most one) based on ordering by service_date, scheduled_departure, and trip_id. The result should include route_id, trip_id, service_date, and batch_number, ordered by route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id. To implement without changing data, compute per-route total trips and a per-row rank, then assign batch_number as 1 when the row's rank is within the first half (ceil(total/2)) and 2 otherwise; routes with a single trip use batch 1. This uses only read operations against the provided schema (routes, trips), and does not require any writes.

results.question: For every visitor, count their sessions, including visitors with no sessions as zero. Return visitor_id, country, session_count, ordered by visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT v.id AS visitor_id, v.country, COUNT(s.id) AS session_count

results.question: For each session referrer, using direct for NULL, report the number of sessions, the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event, and total purchase-event revenue. Count each session once even when it contains multiple events, retain sessions without events, and use zero revenue when there are no purchases. Return referrer, session_count, converting_session_count, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, ordered by referrer alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT
  CASE WHEN s.referrer IS NULL THEN 'direct' ELSE s.referrer END AS referrer,
  COUNT(DISTINCT s.id) AS session_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'purchase' THEN s.id END) AS converting_session_count,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'purchase' THEN e.revenue ELSE 0 END), 2) AS purchase_revenue
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.id
GROUP BY CASE WHEN s.referrer IS NULL THEN 'direct' ELSE s.referrer END
ORDER BY referrer ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: Valid read-only database question. It asks for an aggregated report per session referrer (including NULL) across sessions and purchase events, requiring left join from sessions to events, counting distinct sessions, counting sessions with at least one purchase, and summing purchase revenue. This is a straightforward read-only query over the provided schema.

results.question: For every session, count its events and calculate the span in whole seconds from its earliest to latest event. Return NULL span for a session with no events and zero for one event. Return session_id, event_count, event_span_seconds, ordered by session_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id AS session_id,
       COUNT(e.id) AS event_count,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(e.id) = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE (unixepoch(MAX(e.event_at)) - unixepoch(MIN(e.event_at))) END AS event_span_seconds
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id
ORDER BY s.id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request. It asks to compute, for each session, the number of events and the time span (earliest to latest event) in seconds, with NULL span if there are no events and 0 span if there is exactly one event. It uses only the provided schema. No write or schema changes are requested.

results.question: For each visitor country with at least one session, calculate its session conversion rate: 100 times the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event divided by all sessions from that country. A session with multiple purchase events counts once. Return country, session_count, converting_session_count, conversion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by country alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT country, session_count, converting_session_count, ROUND(100.0 * converting_session_count / session_count, 2) AS conversion_percent
FROM (
  SELECT v.country,
         COUNT(*) AS session_count,
         SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM events e WHERE e.session_id = s.id AND e.event_type = 'purchase') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converting_session_count
  FROM visitors v
  JOIN sessions s ON v.id = s.visitor_id
  GROUP BY v.country
) AS t
ORDER BY country
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only analytical query over the provided schema. It asks to compute, per visitor country, the number of sessions and the number of sessions with at least one purchase event (counted once per session), then the conversion percentage. It involves joins across visitors, sessions, and events and requires aggregation, ordering, and rounding, all within a read-only context.

results.question: For every session, show the previous session start for the same visitor and the elapsed hours since it. Sequence each visitor's sessions by started_at and then session_id ascending, including ties in start time. The first session has NULL for the previous start and gap. Return visitor_id, session_id, started_at, previous_started_at, gap_hours rounded to two decimals, ordered by visitor_id, started_at, session_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT
    s.visitor_id,
    s.id AS session_id,
    s.started_at,
    LAG(s.started_at) OVER (
      PARTITION BY s.visitor_id
      ORDER BY s.started_at, s.id
    ) AS previous_started_at
  FROM sessions AS s
)
SELECT
  visitor_id,
  session_id,
  started_at,
  previous_started_at,
  ROUND((julianday(started_at) - julianday(previous_started_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS gap_hours
FROM t
ORDER BY visitor_id, started_at, session_id
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks for per-session data (previous session start and hours since) using the sessions table (and visitor/session ordering). No writes or admin operations are required. It would be implemented with window functions (lag) and a time difference, returning NULL for the first session per visitor.

results.question: For each UTC calendar day from 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-04 inclusive, show purchase-event revenue, cumulative revenue since 2025-01-01, and the arithmetic mean of that day's and the preceding calendar day's revenue within this reporting period. Include days without purchases as zero; the first day's mean uses only that day. Return day formatted YYYY-MM-DD, purchase_revenue, cumulative_revenue, two_day_mean_revenue, with all revenue values rounded to two decimals, ordered by day ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT date('2025-01-01')
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day')
  FROM days
  WHERE day < '2025-01-04'
), daily AS (
  SELECT d.day as day,
         IFNULL(sum(e.revenue),0) as purchase_revenue
  FROM days d
  LEFT JOIN events e
    ON date(e.event_at) = d.day AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY d.day
), ordered AS (
  SELECT day,
         purchase_revenue,
         SUM(purchase_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as cumulative_revenue
  FROM daily
), with_lag AS (
  SELECT day,
         purchase_revenue,
         cumulative_revenue,
         LAG(purchase_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) as prev_revenue
  FROM ordered
)
SELECT
  day as day,
  ROUND(purchase_revenue,2) as purchase_revenue,
  ROUND(cumulative_revenue,2) as cumulative_revenue,
  CASE WHEN prev_revenue IS NULL THEN ROUND(purchase_revenue,2) ELSE ROUND((purchase_revenue + prev_revenue)/2.0,2) END as two_day_mean_revenue
FROM with_lag
ORDER BY day
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only request to compute per-day purchase revenue, cumulative revenue from 2025-01-01, and a two-day mean for 2025-01-01 to 2025-01-04 using the provided schema. It does not involve data modification and can be answered with a read-only query.

results.question: For every visitor, total their purchase-event revenue, using zero for visitors without purchases or sessions. Rank visitors by unrounded revenue ascending with equal revenues sharing the first position occupied by that tie group, and calculate percentile_fraction as (rank minus one) divided by (number of visitors minus one); use zero if there is only one visitor. Return visitor_id, country, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, percentile_fraction rounded to four decimals, ordered by unrounded purchase revenue and then visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH per_visitor AS (
  SELECT v.id AS visitor_id,
         v.country,
         COALESCE(SUM(e.revenue), 0.0) AS purchase_revenue_raw
  FROM visitors v
  LEFT JOIN sessions s ON s.visitor_id = v.id
  LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.id AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY v.id, v.country
), ranked AS (
  SELECT pv.visitor_id,
         pv.country,
         pv.purchase_revenue_raw,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY pv.purchase_revenue_raw ASC) AS ranking,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS total_visitors
  FROM per_visitor pv
)
SELECT visitor_id,
       country,
       ROUND(purchase_revenue_raw, 2) AS purchase_revenue,
       ROUND(CASE WHEN total_visitors = 1 THEN 0.0 ELSE (ranking - 1.0) / (total_visitors - 1.0) END, 4) AS percentile_fraction
FROM ranked
ORDER BY purchase_revenue_raw ASC, visitor_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The request asks for a read-only aggregation over the provided schema to compute per-visitor purchase revenue from the events table (with zero for non-purchasers), rank by revenue with ties, compute percentile_fraction, and return specific fields. This is a permissible database question that does not require data modification.

results.question: Find unordered pairs of bidders who have both bid on at least two distinct open listings. Return smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id, and shared_listing_count, ordered by those two IDs. Multiple bids by one bidder on one listing count only once.
results.sql:
WITH bidder_listings AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT b.bidder_id, b.listing_id
  FROM bids b
  JOIN listings l ON b.listing_id = l.id
  WHERE l.status = 'open'
),
eligible AS (
  SELECT bidder_id, COUNT(DISTINCT listing_id) AS cnt
  FROM bidder_listings
  GROUP BY bidder_id
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT listing_id) >= 2
),
pairs AS (
  SELECT a.bidder_id AS bidder_min, b.bidder_id AS bidder_max, COUNT(DISTINCT a.listing_id) AS shared_count
  FROM bidder_listings a
  JOIN bidder_listings b ON a.listing_id = b.listing_id AND a.bidder_id < b.bidder_id
  JOIN eligible ea ON a.bidder_id = ea.bidder_id
  JOIN eligible eb ON b.bidder_id = eb.bidder_id
  GROUP BY a.bidder_id, b.bidder_id
)
SELECT bidder_min AS smaller_bidder_id, bidder_max AS larger_bidder_id, shared_count AS shared_listing_count
FROM pairs
ORDER BY smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only question. It asks to identify unordered bidder pairs who have bid on at least two distinct open listings, counting each listing once per pair. We would look at bids joined to listings where listings.status = 'open', consider distinct (listing_id) per bidder, find pairs of bidder_ids that share listing_ids, and emit (min(bidder1,bidder2), max(bidder1,bidder2), count_of_shared_open_listings) for pairs with count >= 2, ordered by the two bidder IDs.

results.question: Find unordered participant pairs with exactly the same set of mandatory questions answered with non-NULL scores. Require that each participant answered at least one mandatory question. Return smaller_participant_id and larger_participant_id, ordered by both IDs.
results.sql:
WITH per_participant AS (
  SELECT p.id AS participant_id,
         (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(qid, ',')
          FROM (
            SELECT r.question_id AS qid
            FROM responses r
            JOIN questions q ON r.question_id = q.id
            WHERE r.participant_id = p.id AND q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
            ORDER BY r.question_id
          ) AS sub
         ) AS qset
  FROM participants p
  WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM responses r
    JOIN questions q ON r.question_id = q.id
    WHERE r.participant_id = p.id AND q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
  )
)
SELECT a.participant_id AS smaller_participant_id,
       b.participant_id AS larger_participant_id
FROM per_participant a
JOIN per_participant b ON a.qset = b.qset
WHERE a.participant_id < b.participant_id
ORDER BY smaller_participant_id, larger_participant_id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request. It asks to identify pairs of participants who have answered exactly the same set of mandatory questions with non-NULL scores, ensuring each participant answered at least one mandatory question, and to return the pair as smaller_id and larger_id. It involves only reading data from the provided tables (participants, questions, responses) and does not require data modification.

results.question: For each registered participant group, compute the percentage of mandatory question-participant combinations that have a non-NULL score. The denominator is all registered participants in the group times the total number of mandatory questions; skips and missing responses are incomplete. Return group_name (Unassigned for NULL) and completion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by group_name. Use NULL if there are no mandatory questions.
results.sql:
WITH mandatory AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM questions WHERE required = 1
),
groups AS (
  SELECT COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name, COUNT(*) AS participant_count
  FROM participants p
  GROUP BY COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned')
),
numerator AS (
  SELECT COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name,
         COUNT(DISTINCT (r.participant_id || ':' || r.question_id)) AS numerator
  FROM responses r
  JOIN questions q ON r.question_id = q.id
  JOIN participants p ON r.participant_id = p.id
  WHERE q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned')
)
SELECT g.group_name,
       CASE WHEN m.cnt = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE ROUND((COALESCE(n.numerator, 0) * 1.0) / (g.participant_count * m.cnt), 2)
       END AS completion_percent
FROM groups g
CROSS JOIN mandatory m
LEFT JOIN numerator n ON n.group_name = g.group_name
ORDER BY g.group_name
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question asking to compute completion percentages per participant group based on the given schema. It requests deriving a percentage from mandatory questions and non-NULL scores, with special handling for NULL group_name (display as Unassigned) and a NULL result when there are no mandatory questions. No data modification or unsupported operations are involved.

results.question: Compute league points for every team from completed matches: 3 per win, 1 per draw, 0 per loss. Return team_id, name, and points, including 0 for teams without completed matches. Order by points descending, then team_id.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name, COALESCE(SUM(
  CASE
    WHEN m.status = 'completed' AND m.home_team_id = t.id THEN
      CASE WHEN m.home_score > m.away_score THEN 3 WHEN m.home_score = m.away_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
    WHEN m.status = 'completed' AND m.away_team_id = t.id THEN
      CASE WHEN m.away_score > m.home_score THEN 3 WHEN m.away_score = m.home_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
    ELSE 0
  END
), 0) AS points
FROM teams t
LEFT JOIN matches m ON m.status = 'completed' AND (m.home_team_id = t.id OR m.away_team_id = t.id)
GROUP BY t.id, t.name
ORDER BY points DESC, t.id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question. It asks to compute league points for every team from completed matches (status = 'completed'), awarding 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, and 0 for a loss, including teams with zero points. results.question: For each team that has won a completed match, identify the strongest opponent it defeated. Strength is that opponent's total league points from all completed matches (3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss). Choose the lowest opponent ID if points tie. Return team_id, opponent_id, and opponent_points, ordered by team_id. Count an opponent once even if defeated repeatedly.
results.sql:
with completed as (
  select id, home_team_id, away_team_id, home_score, away_score
  from matches
  where status = 'completed'
),
points_per_team as (
  -- points earned by each team in each completed match
  select home_team_id as team_id, away_team_id as opponent_id,
         case when home_score>away_score then 3 when home_score=away_score then 1 else 0 end as points
  from completed
  union all
  select away_team_id as team_id, home_team_id as opponent_id,
         case when away_score>home_score then 3 when away_score=home_score then 1 else 0 end as points
  from completed
),
total_points_per_opponent as (
  -- total league points for each opponent_id across all completed matches
  select team_id as opponent_id, sum(points) as opponent_total_points
  from points_per_team
  group by team_id
),
defeated as (
  -- all team/opponent pairs where a winner defeated the opponent (non-draw)
  select distinct
         case when home_score>away_score then home_team_id else away_team_id end as team_id,
         case when home_score>away_score then away_team_id else home_team_id end as opponent_id
  from completed
  where home_score <> away_score
),
defeated_with_points as (

  from defeated d

results.question: For every run, return run_id and target_coverage_percent, in that order, sorted by run_id. Coverage is 100 times the number of distinct target metrics with at least one non-NULL reading for that run divided by the number of defined metrics with non-NULL targets. Include all statuses and runs without readings, use zero coverage when no target is measured, return NULL if there are no target metrics, and round percentages to two decimals.
results.sql:
WITH target_metrics AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM metrics WHERE target IS NOT NULL
), per_run AS (
  SELECT r.id AS run_id,
         COUNT(DISTINCT mm.metric) AS covered
  FROM runs r
  LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT m.run_id, m.metric
    FROM measurements m
    JOIN metrics met ON met.name = m.metric AND met.target IS NOT NULL
    WHERE m.value IS NOT NULL
  ) mm ON mm.run_id = r.id
  GROUP BY r.id
)
SELECT pr.run_id,
       CASE WHEN tm.total = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(pr.covered, 0) / tm.total, 2)
       END AS target_coverage_percent
FROM per_run pr
CROSS JOIN target_metrics tm
ORDER BY pr.run_id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database request. It asks to compute, for every run, a coverage percentage based on target metrics with non-null readings, and to include runs with no readings, with specific rounding and NULL behavior. It does not request any data modification. The query involves runs, measurements, and metrics as defined in the schema.

        FROM measurements m

results.question: Compare treatment and control yield for each experiment using completed runs only. First average non-NULL yield readings within each run, then average those run means within each variant so runs have equal weight. Ignore runs with no known yield and include only experiments with a known mean for both variants. Return experiment_id, control_mean, treatment_mean, and percent_change, in that order. Percent change is 100 times (treatment minus control) divided by control; return NULL when control is zero. Round all three calculated values to two decimals and sort by experiment_id.
results.sql:
WITH per_run AS (
  SELECT
    r.experiment_id,
    r.variant,
    AVG(m.value) AS run_mean
  FROM runs r
  JOIN measurements m ON m.run_id = r.id
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND m.metric = 'yield'
    AND m.value IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY r.id
), per_exp AS (
  SELECT
    e.id AS experiment_id,
    AVG(CASE WHEN pr.variant = 'control' THEN pr.run_mean END) AS control_mean,
    AVG(CASE WHEN pr.variant = 'treatment' THEN pr.run_mean END) AS treatment_mean
  FROM per_run pr
  JOIN experiments e ON e.id = pr.experiment_id
  GROUP BY e.id
  HAVING AVG(CASE WHEN pr.variant = 'control' THEN pr.run_mean END) IS NOT NULL
     AND AVG(CASE WHEN pr.variant = 'treatment' THEN pr.run_mean END) IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  experiment_id,
  ROUND(control_mean, 2) AS control_mean,
  ROUND(treatment_mean, 2) AS treatment_mean,
  CASE WHEN control_mean = 0 THEN NULL
       ELSE ROUND(100.0 * (treatment_mean - control_mean) / control_mean, 2)
  END AS percent_change
FROM per_exp
ORDER BY experiment_id
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database query request. It asks to compare yield between treatment and control by computing, for each experiment, the mean yield per run (ignoring NULLs) for completed runs, then averaging those run means per variant (treat vs control) to give equal weight to runs. It only includes experiments where both variants have a known mean, returns experiment_id, control_mean, treatment_mean, and percent_change (NULL if control is 0), with all values rounded to two decimals, and sorted by experiment_id.

results.question: For each metric with a non-NULL target, find the completed runs whose mean non-NULL reading is closest to that target. Average repeated readings within a run, omit runs without a known reading, compare absolute distances before rounding, and keep all tied runs. Return metric, run_id, mean_value, and distance, in that order. Round mean_value and distance to two decimals and sort by metric ascending, then run_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH per_run AS (
  SELECT m.name AS metric,
         r.id AS run_id,
         AVG(me.value) AS mean_value,
         m.target AS target,
         ABS(AVG(me.value) - m.target) AS distance_raw
  FROM measurements me
  JOIN runs r ON r.id = me.run_id
  JOIN metrics m ON m.name = me.metric
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND m.target IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY m.name, r.id, m.target
  HAVING AVG(me.value) IS NOT NULL
), min_dist AS (
  SELECT metric, MIN(distance_raw) AS min_distance
  FROM per_run
  GROUP BY metric
)
SELECT pr.metric,
       pr.run_id,
       ROUND(pr.mean_value, 2) AS mean_value,
       ROUND(pr.distance_raw, 2) AS distance
FROM per_run pr
JOIN min_dist md ON pr.metric = md.metric AND pr.distance_raw = md.min_distance
ORDER BY pr.metric ASC, pr.run_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is a read-only database question that can be answered from the provided schema. It asks to compute, for each metric with a non-NULL target, the completed runs whose mean (non-NULL) readings for that metric are closest to the target, including ties, and to return metric, run_id, mean_value, and distance with rounding and sorting. It requires aggregations over measurements grouped by run_id and metric, filtering by completed runs and non-NULL readings, and joining to metrics to access the target. No writes or schema changes are requested.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, name, known_cost, and unpriced_hours, in that order. Include all task statuses and dates. SELECT

  p.name,
  COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NOT NULL THEN te.hours * te.billed_rate ELSE 0 END), 2), 0) AS known_cost,
  COALESCE(ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NULL THEN te.hours ELSE 0 END), 2), 0) AS unpriced_hours,

LEFT JOIN tasks t ON t.project_id = p.id

ORDER BY p.id ASC;

results.question: List every direct or indirect prerequisite of task 5. Follow dependency edges recursively, return each prerequisite only once even if reachable through multiple paths, and exclude task 5 itself. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending; include prerequisites of any status.
