      WHEN mt.target IS NOT NULL AND ms.value IS NOT NULL THEN ms.metric
    END) AS measured_targets
  FROM runs AS r
  LEFT JOIN measurements AS ms
    ON ms.run_id = r.id
  LEFT JOIN metrics AS mt
    ON mt.name = ms.metric
  GROUP BY r.id
)
SELECT
  mbr.run_id,
  CASE
    WHEN tmc.total_targets = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND(100.0 * mbr.measured_targets / tmc.total_targets, 2)
  END AS target_coverage_percent
FROM measured_targets_by_run AS mbr
CROSS JOIN target_metric_count AS tmc
ORDER BY mbr.run_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available runs, measurements, and metrics tables, requiring aggregation, handling NULLs, and sorting.

results.question: Find completed runs that have at least one non-NULL reading for every defined metric whose target is non-NULL. If there are no target metrics, all completed runs qualify. Return run_id and experiment_id, in that order, sorted by run_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS run_id, r.experiment_id
FROM runs AS r
WHERE r.status = 'completed'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM metrics AS mt
    WHERE mt.target IS NOT NULL
      AND NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM measurements AS m
        WHERE m.run_id = r.id
          AND m.metric = mt.name
          AND m.value IS NOT NULL
      )
  )
ORDER BY r.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available runs, measurements, and metrics tables, including filtering completed runs and checking non-NULL readings for metrics with non-NULL targets.

results.question: Compare treatment and control yield for each experiment using completed runs only. First average non-NULL yield readings within each run, then average those run means within each variant so runs have equal weight. Ignore runs with no known yield and include only experiments with a known mean for both variants. Return experiment_id, control_mean, treatment_mean, and percent_change, in that order. Percent change is 100 times (treatment minus control) divided by control; return NULL when control is zero. Round all three calculated values to two decimals and sort by experiment_id.
results.sql:
WITH run_yield_means AS (
  SELECT
    r.id AS run_id,
    r.experiment_id,
    r.variant,
    AVG(m.value) AS run_yield_mean
  FROM runs AS r
  JOIN measurements AS m
    ON m.run_id = r.id
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND m.metric = 'yield'
    AND m.value IS NOT NULL
    AND r.variant IN ('control', 'treatment')
  GROUP BY r.id, r.experiment_id, r.variant
), variant_means AS (
  SELECT
    experiment_id,
    variant,
    AVG(run_yield_mean) AS variant_mean
  FROM run_yield_means
  GROUP BY experiment_id, variant
), pivoted AS (
  SELECT
    experiment_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN variant = 'control' THEN variant_mean END) AS control_mean,
    MAX(CASE WHEN variant = 'treatment' THEN variant_mean END) AS treatment_mean
  FROM variant_means
  GROUP BY experiment_id
)
SELECT
  experiment_id,
  ROUND(control_mean, 2) AS control_mean,
  ROUND(treatment_mean, 2) AS treatment_mean,
  CASE
    WHEN control_mean = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND(100.0 * (treatment_mean - control_mean) / control_mean, 2)
  END AS percent_change
FROM pivoted
WHERE control_mean IS NOT NULL
  AND treatment_mean IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY experiment_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available experiments, runs, and measurements tables, with filtering, aggregation, joins, calculations, rounding, and sorting over existing columns.

results.question: For each metric with a non-NULL target, find the completed runs whose mean non-NULL reading is closest to that target. Average repeated readings within a run, omit runs without a known reading, compare absolute distances before rounding, and keep all tied runs. Return metric, run_id, mean_value, and distance, in that order. Round mean_value and distance to two decimals and sort by metric ascending, then run_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH run_metric_means AS (
  SELECT
    m.metric,
    m.run_id,
    AVG(m.value) AS mean_value,
    mt.target,
    ABS(AVG(m.value) - mt.target) AS distance
  FROM measurements AS m
  JOIN runs AS r
    ON r.id = m.run_id
  JOIN metrics AS mt
    ON mt.name = m.metric
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND mt.target IS NOT NULL
    AND m.value IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY m.metric, m.run_id, mt.target
), closest AS (
  SELECT
    metric,
    run_id,
    mean_value,
    distance,
    MIN(distance) OVER (PARTITION BY metric) AS min_distance
  FROM run_metric_means
)
SELECT
  metric,
  run_id,
  ROUND(mean_value, 2) AS mean_value,
  ROUND(distance, 2) AS distance
FROM closest
WHERE distance = min_distance
ORDER BY metric ASC, run_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available experiments, runs, measurements, and metrics tables, with aggregation, filtering, tie handling, rounding, and sorting over existing columns.

results.question: List tasks with no assignee, including every status. Return task_id, project_id, title, and due_date, in that order, keeping NULL due dates. Sort by task_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS task_id, project_id, title, due_date
FROM tasks
WHERE assignee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available tasks table columns.

results.question: For every person, total the hours they personally logged across all tasks and dates, regardless of task status or assignment. Return person_id, name, and total_hours, in that order; use zero for people with no entries, round hours to two decimals, and sort by person_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS person_id,
  p.name,
  ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(te.hours), 0), 2) AS total_hours
FROM people AS p
LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te
  ON te.person_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the people and time_entries tables, with aggregation and sorting requested.

results.question: List tasks with no due date, regardless of status. Return task_id, title, and status, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS task_id, title, status
FROM tasks
WHERE due_date IS NULL
ORDER BY id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the tasks table and available columns: id, title, status, and due_date.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, name, known_cost, and unpriced_hours, in that order. Include all task statuses and dates. Known cost is the sum of hours times billed_rate for entries with a non-NULL rate; unpriced hours are hours with a NULL rate. Use zero for missing totals and projects with no work, round both totals to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS project_id,
  p.name AS name,
  ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NOT NULL THEN te.hours * te.billed_rate ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS known_cost,
  ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN te.id IS NOT NULL AND te.billed_rate IS NULL THEN te.hours ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS unpriced_hours
FROM projects AS p
LEFT JOIN tasks AS t
  ON t.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te
  ON te.task_id = t.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available projects, tasks, and time_entries tables, with aggregation and handling of NULL billed rates.

results.question: Find tasks whose own status is not done and whose direct prerequisites are all done. Tasks without prerequisites qualify. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending. Consider only direct prerequisites, regardless of the task due date or assignee.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS task_id, t.title
FROM tasks AS t
WHERE t.status <> 'done'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM dependencies AS d
    JOIN tasks AS prereq ON prereq.id = d.depends_on
    WHERE d.task_id = t.id
      AND prereq.status <> 'done'
  )
ORDER BY t.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the tasks and dependencies tables, with available status, title, and task_id information.

results.question: Find direct dependency edges for which the dependent task and its prerequisite have the same non-NULL assignee, regardless of task status. Return task_id, depends_on, and assignee_id, in that order. Sort by task_id ascending, then depends_on ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  d.task_id,
  d.depends_on,
  t.assignee_id
FROM dependencies AS d
JOIN tasks AS t
  ON t.id = d.task_id
JOIN tasks AS prereq
  ON prereq.id = d.depends_on
WHERE t.assignee_id IS NOT NULL
  AND t.assignee_id = prereq.assignee_id
ORDER BY d.task_id ASC, d.depends_on ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the dependencies and tasks tables to compare assignees and return sorted dependency edges.

results.question: Which projects contain at least one task but no task with status blocked? Return project_id and name, in that order, sorted by project_id ascending. Projects with no tasks must be excluded.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS project_id, p.name
FROM projects AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM tasks AS t
  WHERE t.project_id = p.id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM tasks AS t
  WHERE t.project_id = p.id
    AND t.status = 'blocked'
)
ORDER BY project_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the available projects and tasks tables, with filtering, grouping, and sorting.

results.question: List every direct or indirect prerequisite of task 5. Follow dependency edges recursively, return each prerequisite only once even if reachable through multiple paths, and exclude task 5 itself. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending; include prerequisites of any status.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE prereqs(task_id, path) AS (
  SELECT d.depends_on, ',' || 5 || ',' || d.depends_on || ','
  FROM dependencies AS d
  WHERE d.task_id = 5
    AND d.depends_on <> 5
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.depends_on, p.path || d.depends_on || ','
  FROM prereqs AS p
  JOIN dependencies AS d ON d.task_id = p.task_id
  WHERE d.depends_on <> 5
    AND instr(p.path, ',' || d.depends_on || ',') = 0
)
SELECT DISTINCT t.id AS task_id, t.title
FROM prereqs AS p
JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = p.task_id
ORDER BY task_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the tasks and dependencies tables, including recursive traversal and sorting.

results.question: Find the task with the greatest known cost within each project, keeping all tied tasks and omitting projects with no tasks. Include every task status and date. A task known cost is the sum of hours times non-NULL billed_rate, or zero when it has no priced entries. Compare unrounded costs. Return project_id, task_id, title, and known_cost, in that order, round known_cost to two decimals, and sort by project_id then task_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_costs AS (
  SELECT
    t.project_id,
    t.id AS task_id,
    t.title,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NOT NULL THEN te.hours * te.billed_rate END), 0) AS known_cost
  FROM tasks AS t
  LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te
    ON te.task_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.project_id, t.id, t.title
), ranked AS (
  SELECT
    project_id,
    task_id,
    title,
    known_cost,
    MAX(known_cost) OVER (PARTITION BY project_id) AS max_known_cost
  FROM task_costs
)
SELECT
  project_id,
  task_id,
  title,
  ROUND(known_cost, 2) AS known_cost
FROM ranked
WHERE known_cost = max_known_cost
ORDER BY project_id ASC, task_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available projects, tasks, and time_entries tables, including aggregation, handling NULL billed rates, ties, rounding, and sorting.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, task_count, dependency_edge_count, and total_hours, in that order. Count each task once, count each direct dependency edge once for the project owning its dependent task, and sum each time entry once. Include all statuses and dates, preserve projects without tasks with zero totals, round hours to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_counts AS (
  SELECT
    project_id,
    COUNT(*) AS task_count
  FROM tasks
  GROUP BY project_id
), dependency_counts AS (
  SELECT
    t.project_id,
    COUNT(*) AS dependency_edge_count
  FROM tasks AS t
  JOIN dependencies AS d
    ON d.task_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.project_id
), hour_totals AS (
  SELECT
    t.project_id,
    ROUND(SUM(te.hours), 2) AS total_hours
  FROM tasks AS t
  JOIN time_entries AS te
    ON te.task_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.project_id
)
SELECT
  p.id AS project_id,
  COALESCE(tc.task_count, 0) AS task_count,
  COALESCE(dc.dependency_edge_count, 0) AS dependency_edge_count,
  COALESCE(ht.total_hours, 0.0) AS total_hours
FROM projects AS p
LEFT JOIN task_counts AS tc
  ON tc.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN dependency_counts AS dc
  ON dc.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN hour_totals AS ht
  ON ht.project_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available projects, tasks, dependencies, and time_entries tables, requiring aggregation and preservation of projects without tasks.

results.question: List product ID, name, and current catalog price for products priced at least 50, ordered by product ID.
results.sql:
SELECT id, name, price AS current_catalog_price
FROM products
WHERE price >= 50
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The products table contains product IDs, names, and catalog prices, so the requested filtered and ordered list can be answered.
critique_issues: The query still has LIMIT 1000, which can omit qualifying products. Remove the LIMIT to list all products priced at least 50.

results.question: Count orders in each status. Return status and order count, sorted alphabetically by status.
results.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The orders table includes a status column, so the number of orders can be counted for each status and sorted alphabetically.

results.question: Which customer regions are present? Return each distinct region once, alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT DISTINCT region FROM customers ORDER BY region ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This asks for the distinct customer regions, sorted alphabetically; the customers table contains the region column.

results.question: Return every customer ID, name, and completed-order revenue rounded to two decimals, including zero for customers without completed sales. Use item quantities and historical unit prices. Sort by customer ID.
results.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
  AND o.status = 'completed'
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using customers, orders, and order_items, including customers with no completed orders and revenue calculated from quantities and historical unit prices.

results.question: Which three products sold the most units in completed orders? Return product ID, name, and units. Exclude products without completed item lines; sort units descending, then product ID ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.name, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN orders AS o ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units DESC, p.id ASC
LIMIT 3
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes order status, item quantities, and product IDs and names, so this can be answered by summing units in completed orders and sorting as requested.

results.question: Which completed orders have an item total strictly above 100? Return order ID and total rounded to two decimals, sorted by order ID. Calculate totals from quantity times historical unit price.
results.sql:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY o.id
HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 100
ORDER BY o.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes order status and item quantities and historical unit prices, so completed-order totals can be calculated and filtered as requested.

results.question: Which customers have both a completed order and a cancelled order? Return customer ID and name once each, ordered by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.status = 'completed'
)
AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.status = 'cancelled'
)
ORDER BY c.id
results.classification_explanation: The orders table contains customer IDs and order statuses, and the customers table provides customer names, so customers with both completed and cancelled orders can be identified and ordered by ID.

results.question: For each month with completed orders, return YYYY-MM, revenue rounded to two decimals, and percentage change from the previous month present in the result, rounded to two decimals. Revenue uses historical item prices; empty orders contribute zero. Return NULL for the first change or a zero prior revenue. Sort by month.
results.sql:
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_at) AS month,
    SUM(COALESCE(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price, 0)) AS revenue
  FROM orders AS o
  LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_at)
),
with_previous AS (
  SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS previous_revenue
  FROM monthly_revenue
)
SELECT
  month,
  ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
  CASE
    WHEN previous_revenue IS NULL OR previous_revenue = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND((revenue - previous_revenue) * 100.0 / previous_revenue, 2)
  END AS percentage_change
FROM with_previous
ORDER BY month
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains order dates, statuses, and historical item prices and quantities, sufficient to calculate monthly completed-order revenue and its percentage change from the previous month in the result.

results.question: Find the product or products with the highest completed-order revenue within each category, including ties. Include all catalog products in the comparison with zero revenue when unsold. Return category, product ID, name, and revenue rounded to two decimals; sort category then product ID. Use historical item prices.
results.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    p.category,
    p.id AS product_id,
    p.name,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN o.id IS NOT NULL THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 0) AS revenue
  FROM products AS p
  LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.id, p.category, p.name
), ranked AS (
  SELECT
    category,
    product_id,
    name,
    revenue,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank
  FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT category, product_id, name, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE revenue_rank = 1
ORDER BY category, product_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available products, orders, and order_items data. Historical revenue can be calculated from item quantities and unit prices for completed orders, while including unsold catalog products with zero revenue and retaining ties.

results.question: Which customers have bought every catalog product in the Home category through completed orders? Require the Home category to contain at least one product. Return customer ID and name, ordered by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM products AS hp
    WHERE hp.category = 'Home'
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM products AS hp
    WHERE hp.category = 'Home'
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM orders AS o
          JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
          WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
            AND o.status = 'completed'
            AND oi.product_id = hp.id
      )
)
ORDER BY c.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains the customer, order, order-item, and product data needed to find customers who purchased every Home product through completed orders, with the requested ordering.

results.question: List employee ID and name for employees hired from 2021-01-01 through 2022-12-31 inclusive, ordered by employee ID.
results.sql:
SELECT id, name
FROM employees
WHERE hired_at >= '2021-01-01'
  AND hired_at < '2023-01-01'
ORDER BY id;
results.classification_explanation: The employee table includes employee IDs, names, and hire dates, so this read-only request can be answered.

results.question: Return each department ID, name, and average salary rounded to two decimals. Include departments without employees with NULL average salary; order by department ID.
results.sql:
SELECT d.id, d.name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS average_salary
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY d.id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available departments and employees data.

results.question: Return every distinct employee job title, sorted alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT DISTINCT title FROM employees ORDER BY title ASC
results.classification_explanation: Employee job titles are available in the employees table.

results.question: For every employee, return employee ID, employee name, and direct manager name. Return NULL manager name when there is no manager. Order by employee ID.
results.sql:
SELECT e.id AS employee_id, e.name AS employee_name, m.name AS manager_name
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.id;
results.classification_explanation: The employee and manager names and IDs are available in the employees table, including employees with no manager.

results.question: Which employees earn strictly more than the average salary in their own department? Exclude unassigned employees. Return employee ID, name, department ID, and salary; sort by employee ID.
results.sql:
SELECT e.id AS employee_id, e.name, e.department_id, e.salary
FROM employees AS e
WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL
  AND e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees AS e2
    WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id
  )
ORDER BY e.id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the employees table and department assignments.

results.question: Return every department ID, name, and total hours logged by its own employees in May 2025, including zero for departments without matching logs. Attribute hours to the employee department regardless of the project department. Sort by department ID.
results.sql:
SELECT d.id AS department_id, d.name AS department_name, COALESCE(SUM(wl.hours), 0) AS total_hours
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.id
LEFT JOIN work_logs AS wl
  ON wl.employee_id = e.id
  AND wl.worked_at >= '2025-05-01'
  AND wl.worked_at < '2025-06-01'
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY d.id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request. Department and employee data can be joined with work logs, filtered to May 2025, and aggregated by employee department, including departments with no matching logs.

results.question: Which employees have no work logs during May 2025? Return employee ID and name, ordered by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name
FROM employees AS e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM work_logs AS w
  WHERE w.employee_id = e.id
    AND w.worked_at >= '2025-05-01'
    AND w.worked_at < '2025-06-01'
)
ORDER BY e.id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes employee IDs and names, plus work-log dates, so employees with no logs during May 2025 can be identified and ordered by ID.

results.question: Trace the reporting chain above employee 7. Return manager employee ID, manager name, and distance, where the direct manager is distance 1. Exclude employee 7; sort by distance ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE chain(manager_id, distance, path) AS (
  SELECT manager_id, 1, printf(',%d,%d,', id, manager_id)
  FROM employees
  WHERE id = 7 AND manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.manager_id, c.distance + 1, c.path || e.manager_id || ','
  FROM chain AS c
  JOIN employees AS e ON e.id = c.manager_id
  WHERE e.manager_id IS NOT NULL
    AND instr(c.path, printf(',%d,', e.manager_id)) = 0
)
SELECT c.manager_id AS manager_employee_id, e.name AS manager_name, c.distance
FROM chain AS c
JOIN employees AS e ON e.id = c.manager_id
ORDER BY c.distance ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The employee reporting chain can be derived from the employees table’s manager_id relationship, returning each manager’s ID, name, and distance.

results.question: Within each non-NULL department, return employees in the top two distinct salary levels, including everyone tied at either level. Return department ID, employee ID, name, salary, and dense salary rank. Sort by department ID, rank, then employee ID.
results.sql:
WITH ranked_employees AS (
  SELECT
    department_id,
    id AS employee_id,
    name,
    salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
      PARTITION BY department_id
      ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS salary_rank
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, salary, salary_rank
FROM ranked_employees
WHERE salary_rank <= 2
ORDER BY department_id, salary_rank, employee_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the employees table; it asks for the top two distinct salary levels within each non-NULL department, including ties.

results.question: For each employee assigned to a department, return department ID, employee ID, name, all-time logged hours, and percentage of that department's logged hours rounded to two decimals. Include employees with zero hours; return 0 percent when a department has no hours. Sort by department ID then employee ID.
results.sql:
WITH employee_hours AS (
  SELECT
    e.department_id,
    e.id AS employee_id,
    e.name,
    COALESCE(SUM(w.hours), 0) AS logged_hours
  FROM employees AS e
  LEFT JOIN work_logs AS w ON w.employee_id = e.id
  WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY e.department_id, e.id, e.name
), department_hours AS (
  SELECT department_id, SUM(logged_hours) AS total_hours
  FROM employee_hours
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT
  eh.department_id,
  eh.employee_id,
  eh.name,
  eh.logged_hours,
  CASE
    WHEN dh.total_hours = 0 THEN 0
    ELSE ROUND(100.0 * eh.logged_hours / dh.total_hours, 2)
  END AS department_hours_percentage
FROM employee_hours AS eh
JOIN department_hours AS dh ON dh.department_id = eh.department_id
ORDER BY eh.department_id, eh.employee_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains employee departments and work logs, so the requested all-time hours and each employee’s share of their department’s logged hours can be calculated, including zero-hour employees.

results.question: Return ID and name of students majoring in CS or Math whose names contain the letter a, ignoring ASCII case. Order by student ID.
results.sql:
SELECT id, name
FROM students
WHERE major IN ('CS', 'Math')
  AND lower(name) LIKE '%a%'
ORDER BY id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the students table.

results.question: Sort all courses by credits descending, breaking ties by course ID ascending. Return the third and fourth rows of that ordering, with course ID, title, and credits in that order.
results.sql:
SELECT id, title, credits
FROM courses
ORDER BY credits DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the courses table and its available columns.

results.question: Count enrollment records in each status across all terms. Return status and count, ordered by status.
results.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM enrollments
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
results.classification_explanation: The enrollment table contains status and term fields, so counting enrollment records by status across all terms is answerable.

results.question: For every student, return student ID, name, and credit-weighted average score rounded to two decimals across completed enrollments with a non-NULL score. Count repeat completions separately. Return NULL when no eligible grades exist. Sort by student ID.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id AS student_id, s.name, ROUND(SUM(e.score * c.credits) / NULLIF(SUM(c.credits), 0), 2) AS credit_weighted_average_score
FROM students AS s
LEFT JOIN enrollments AS e
  ON e.student_id = s.id
  AND e.status = 'completed'
  AND e.score IS NOT NULL
LEFT JOIN courses AS c
  ON c.id = e.course_id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available students, enrollments, and courses tables. Completed enrollments with non-NULL scores can be weighted by course credits, with repeats counted separately.

results.question: For every course, return course ID, title, and number of non-withdrawn enrollment records in 2025-Spring, including zero. Sort by course ID.
results.sql:
SELECT c.id AS course_id, c.title, COUNT(e.term) AS enrollment_count
FROM courses AS c
LEFT JOIN enrollments AS e
  ON e.course_id = c.id
  AND e.term = '2025-Spring'
  AND e.status <> 'withdrawn'
GROUP BY c.id, c.title
ORDER BY c.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every course and counting its non-withdrawn enrollment records for 2025-Spring, including courses with zero records.

results.question: Which students have never completed any enrollment? Return student ID and name, sorted by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name
FROM students AS s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM enrollments AS e
    WHERE e.student_id = s.id
      AND e.status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY s.id;
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered from the students and enrollments tables by identifying students with no completed enrollment and sorting their IDs.

results.question: For every instructor, return instructor ID, name, number of assigned catalog courses, and total credits of those courses. Include instructors with no courses using zero counts and zero credits. Count each catalog course once regardless of enrollments; sort by instructor ID.
results.sql:
SELECT i.id AS instructor_id, i.name, COUNT(c.id) AS course_count, COALESCE(SUM(c.credits), 0) AS total_credits
FROM instructors AS i
LEFT JOIN courses AS c ON c.instructor_id = i.id
GROUP BY i.id, i.name
ORDER BY i.id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the instructors and courses tables. It asks for a per-instructor course count and credit total, including instructors with no assigned courses.

results.question: Which students have completed every required course in their own major in any term? Exclude majors with no required courses. Return student ID and name, sorted by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name
FROM students AS s
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM courses AS required_course
    WHERE required_course.major = s.major
      AND required_course.is_required = 1
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM courses AS required_course
    WHERE required_course.major = s.major
      AND required_course.is_required = 1
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM enrollments AS e
          WHERE e.student_id = s.id
            AND e.course_id = required_course.id
            AND e.status = 'completed'
      )
)
ORDER BY s.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains students, required courses by major, and enrollment statuses, so this can be answered by checking whether each student has completed every required course in their major in at least one term, excluding majors with no required courses.

results.question: For each term, find the course or courses with the highest average score among completed enrollments with non-NULL scores, retaining ties before rounding. Return term, course ID, title, and average score rounded to two decimals; sort by term then course ID.
results.sql:
WITH course_averages AS (
  SELECT e.term, c.id AS course_id, c.title, AVG(e.score) AS average_score
  FROM enrollments AS e
  JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id
  WHERE e.status = 'completed'
    AND e.score IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY e.term, c.id, c.title
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, MAX(average_score) OVER (PARTITION BY term) AS highest_average
  FROM course_averages
)
SELECT term, course_id, title, ROUND(average_score, 2) AS average_score
FROM ranked
WHERE average_score = highest_average
ORDER BY term, course_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only query using the available enrollment and course data, with aggregation, tie handling, rounding, and sorting.

results.question: Among distinct students with a non-withdrawn enrollment in 2024-Fall, how many also have a non-withdrawn enrollment in 2025-Spring? Return one row with cohort student count, retained student count, and retention percent rounded to two decimals. A student counts once per group; return NULL percent for an empty cohort.
results.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT student_id
  FROM enrollments
  WHERE term = '2024-Fall'
    AND status <> 'withdrawn'
    AND student_id IS NOT NULL
), retained AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT c.student_id
  FROM cohort AS c
  JOIN enrollments AS e
    ON e.student_id = c.student_id
  WHERE e.term = '2025-Spring'
    AND e.status <> 'withdrawn'
)
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cohort) AS cohort_student_count,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retained) AS retained_student_count,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retained)
    / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cohort), 0),
    2
  ) AS retention_percent;
results.classification_explanation: The enrollment table contains student IDs, terms, and statuses, so the cohort, retained-student count, and retention percentage can be calculated, including a NULL percentage for an empty cohort.

results.question: List book ID, title, and publication year for all books, ordered by publication year descending then book ID ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id, title, published_year FROM books ORDER BY published_year DESC, id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The books table contains book ID, title, and publication year, and supports the requested ordering.

results.question: Which loans were active at the end of 2025-06-30? A loan is active if loaned on or before that date and not returned by that date. Return loan ID and book ID, ordered by loan ID.
results.sql:
SELECT id, book_id
FROM loans
WHERE date(loaned_at) <= date('2025-06-30')
  AND (returned_at IS NULL OR date(returned_at) > date('2025-06-30'))
ORDER BY id;
results.classification_explanation: The loans table includes loan and return dates, so the requested loans can be identified and ordered by loan ID.

results.question: Return author ID, author name, and number of catalog book titles for every author, including authors with zero titles. Order by author ID.
results.sql:
SELECT a.id AS author_id, a.name AS author_name, COUNT(b.id) AS book_title_count
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes authors and books, so the catalog title count for each author—including authors with no books—can be determined.

results.question: For loans active at the end of 2025-06-30 whose due date is strictly earlier than that date, return loan ID, member name, book title, and integer days overdue as of 2025-06-30. A return after that date still counts as active. Sort by loan ID.
results.sql:
SELECT l.id AS loan_id, m.name AS member_name, b.title AS book_title, CAST(julianday('2025-06-30') - julianday(date(l.due_at)) AS INTEGER) AS days_overdue
FROM loans AS l
JOIN members AS m ON m.id = l.member_id
JOIN books AS b ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE date(l.loaned_at) <= '2025-06-30'
  AND (l.returned_at IS NULL OR date(l.returned_at) > '2025-06-30')
  AND date(l.due_at) < '2025-06-30'
ORDER BY l.id
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains the loan, member, and book data needed; overdue days can be calculated from due_at and the specified date, while returned_at determines whether a loan was active at the end of that date.
critique_issues: The query still has `LIMIT 1000`, which can omit qualifying loans. Remove the limit to return all matching loans.

results.question: For every member, return member ID, name, returned-loan count, and average loan duration in days rounded to two decimals. Use all loans with a recorded return, including July returns. Return zero count and NULL average when none are returned; sort by member ID.
results.sql: SELECT m.id AS member_id, m.name, COUNT(CASE WHEN l.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN 1 END) AS returned_loan_count, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN l.returned_at IS NOT NULL THEN julianday(l.returned_at) - julianday(l.loaned_at) END), 2) AS average_loan_duration_days FROM members AS m LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY m.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains member, loan, and return-date data needed to count returned loans and calculate average loan duration, including members with no returned loans.

results.question: Find all book titles tied for the highest number of loan records across all dates. Exclude titles never borrowed. Return book ID, title, and loan count; order by book ID.
results.sql:
WITH loan_counts AS (
  SELECT b.id AS book_id, b.title, COUNT(l.id) AS loan_count
  FROM books AS b
  JOIN loans AS l ON l.book_id = b.id
  GROUP BY b.id, b.title
), max_count AS (
  SELECT MAX(loan_count) AS loan_count
  FROM loan_counts
)
SELECT lc.book_id, lc.title, lc.loan_count
FROM loan_counts AS lc
JOIN max_count AS mc ON lc.loan_count = mc.loan_count
ORDER BY lc.book_id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes books and loans, so the titles with the highest number of loan records can be found and returned with their book IDs and loan counts.

results.question: Which members have borrowed titles from at least two different authors across all dates? Return member ID and name, ordered by member ID.
results.sql:
SELECT m.id AS member_id, m.name
FROM members AS m
JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books AS b ON b.id = l.book_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT b.author_id) >= 2

results.classification_explanation: The schema contains member, loan, book, and author data needed to identify members who borrowed titles by at least two different authors and return their IDs and names ordered by ID.

results.question: For each loan, return member ID, loan ID, loan date, and integer days since that member's previous loan date. Order a member's loans by loan date then loan ID, and use NULL for the first loan. Sort the result by member ID, loan date, then loan ID.
results.sql:
WITH ordered_loans AS (
  SELECT
    member_id,
    id AS loan_id,
    loaned_at AS loan_date,
    LAG(loaned_at) OVER (
      PARTITION BY member_id
      ORDER BY loaned_at, id
    ) AS previous_loan_date
  FROM loans
)
SELECT
  member_id,
  loan_id,
  loan_date,
  CASE
    WHEN previous_loan_date IS NULL THEN NULL
    ELSE CAST(julianday(date(loan_date)) - julianday(date(previous_loan_date)) AS INTEGER)
  END AS days_since_previous_loan
FROM ordered_loans
ORDER BY member_id, loan_date, loan_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the loans table; the days since each member’s previous loan can be calculated from the loan dates.

results.question: For each book, return book ID, title, and copies available at the end of 2025-06-30. Subtract loans started on or before that date and not returned by that date from total copies. Include titles with no active loans; order by book ID.
results.sql:
SELECT
  b.id AS book_id,
  b.title,
  b.total_copies - COUNT(l.id) AS copies_available
FROM books AS b
LEFT JOIN loans AS l
  ON l.book_id = b.id
  AND date(l.loaned_at) <= date('2025-06-30')
  AND (l.returned_at IS NULL OR date(l.returned_at) > date('2025-06-30'))
GROUP BY b.id, b.title, b.total_copies
ORDER BY b.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains book copy counts and loan start and return dates, so available copies on 2025-06-30 can be calculated for every book, including books with no active loans.

results.question: Which delivered shipments arrived strictly after their promised timestamp? Return shipment ID, customer name, and hours late rounded to two decimals; sort by shipment ID.

results.question: For every carrier, return carrier ID, name, and total cost divided by total weight of its non-cancelled shipments, rounded to two decimals. Return NULL when total weight is zero or no eligible shipments exist. Sort by carrier ID.
results.sql: SELECT c.id AS carrier_id, c.name, CASE WHEN COALESCE(SUM(s.weight_kg), 0) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE ROUND(SUM(s.cost) / SUM(s.weight_kg), 2) END AS cost_per_kg FROM carriers AS c LEFT JOIN shipments AS s ON s.carrier_id = c.id AND s.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id

results.question: Which customers have used at least two different non-NULL carriers on non-cancelled shipments? Return customer ID, name, and distinct carrier count; sort by customer ID.

results.question: Which non-cancelled shipments have no tracking events? Return shipment ID and customer name, ordered by shipment ID.

results.question: For every shipment, return shipment ID, latest event type, and latest event timestamp. Choose the highest event ID when timestamps tie; return NULL event fields when no events exist. Sort by shipment ID.
results.sql: WITH ranked_events AS (SELECT shipment_id, event_type, occurred_at, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shipment_id ORDER BY occurred_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM tracking_events) SELECT s.id AS shipment_id, re.event_type AS latest_event_type, re.occurred_at AS latest_event_timestamp FROM shipments AS s LEFT JOIN ranked_events AS re ON re.shipment_id = s.id AND re.rn = 1 ORDER BY s.id

results.question: For shipments with both picked_up and delivered tracking events, return shipment ID and hours from the first picked_up event to the first delivered event rounded to two decimals. Use event timestamps, not shipment timestamps; sort by shipment ID.
results.sql:
WITH event_times AS (
  SELECT
    shipment_id,
    MIN(CASE WHEN event_type = 'picked_up' THEN occurred_at END) AS first_picked_up,
    MIN(CASE WHEN event_type = 'delivered' THEN occurred_at END) AS first_delivered
  FROM tracking_events
  WHERE event_type IN ('picked_up', 'delivered')
  GROUP BY shipment_id
)
SELECT
  shipment_id,
  ROUND((julianday(first_delivered) - julianday(first_picked_up)) * 24, 2) AS hours
FROM event_times
WHERE first_picked_up IS NOT NULL
  AND first_delivered IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY shipment_id
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The tracking_events table contains shipment IDs, event types, and event timestamps, so the requested elapsed hours can be calculated for shipments with both event types and sorted by shipment ID.
critique_issues: The query still has `LIMIT 1000`, which can omit qualifying shipments even though the request asks for all of them. Remove the `LIMIT` clause.

results.question: For each non-NULL carrier and each shipping date with non-cancelled shipments, return carrier ID, shipping date as YYYY-MM-DD, daily shipped weight, and cumulative shipped weight through that date for the carrier. Do not add missing dates. Sort by carrier ID then date.
results.sql:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT
    carrier_id,
    date(shipped_at) AS shipping_date,
    SUM(weight_kg) AS daily_shipped_weight
  FROM shipments
  WHERE carrier_id IS NOT NULL
    AND status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY carrier_id, date(shipped_at)
)
SELECT
  carrier_id,
  shipping_date,
  daily_shipped_weight,
  SUM(daily_shipped_weight) OVER (
    PARTITION BY carrier_id
    ORDER BY shipping_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS cumulative_shipped_weight
FROM daily
ORDER BY carrier_id, shipping_date
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes carrier IDs, shipment dates, weights, and statuses, so daily and cumulative shipped weight for non-cancelled shipments can be calculated and sorted as requested.

results.question: For every completed appointment, return appointment_id, patient name, fee, total payments, and balance_due. results.question: Produce a reconciliation list containing every appointment and every payment, matching payments to appointments when possible. Keep one row per matched payment, appointments with no payment, and unallocated payments. Return appointment_id, payment_id, and amount; leave missing values NULL. Order by appointment_id with NULLs last, then payment_id.
results.sql:
WITH reconciliation AS (
    SELECT a.appointment_id, p.payment_id, p.amount
    FROM appointments AS a
    LEFT JOIN payments AS p
        ON p.appointment_id = a.appointment_id

    UNION ALL

    SELECT NULL AS appointment_id, p.payment_id, p.amount
    FROM payments AS p
    LEFT JOIN appointments AS a
        ON a.appointment_id = p.appointment_id
    WHERE a.appointment_id IS NULL
)
SELECT appointment_id, payment_id, amount
FROM reconciliation
ORDER BY (appointment_id IS NULL), appointment_id, payment_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request. The available appointments and payments tables support matching payments to appointments, including unmatched appointments and unallocated payments, and returning the requested fields in the specified order.

results.question: Within each specialty, find the completed appointment or appointments with the highest fee, including ties. Return specialty, appointment_id, and fee, ordered by specialty and then appointment_id.
results.sql:
WITH ranked_appointments AS (
  SELECT c.specialty, a.appointment_id, a.fee,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.specialty ORDER BY a.fee DESC) AS fee_rank
  FROM appointments AS a
  JOIN clinicians AS c ON c.clinician_id = a.clinician_id
  WHERE a.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT specialty, appointment_id, fee
FROM ranked_appointments
WHERE fee_rank = 1
ORDER BY specialty, appointment_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using appointments and clinicians; it asks for the highest-fee completed appointment(s) within each specialty, including ties.

results.question: Which patients have at least one completed appointment and have fully paid every completed appointment? An appointment is fully paid when its summed payments are at least its fee; missing payments count as zero. Ignore appointments of other statuses. Return patient_id and name, ordered by patient_id.
results.sql:
WITH payment_totals AS (
  SELECT appointment_id, SUM(amount) AS total_paid
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY appointment_id
)
SELECT p.patient_id, p.name
FROM patients AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM appointments AS a
  WHERE a.patient_id = p.patient_id
    AND a.status = 'completed'
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM appointments AS a
  LEFT JOIN payment_totals AS pt
    ON pt.appointment_id = a.appointment_id
  WHERE a.patient_id = p.patient_id
    AND a.status = 'completed'
    AND COALESCE(pt.total_paid, 0) < a.fee
)
ORDER BY p.patient_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question. The available tables support identifying patients with completed appointments and checking each completed appointment's summed payments against its fee, treating missing payments as zero.

results.question: For every customer, return customer_id, name, and the combined current balance of all their accounts, including closed accounts. Current balance is opening_balance plus all ledger entries. Customers without accounts should show zero. Round the combined balance to two decimals and order by customer_id.
results.sql:
WITH account_balances AS (
    SELECT a.account_id,
           a.customer_id,
           a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(le.amount), 0) AS current_balance
    FROM accounts AS a
    LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS le ON le.account_id = a.account_id

results.question: Find accounts with at least two negative ledger entries, including fees as well as withdrawals. Return account_number, negative_entry_count, and the positive total of money removed, rounded to two decimals. Use all posting dates and order by account_number.

results.question: For every account, count ledger entries posted on or before March 31, 2025, and sum their signed amounts. results.question: Compare each account with its March 31, 2025 statement when the statement ending balance is known. Show only mismatches after rounding both balances to two decimals. The book balance is opening_balance plus postings through March 31. Return account_number, book_balance, statement_balance, and the rounded book balance minus the rounded statement balance as difference. Round every monetary output to two decimals. Order by account_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH book_balances AS (
  SELECT
    a.account_number,
    a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(CASE
      WHEN date(le.posted_at) <= date('2025-03-31') THEN le.amount
      ELSE 0
    END), 0) AS book_balance
  FROM accounts AS a
  LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS le ON le.account_id = a.account_id
  GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_number, a.opening_balance
), comparisons AS (
  SELECT
    b.account_number,
    ROUND(b.book_balance, 2) AS book_balance,
    ROUND(s.ending_balance, 2) AS statement_balance
  FROM book_balances AS b
  JOIN statements AS s ON s.account_number = b.account_number
  WHERE date(s.statement_date) = date('2025-03-31')
    AND s.ending_balance IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  account_number,
  book_balance,
  statement_balance,
  ROUND(book_balance - statement_balance, 2) AS difference
FROM comparisons
WHERE book_balance <> statement_balance
ORDER BY account_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only comparison using accounts, ledger_entries, and statements, with date filtering, rounding, and sorting.

results.question: Reconcile all local accounts with all imported statements dated March 31, 2025, retaining unmatched records on either side. Return account_number, book_balance, statement_balance, and the rounded book balance minus the rounded statement balance as difference. Book balance uses opening_balance plus postings through March 31. Round monetary outputs to two decimals; use NULL for a missing book balance, a missing or unknown statement balance, and any difference involving NULL. Order by account_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH book AS (
  SELECT
    a.account_number,
    a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN date(le.posted_at) <= '2025-03-31' THEN le.amount ELSE 0 END), 0) AS balance
  FROM accounts AS a
  LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS le ON le.account_id = a.account_id
  GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_number, a.opening_balance
), march_statements AS (
  SELECT account_number, ending_balance
  FROM statements
  WHERE date(statement_date) = '2025-03-31'
), reconciled AS (
  SELECT
    b.account_number,
    ROUND(b.balance, 2) AS book_balance,
    ROUND(s.ending_balance, 2) AS statement_balance
  FROM book AS b
  LEFT JOIN march_statements AS s ON s.account_number = b.account_number
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    s.account_number,
    NULL AS book_balance,
    ROUND(s.ending_balance, 2) AS statement_balance
  FROM march_statements AS s
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM book AS b WHERE b.account_number = s.account_number
  )
)
SELECT
  account_number,
  book_balance,
  statement_balance,
  CASE
    WHEN book_balance IS NULL OR statement_balance IS NULL THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND(book_balance - statement_balance, 2)
  END AS difference
FROM reconciled
ORDER BY account_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only reconciliation using the available accounts, ledger entries, and statements tables. The requested balances, unmatched records, rounding, NULL handling, and ordering can be computed from the schema.

results.question: Find open accounts whose current balance is strictly below the average current balance of open accounts of the same kind. Current balance includes opening_balance and all postings; include accounts with no entries in the comparison. Compare unrounded balances. Return account_number, kind, and current_balance rounded to two decimals, ordered by account_number.
results.sql:
WITH current_balances AS (
    SELECT
        a.account_number,
        a.kind,
        a.status,
        a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(le.amount), 0) AS current_balance
    FROM accounts AS a
    LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS le ON le.account_id = a.account_id
    GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_number, a.kind, a.status, a.opening_balance
), open_balances AS (
    SELECT
        account_number,
        kind,
        current_balance,
        AVG(current_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY kind) AS average_balance
    FROM current_balances
    WHERE status = 'open'
)
SELECT account_number, kind, ROUND(current_balance, 2) AS current_balance
FROM open_balances
WHERE current_balance < average_balance
ORDER BY account_number
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying open accounts and calculating each current balance from its opening balance plus all ledger postings, including accounts with no entries, then comparing balances by account kind.

results.question: Show paid invoice revenue by billing month, using the historical invoice amounts. Return month as YYYY-MM and revenue rounded to two decimals. Include only months with paid invoices and order chronologically.
results.sql:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', billed_on) AS month, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM invoices
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', billed_on)
ORDER BY month;
results.classification_explanation: The invoices table includes billing dates, historical invoice amounts, and statuses, so paid revenue can be grouped by month and rounded as requested.

results.question: For every customer, return customer_id, name, and total paid invoice amount across all their subscriptions, regardless of subscription status. Include customers with no paid invoices as zero, round the total to two decimals, and order by customer_id.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(i.amount), 0), 2) AS total_paid_invoice_amount
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN invoices AS i ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id AND i.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports joining customers to subscriptions and invoices, filtering for paid invoices, and including customers without paid invoices with a zero total.

results.question: For every plan, including plans with no active subscriptions, return plan_id, name, and active_subscription_count. Count status active only and order by plan_id.
results.sql:
SELECT p.plan_id, p.name, COUNT(s.subscription_id) AS active_subscription_count
FROM plans AS p
LEFT JOIN subscriptions AS s
  ON s.plan_id = p.plan_id
 AND s.status = 'active'
GROUP BY p.plan_id, p.name
ORDER BY p.plan_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting active subscriptions for every plan, including plans with none.

results.question: Which subscriptions exceeded their plan included_units allowance during January 2025? Ignore subscription status. Return subscription_id, plan name, January units used, and units above the allowance. Include only positive overages and order by subscription_id.
results.sql:
SELECT s.subscription_id, p.name AS plan_name, SUM(u.units) AS january_units_used, SUM(u.units) - p.included_units AS units_above_allowance
FROM subscriptions AS s
JOIN plans AS p ON p.plan_id = s.plan_id
JOIN usage_events AS u ON u.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
WHERE u.used_on >= '2025-01-01' AND u.used_on < '2025-02-01'
GROUP BY s.subscription_id, p.name, p.included_units
HAVING SUM(u.units) > p.included_units
ORDER BY s.subscription_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question. The available tables provide subscription plans and included units, along with dated usage events to calculate January 2025 usage and overages.

results.question: Find customers whose open invoices total at least 50 across all subscriptions. Return customer_id, name, open_invoice_count, and open_amount rounded to two decimals, ordered by customer_id. Exclude paid and void invoices.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(i.invoice_id) AS open_invoice_count, ROUND(SUM(i.amount), 2) AS open_amount
FROM customers AS c
JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN invoices AS i ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
WHERE LOWER(i.status) NOT IN ('paid', 'void')
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(i.amount) >= 50
ORDER BY c.customer_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the available customers, subscriptions, and invoices tables.

results.question: Find subscriptions that have at least one usage event but have never had an invoice of any status. Return subscription_id, customer name, and plan name, ordered by subscription_id.
results.sql:
SELECT s.subscription_id, c.name AS customer_name, p.name AS plan_name
FROM subscriptions AS s
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
JOIN plans AS p ON p.plan_id = s.plan_id
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM usage_events AS ue
    WHERE ue.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM invoices AS i
    WHERE i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
)
ORDER BY s.subscription_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the available subscriptions, usage_events, invoices, customers, and plans tables.

results.question: Show each paid invoice together with the running paid revenue for its customer across all subscriptions. Apply invoices in billed_on then invoice_id order within each customer. Return customer_id, invoice_id, billed_on, and running_paid_amount rounded to two decimals. Order by customer_id, billed_on, and invoice_id.
results.sql:
SELECT s.customer_id, i.invoice_id, i.billed_on,
       ROUND(SUM(i.amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY s.customer_id
           ORDER BY i.billed_on, i.invoice_id
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 2) AS running_paid_amount
FROM invoices AS i
JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.subscription_id = i.subscription_id
WHERE i.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY s.customer_id, i.billed_on, i.invoice_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the customers, subscriptions, and invoices tables. It asks for paid invoices and a per-customer running total ordered by billing date and invoice ID.

results.question: Which customers have at least one subscription and have at least one paid invoice for every subscription they have ever held, including cancelled or paused subscriptions? Return customer_id and name, ordered by customer_id.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM subscriptions AS s
    WHERE s.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM subscriptions AS s
    WHERE s.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM invoices AS i
          WHERE i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
            AND i.status = 'paid'
      )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is answerable using the customers, subscriptions, and invoices tables. Subscription status can be ignored to include all subscriptions, and paid invoices can be checked for each subscription.

results.question: Which high-priority tickets currently have status open? Return ticket_id, opened_at, and assigned_agent_id, retaining NULL for unassigned tickets. Sort by opened_at ascending, then ticket_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT ticket_id, opened_at, assigned_agent_id
FROM tickets
WHERE priority = 'high'
  AND status = 'open'
ORDER BY opened_at ASC, ticket_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the tickets table and its available columns.

results.question: Count closed tickets for each priority that has at least one closed ticket. Return priority and closed_ticket_count, sorted by priority alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT priority, COUNT(*) AS closed_ticket_count
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'closed'
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY priority ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains ticket status and priority, so this closed-ticket count by priority can be answered.

results.question: List the agents in team 1. Return agent_id and name, sorted by name alphabetically, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT agent_id, name
FROM agents
WHERE team_id = 1
ORDER BY name ASC, agent_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The agents table includes team_id, agent_id, and name, so this is an answerable read-only request.

results.question: For every team, count its unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending, including tickets without an assigned agent. Include teams with zero unresolved tickets. Return team_id, team_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT teams.team_id, teams.name AS team_name, COUNT(tickets.ticket_id) AS unresolved_ticket_count
FROM teams
LEFT JOIN tickets
  ON tickets.team_id = teams.team_id
  AND tickets.status IN ('open', 'pending')
GROUP BY teams.team_id, teams.name
ORDER BY teams.team_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the teams and tickets tables; it specifies the unresolved statuses, includes unassigned tickets and teams with zero tickets, and provides the requested output and sorting.

results.question: For every customer, report the number of tickets of any status and the number of those tickets with no assigned agent. Include customers without tickets with both counts zero. Return customer_id, customer_name, ticket_count, and unassigned_ticket_count, sorted by customer_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name AS customer_name, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS ticket_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN t.ticket_id IS NOT NULL AND t.assigned_agent_id IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS unassigned_ticket_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN tickets AS t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the customers and tickets tables, including customers with no tickets.

results.question: For each ticket that has received an agent_reply event, find its earliest agent reply and the elapsed hours from opening to that reply. Ignore other event types. Return ticket_id, first_reply_at, and response_hours rounded to two decimal places, sorted by ticket_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       MIN(e.created_at) AS first_reply_at,
       ROUND((julianday(MIN(e.created_at)) - julianday(t.opened_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS response_hours
FROM tickets AS t
JOIN ticket_events AS e ON e.ticket_id = t.ticket_id
WHERE e.event_type = 'agent_reply'
GROUP BY t.ticket_id, t.opened_at
ORDER BY t.ticket_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using tickets and ticket_events, with an elapsed-time calculation and filtering for agent_reply events.

results.question: Which agents are assigned at least two tickets with status closed? Return agent_id, agent_name, and closed_ticket_count. Sort by closed_ticket_count descending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS closed_ticket_count
FROM agents AS a
JOIN tickets AS t ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
WHERE t.status = 'closed'
GROUP BY a.agent_id, a.name
HAVING COUNT(t.ticket_id) >= 2
ORDER BY closed_ticket_count DESC, a.agent_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question. The available tables include agents and tickets, with the fields needed to identify assigned agents, count their closed tickets, and sort the results as requested.

results.question: Find the oldest unresolved ticket, meaning status open or pending, for each team that has one. Exclude tickets without a team. If a team has several tickets opened at the same time, choose the lowest ticket_id. Return team_id, team_name, ticket_id, and opened_at, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked_tickets AS (
  SELECT
    t.team_id,
    tm.name AS team_name,
    t.ticket_id,
    t.opened_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY t.team_id
      ORDER BY t.opened_at ASC, t.ticket_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM tickets AS t
  JOIN teams AS tm ON tm.team_id = t.team_id
  WHERE t.team_id IS NOT NULL
    AND t.status IN ('open', 'pending')
)
SELECT team_id, team_name, ticket_id, opened_at
FROM ranked_tickets
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY team_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available tickets and teams tables.

results.question: Build a complete assignment roster showing every ticket of any status with its assigned agent, every unassigned ticket with NULL agent fields, and every agent with no tickets with NULL ticket fields. Return agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, and status. Sort by agent_id ascending with NULL agents last, then ticket_id ascending with NULL tickets last.
results.sql:
SELECT agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, status
FROM (
    SELECT a.agent_id AS agent_id,
           a.name AS agent_name,
           t.ticket_id AS ticket_id,
           t.status AS status
    FROM tickets AS t
    LEFT JOIN agents AS a ON a.agent_id = t.assigned_agent_id

    UNION ALL

    SELECT a.agent_id AS agent_id,
           a.name AS agent_name,
           NULL AS ticket_id,
           NULL AS status
    FROM agents AS a
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM tickets AS t
        WHERE t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
    )
)
ORDER BY (agent_id IS NULL), agent_id ASC,
         (ticket_id IS NULL), ticket_id ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the tickets and agents tables, including unassigned tickets and agents without tickets.
critique_issues: `LIMIT 1000` can omit rows, so the roster may not be complete. Remove the `LIMIT` clause.

results.question: For each team, identify all agents tied for the largest number of assigned unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending. Exclude teams where every agent has zero assigned unresolved tickets. Count workload by the agent's team, and ignore unassigned tickets. Return team_id, team_name, agent_id, agent_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH agent_workloads AS (
  SELECT
    a.team_id,
    a.agent_id,
    a.name AS agent_name,
    COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS unresolved_ticket_count
  FROM agents AS a
  LEFT JOIN tickets AS t
    ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
   AND t.status IN ('open', 'pending')
  GROUP BY a.team_id, a.agent_id, a.name
), ranked_workloads AS (
  SELECT
    team_id,
    agent_id,
    agent_name,
    unresolved_ticket_count,
    MAX(unresolved_ticket_count) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_max_count
  FROM agent_workloads
)
SELECT
  rw.team_id,
  tm.name AS team_name,
  rw.agent_id,
  rw.agent_name,
  rw.unresolved_ticket_count
FROM ranked_workloads AS rw
JOIN teams AS tm ON tm.team_id = rw.team_id
WHERE rw.unresolved_ticket_count > 0
  AND rw.unresolved_ticket_count = rw.team_max_count
ORDER BY rw.team_id ASC, rw.agent_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available teams, agents, and tickets tables.

results.question: Which rooms have a current nightly_rate of 160 or less? Return room_number, room_type, and nightly_rate. Sort by nightly_rate descending, then room_number ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT room_number, room_type, nightly_rate
FROM rooms
WHERE nightly_rate <= 160
ORDER BY nightly_rate DESC, room_number ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only question about the rooms table and its available columns.

results.question: List confirmed bookings whose check-in date falls in February or March 2025. Return booking_id, check_in, and check_out, sorted by check_in ascending, then booking_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT booking_id, check_in, check_out
FROM bookings
WHERE status = 'confirmed'
  AND check_in >= '2025-02-01'
  AND check_in < '2025-04-01'
ORDER BY check_in ASC, booking_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The bookings table contains status, check_in, and check_out, so confirmed bookings in February or March 2025 can be listed and sorted as requested.

results.question: For each checked_out booking, calculate its number of nights and booking value using booked_nightly_rate. Checkout day is excluded. Return booking_id, nights as an integer, and booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT booking_id, CAST(julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in) AS INTEGER) AS nights, ROUND((julianday(check_out) - julianday(check_in)) * booked_nightly_rate, 2) AS booking_value
FROM bookings
WHERE status = 'checked_out'
ORDER BY booking_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request. The bookings table contains the status, check-in and check-out dates, and booked nightly rate needed to calculate nights and booking value.

results.question: For every room, count checked_out bookings and their total nights, excluding checkout days. Include rooms without checked_out bookings with both totals zero. Return room_id, room_number, completed_booking_count, and total_nights as an integer, sorted by room_number ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  r.room_id,
  r.room_number,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN b.status = 'checked_out' THEN 1 END) AS completed_booking_count,
  COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'checked_out' THEN CAST(julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in) AS INTEGER) ELSE 0 END), 0) AS total_nights
FROM rooms AS r
LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.room_id = r.room_id
GROUP BY r.room_id, r.room_number
ORDER BY r.room_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every room and aggregating its checked_out bookings, counting bookings and summing nights between check-in and checkout dates, with zero totals for rooms without matching bookings.

results.question: For every guest, total the booking value of their checked_out stays, using each booking's historical booked_nightly_rate multiplied by nights and excluding checkout days. Include guests with no checked_out stays with a zero total. Return guest_id, guest_name, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  g.guest_id,
  g.name AS guest_name,
  ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'checked_out' THEN b.booked_nightly_rate * (julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in)) ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS completed_booking_value
FROM guests AS g
LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.guest_id = g.guest_id
GROUP BY g.guest_id, g.name
ORDER BY g.guest_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains guest and booking data needed to total checked_out stays using each booking's historical nightly rate and the number of nights between check-in and check-out, while including guests with no qualifying stays.

results.question: How much net cash has been received for checked_out bookings in each room type? Sum signed payments so refunds reduce the total; exclude payments for other booking statuses and unallocated payments. Only include room types with at least one qualifying payment. Return room_type and net_payments rounded to two decimal places, sorted by room_type alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT r.room_type, ROUND(SUM(p.amount), 2) AS net_payments
FROM payments AS p
JOIN bookings AS b ON b.booking_id = p.booking_id
JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = b.room_id
WHERE b.status = 'checked_out'
GROUP BY r.room_type
ORDER BY r.room_type ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports this read-only aggregation: payments can be joined to bookings and rooms, filtered to checked_out bookings with allocated payments, and summed by room type. Signed payment amounts can account for refunds.

results.question: Which checked_out bookings still have a positive outstanding balance? Balance equals nights excluding checkout day times booked_nightly_rate, minus all signed payments for that booking; treat no payments as zero. Return booking_id, guest_name, room_number, and outstanding_balance rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending. Test positivity before rounding.
results.sql:
WITH booking_balances AS (
    SELECT
        b.booking_id,
        g.name AS guest_name,
        r.room_number,
        (julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in)) * b.booked_nightly_rate
            - COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) AS outstanding_balance
    FROM bookings AS b
    JOIN guests AS g ON g.guest_id = b.guest_id
    JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = b.room_id
    LEFT JOIN payments AS p ON p.booking_id = b.booking_id
    WHERE b.status = 'checked_out'
    GROUP BY b.booking_id, g.name, r.room_number, b.check_in, b.check_out, b.booked_nightly_rate
)
SELECT
    booking_id,
    guest_name,
    room_number,
    ROUND(outstanding_balance, 2) AS outstanding_balance
FROM booking_balances
WHERE outstanding_balance > 0
ORDER BY booking_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema provides the booking status and dates, booked nightly rate, payments, guest names, and room numbers needed to calculate and return the requested balances.

results.question: Find overlapping pairs of bookings for the same room, considering only confirmed and checked_out bookings. A booking occupies [check_in, check_out), so a checkout on another booking's check-in date is not an overlap. Return each pair once, with the lower booking_id first. Return room_number, first_booking_id, and second_booking_id, sorted by room_number, first_booking_id, then second_booking_id, all ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.room_number, b1.booking_id AS first_booking_id, b2.booking_id AS second_booking_id
FROM bookings AS b1
JOIN bookings AS b2
  ON b1.room_id = b2.room_id
 AND b1.booking_id < b2.booking_id
 AND b1.check_in < b2.check_out
 AND b2.check_in < b1.check_out
JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = b1.room_id
WHERE b1.status IN ('confirmed', 'checked_out')
  AND b2.status IN ('confirmed', 'checked_out')
ORDER BY r.room_number ASC, first_booking_id ASC, second_booking_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The bookings and rooms tables contain the fields needed to identify same-room date overlaps, filter by booking status, and return the requested columns in order.

results.question: Within each room type, find every room tied for the highest total booking value from checked_out stays. Use historical booked_nightly_rate times nights excluding checkout days, and assign zero to rooms without checked_out stays; if every room in a type has zero, return all of them. Return room_type, room_number, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places. Rank using unrounded totals and sort by room_type alphabetically, then room_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH room_values AS (
    SELECT
        r.room_type,
        r.room_number,
        COALESCE(SUM(
            CASE WHEN b.status = 'checked_out'
                 THEN b.booked_nightly_rate * (julianday(b.check_out) - julianday(b.check_in))
                 ELSE 0
            END
        ), 0) AS total_value
    FROM rooms AS r
    LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.room_id = r.room_id
    GROUP BY r.room_id, r.room_type, r.room_number
), ranked_rooms AS (
    SELECT
        room_type,
        room_number,
        total_value,
        MAX(total_value) OVER (PARTITION BY room_type) AS highest_value
    FROM room_values
)
SELECT
    room_type,
    room_number,
    ROUND(total_value, 2) AS completed_booking_value
FROM ranked_rooms
WHERE total_value = highest_value
ORDER BY room_type ASC, room_number ASC
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rooms);
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question. The schema provides room types, room numbers, booking status, check-in and check-out dates, and historical booked nightly rates needed to calculate completed stay values and identify tied maxima.

results.question: Which guests have at least two checked_out stays and an average stay length strictly above the average length across all checked_out bookings? Compute nights excluding checkout day, and compare the unrounded averages; the overall average is per booking, not per guest. Return guest_id, guest_name, and average_nights rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH checked_out AS (
    SELECT booking_id, guest_id,
           julianday(date(check_out)) - julianday(date(check_in)) AS nights
    FROM bookings
    WHERE status = 'checked_out'
), guest_averages AS (
    SELECT guest_id, COUNT(*) AS stay_count, AVG(nights) AS average_nights
    FROM checked_out
    GROUP BY guest_id
), overall_average AS (
    SELECT AVG(nights) AS average_nights
    FROM checked_out
)
SELECT ga.guest_id,
       g.name AS guest_name,
       ROUND(ga.average_nights, 2) AS average_nights
FROM guest_averages AS ga
JOIN guests AS g ON g.guest_id = ga.guest_id
CROSS JOIN overall_average AS oa
WHERE ga.stay_count >= 2
  AND ga.average_nights > oa.average_nights
ORDER BY ga.guest_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using bookings and guests, with stay lengths calculated from check-in and check-out dates.

results.question: List raw parts with a unit cost of at least 3. Return part_id, name, unit_cost, ordered by unit_cost descending and then part_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS part_id, name, unit_cost FROM parts WHERE kind = 'raw' AND unit_cost >= 3 ORDER BY unit_cost DESC, id ASC LIMIT 100
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the parts table. The schema includes part IDs, names, unit costs, and kind, so raw parts can be filtered by kind and unit cost, then ordered as requested.
