critique_issues: The LIMIT 100 may omit qualifying raw parts, but the request asks to list them all. Remove the LIMIT clause.

results.question: List work orders whose status is planned or in_progress and whose due date is before 2025-02-15. Return work_order_id, part_id, quantity, due_date, ordered by due_date and then work_order_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS work_order_id, part_id, quantity, due_date
FROM work_orders
WHERE status IN ('planned', 'in_progress')
  AND due_date < '2025-02-15'
ORDER BY due_date ASC, id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The requested work order fields and filters are available in the schema.

results.question: Count work orders in each status that occurs. Return status, work_order_count, ordered by status alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS work_order_count
FROM work_orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only aggregation over the work_orders table, grouping work orders by status and ordering the results alphabetically.

results.question: For every part, report the total quantity on work orders with status planned or in_progress, using zero when there are none. Return part_id, name, active_quantity, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS part_id, p.name, COALESCE(SUM(wo.quantity), 0) AS active_quantity
FROM parts AS p
LEFT JOIN work_orders AS wo
  ON wo.part_id = p.id
 AND wo.status IN ('planned', 'in_progress')
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the parts and work_orders tables, with aggregation and status filtering.

results.question: Show completed work orders that finished after their due date. Return work_order_id, part_name, days_late as an integer calendar-day difference, quantity, ordered by work_order_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT wo.id AS work_order_id, p.name AS part_name, CAST(julianday(date(wo.completed_date)) - julianday(date(wo.due_date)) AS INTEGER) AS days_late, wo.quantity FROM work_orders AS wo JOIN parts AS p ON p.id = wo.part_id WHERE wo.status = 'completed' AND date(wo.completed_date) > date(wo.due_date) ORDER BY wo.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available work_orders and parts tables contain the completion date, due date, quantity, work order ID, and part name needed to identify late completed orders and return the requested calendar-day difference.

results.question: For every part classified as assembly, count its distinct direct component parts and sum their direct quantities per one assembly unit. Use zero for both values when the assembly has no components. Return part_id, name, component_count, component_quantity, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS part_id, p.name, COUNT(b.component_part_id) AS component_count, COALESCE(SUM(b.quantity), 0) AS component_quantity
FROM parts AS p
LEFT JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = p.id
WHERE p.kind = 'assembly'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The parts and BOM tables provide assembly classifications and direct component quantities, including assemblies with no components.

results.question: For each part with at least one completed work order, show the total completed quantity and the number of distinct direct component parts in its bill of materials. The completed quantity must count each work order once; a part without direct components has a component count of zero. Return part_id, name, completed_quantity, component_count, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH completed_orders AS (
    SELECT part_id, SUM(quantity) AS completed_quantity
    FROM work_orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY part_id
), component_counts AS (
    SELECT parent_part_id, COUNT(DISTINCT component_part_id) AS component_count
    FROM bom
    GROUP BY parent_part_id
)
SELECT p.id AS part_id,
       p.name,
       co.completed_quantity,
       COALESCE(cc.component_count, 0) AS component_count
FROM completed_orders co
JOIN parts p ON p.id = co.part_id
LEFT JOIN component_counts cc ON cc.parent_part_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is answerable from the available parts, work_orders, and bom tables.

results.question: For each completed work order, show the previous completed work order date for the same part and the integer calendar-day gap from it. Within each part, sequence completed orders by completed_date and then work_order_id ascending; the first order has NULL for the previous date and gap. Return part_id, work_order_id, completed_date, previous_completed_date, gap_days, ordered by part_id, completed_date, work_order_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH completed_orders AS (
    SELECT
        part_id,
        id AS work_order_id,
        completed_date,
        LAG(completed_date) OVER (
            PARTITION BY part_id
            ORDER BY completed_date, id
        ) AS previous_completed_date
    FROM work_orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT
    part_id,
    work_order_id,
    completed_date,
    previous_completed_date,
    CASE
        WHEN previous_completed_date IS NULL OR completed_date IS NULL THEN NULL
        ELSE CAST(
            julianday(date(completed_date)) - julianday(date(previous_completed_date))
            AS INTEGER
        )
    END AS gap_days
FROM completed_orders
ORDER BY part_id, completed_date, work_order_id
results.classification_explanation: The work_orders table contains the part, order ID, completion date, and status needed to identify completed orders and calculate the prior completion date and calendar-day gap.

results.question: Calculate the leaf-material requirements for building three Desk lamps (part_id 1). A leaf material is a descendant with no components of its own. Multiply quantities along each path, add quantities when a leaf appears along multiple paths, and price the resulting quantity at the leaf part's unit_cost. Return leaf_part_id, name, required_quantity, material_cost rounded to two decimal places, ordered by leaf_part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE requirements(part_id, required_quantity, path) AS (
    SELECT b.component_part_id,
           3.0 * b.quantity,
           ',' || 1 || ',' || b.component_part_id || ','
    FROM bom AS b
    WHERE b.parent_part_id = 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT b.component_part_id,
           r.required_quantity * b.quantity,
           r.path || b.component_part_id || ','
    FROM requirements AS r
    JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = r.part_id
    WHERE instr(r.path, ',' || b.component_part_id || ',') = 0
)
SELECT p.id AS leaf_part_id,
       p.name,
       SUM(r.required_quantity) AS required_quantity,
       ROUND(SUM(r.required_quantity) * p.unit_cost, 2) AS material_cost
FROM requirements AS r
JOIN parts AS p ON p.id = r.part_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM bom AS b
    WHERE b.parent_part_id = p.id
)
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, p.unit_cost
ORDER BY leaf_part_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The parts and BOM tables support traversing component relationships, summing quantities for leaf materials, and calculating their material costs.

results.question: For every ancestor part that has components, list all its direct and indirect descendant parts. For one unit of the ancestor, multiply quantities along each path and add the quantities across all paths to the same descendant. Exclude the ancestor itself. Return ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, required_quantity, ordered by ancestor_part_id and then descendant_part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE descendants(ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, required_quantity, path) AS (
    SELECT
        parent_part_id,
        component_part_id,
        quantity,
        ',' || parent_part_id || ',' || component_part_id || ','
    FROM bom
    UNION ALL
    SELECT
        d.ancestor_part_id,
        b.component_part_id,
        d.required_quantity * b.quantity,
        d.path || b.component_part_id || ','
    FROM descendants AS d
    JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = d.descendant_part_id
    WHERE instr(d.path, ',' || b.component_part_id || ',') = 0
)
SELECT
    ancestor_part_id,
    descendant_part_id,
    SUM(required_quantity) AS required_quantity
FROM descendants
GROUP BY ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id
ORDER BY ancestor_part_id ASC, descendant_part_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The BOM table supports finding direct and indirect descendants, multiplying quantities along each path, and summing quantities for the same ancestor-descendant pair.

results.question: List products with a reorder level of at least five units. Return product_id, sku, name, reorder_level, ordered by reorder_level descending and then product_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS product_id, sku, name, reorder_level
FROM products
WHERE reorder_level >= 5
ORDER BY reorder_level DESC, product_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the products table and its available columns.

results.question: List recorded movements with a negative quantity change during January 2025, regardless of reason. Return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, ordered by movement_date and then movement_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change
FROM movements
WHERE quantity_change < 0
  AND movement_date >= '2025-01-01'
  AND movement_date < '2025-02-01'
ORDER BY movement_date ASC, id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the movements table and its available columns.

results.question: For each warehouse with at least one stock record, total its on-hand units across those records. Return warehouse_id, total_on_hand, ordered by warehouse_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT warehouse_id, SUM(on_hand) AS total_on_hand
FROM stock
GROUP BY warehouse_id
ORDER BY warehouse_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains warehouse and stock records with the fields needed to total on-hand units per warehouse and order the results by warehouse_id.

results.question: For every warehouse, show its total on-hand units and number of stock records. Count a stock record even when on_hand is zero; report zero for both metrics when the warehouse has no records. Return warehouse_id, name, total_on_hand, stock_record_count, ordered by warehouse_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT w.id AS warehouse_id, w.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.on_hand), 0) AS total_on_hand, COUNT(s.product_id) AS stock_record_count
FROM warehouses AS w
LEFT JOIN stock AS s ON s.warehouse_id = w.id
GROUP BY w.id, w.name
ORDER BY w.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This read-only request is answerable from the warehouses and stock tables, including warehouses with no stock records.

results.question: List every warehouse/product combination, treating a missing stock record as zero units on hand. Return warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, ordered by warehouse_id and then product_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT w.id AS warehouse_id, p.id AS product_id, COALESCE(s.on_hand, 0) AS on_hand
FROM warehouses AS w
CROSS JOIN products AS p
LEFT JOIN stock AS s
  ON s.warehouse_id = w.id
 AND s.product_id = p.id
ORDER BY warehouse_id ASC, product_id ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using the available warehouses, products, and stock tables; missing stock records can be treated as zero.
critique_issues: `LIMIT 1000` can omit warehouse/product combinations, contrary to “List every.” Remove the limit.

results.question: For every product, show total current on-hand units across warehouses and the net sum of all quantity changes recorded during January 2025. Compute the two totals independently, using zero when a product has no stock or no January movements. Return product_id, name, total_on_hand, january_net_change, ordered by product_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.name, COALESCE(s.total_on_hand, 0) AS total_on_hand, COALESCE(m.january_net_change, 0) AS january_net_change
FROM products AS p
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(on_hand) AS total_on_hand
    FROM stock
    GROUP BY product_id
) AS s ON s.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity_change) AS january_net_change
    FROM movements
    WHERE movement_date >= '2025-01-01' AND movement_date < '2025-02-01'
    GROUP BY product_id
) AS m ON m.product_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains product, stock, and movement data needed to calculate both totals independently for every product, including products with no matching stock or January 2025 movements.

results.question: Find existing stock records whose last count was before 2025-01-10 or whose last-count date is unknown. Return warehouse_id, warehouse_name, product_id, product_name, on_hand, last_counted, ordered by warehouse_id and then product_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT s.warehouse_id, w.name AS warehouse_name, s.product_id, p.name AS product_name, s.on_hand, s.last_counted
FROM stock AS s
JOIN warehouses AS w ON w.id = s.warehouse_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.id = s.product_id
WHERE s.last_counted < '2025-01-10'
   OR s.last_counted IS NULL
ORDER BY s.warehouse_id ASC, s.product_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the stock, warehouses, and products tables; it specifies the date condition, requested fields, and ordering.

results.question: For every movement at warehouse 1, calculate the running net quantity change for that product, beginning at zero before its first recorded movement. Sequence each product's movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, running_net_change, ordered by product_id, movement_date, movement_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, SUM(quantity_change) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY movement_date ASC, id ASC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_net_change FROM movements WHERE warehouse_id = 1 ORDER BY product_id ASC, movement_date ASC, id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using movements.id as the movement_id, with a running total per product ordered by movement_date and id.

results.question: Rank existing stock records within each warehouse by on_hand descending. Equal quantities share a rank and the next different quantity receives the next consecutive rank with no gaps. Return warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, stock_rank, ordered by warehouse_id, stock_rank, product_id ascending.
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the available stock table.

results.question: For each movement whose reason is outbound, show the date of the immediately following recorded movement for the same warehouse and product, considering all reasons when finding that following movement. Sequence movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, next_movement_date, gap_days as an integer calendar-day difference; use NULL for the final two columns if there is no later movement. Order by movement_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH sequenced AS (
    SELECT
        id,
        warehouse_id,
        product_id,
        movement_date,
        reason,
        LEAD(movement_date) OVER (
            PARTITION BY warehouse_id, product_id
            ORDER BY movement_date ASC, id ASC
        ) AS next_movement_date
    FROM movements
)
SELECT
    id AS movement_id,
    warehouse_id,
    product_id,
    movement_date,
    next_movement_date,
    CASE
        WHEN next_movement_date IS NOT NULL
        THEN CAST(julianday(date(next_movement_date)) - julianday(date(movement_date)) AS INTEGER)
        ELSE NULL
    END AS gap_days
FROM sequenced
WHERE reason = 'outbound'
ORDER BY movement_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request. The movement_id refers to movements.id, and the requested sequencing and calendar-day gap can be derived from the available movement dates.

results.question: List meters with no retirement date. Return meter_id, label, site_id, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS meter_id, label, site_id
FROM meters
WHERE retired_on IS NULL
ORDER BY meter_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the meters table.

results.question: List nonmissing energy readings recorded on 2025-01-02 UTC. Return reading_id, meter_id, reading_at, reading_kwh, ordered by reading_at and then reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS reading_id, meter_id, reading_at, reading_kwh
FROM readings
WHERE reading_at >= '2025-01-02T00:00:00Z'
  AND reading_at < '2025-01-03T00:00:00Z'
  AND reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY reading_at ASC, id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the readings table and its available columns.
critique_issues: `LIMIT 1000` may omit qualifying readings, but the request asks for the full list. Remove the `LIMIT` clause.

results.question: For every meter represented in the readings table, count its nonmissing readings and show their minimum and maximum kWh values. A meter with only missing readings has count zero and NULL minimum and maximum. Return meter_id, valid_reading_count, minimum_kwh, maximum_kwh, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT meter_id,
       COUNT(reading_kwh) AS valid_reading_count,
       MIN(reading_kwh) AS minimum_kwh,
       MAX(reading_kwh) AS maximum_kwh
FROM readings
GROUP BY meter_id
ORDER BY meter_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the readings table; it asks for counts and minimum/maximum values of nonmissing readings, grouped by meter_id.

results.question: For every site, report its total number of meters and the number with no retirement date. Sites without meters should have zero for both counts. Return site_id, name, meter_count, active_meter_count, ordered by site_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id AS site_id, s.name, COUNT(m.id) AS meter_count, SUM(CASE WHEN m.id IS NOT NULL AND m.retired_on IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS active_meter_count
FROM sites AS s
LEFT JOIN meters AS m ON m.site_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the sites and meters tables, including sites with no meters.

results.question: List meters that have no nonmissing energy reading, including meters with no reading records and meters whose records are all missing. Return meter_id, label, site_name, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT m.id AS meter_id, m.label, s.name AS site_name
FROM meters AS m
JOIN sites AS s ON s.id = m.site_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM readings AS r
    WHERE r.meter_id = m.id
      AND r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
)
ORDER BY m.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains meters, readings, and sites, so it can identify meters with no readings or only missing energy readings and return the requested fields in meter_id order.

results.question: For every meter with at least two nonmissing readings, report the minimum reading, maximum reading, and observed kWh range defined as maximum minus minimum. Return site_id, meter_id, label, minimum_kwh, maximum_kwh, observed_range_kwh rounded to two decimal places, ordered by site_id and then meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT m.site_id, m.id AS meter_id, m.label, ROUND(MIN(r.reading_kwh), 2) AS minimum_kwh, ROUND(MAX(r.reading_kwh), 2) AS maximum_kwh, ROUND(MAX(r.reading_kwh) - MIN(r.reading_kwh), 2) AS observed_range_kwh
FROM meters AS m
JOIN readings AS r ON r.meter_id = m.id
WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY m.id, m.site_id, m.label
HAVING COUNT(r.reading_kwh) >= 2
ORDER BY m.site_id ASC, m.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The request asks for a read-only calculation using available meter and reading data.

results.question: For each nonmissing reading with a matching regional tariff, show the tariff effective on that reading's UTC calendar date. The valid_from date is inclusive, valid_to is exclusive, and NULL valid_to has no upper limit. Return reading_id, meter_id, reading_date formatted YYYY-MM-DD, price_per_kwh, ordered by reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS reading_id,
       m.id AS meter_id,
       date(r.reading_at) AS reading_date,
       t.price_per_kwh
FROM readings AS r
JOIN meters AS m ON m.id = r.meter_id
JOIN sites AS s ON s.id = m.site_id
JOIN tariffs AS t
  ON t.region = s.region
 AND t.valid_from <= date(r.reading_at)
 AND (t.valid_to IS NULL OR date(r.reading_at) < t.valid_to)
WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY reading_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available readings, meters, sites, and tariffs tables.

results.question: Within each meter, sequence nonmissing readings by reading_at and then reading_id ascending and form intervals between consecutive nonmissing readings. Omit the first reading. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, elapsed_hours rounded to two decimals, consumed_kwh as current minus previous reading rounded to two decimals, average_kw as consumed_kwh divided by elapsed hours rounded to three decimals. Use NULL average_kw for zero elapsed hours. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH nonmissing AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        id AS reading_id,
        reading_at,
        reading_kwh,
        LAG(reading_at) OVER (
            PARTITION BY meter_id
            ORDER BY reading_at, id
        ) AS previous_reading_at,
        LAG(reading_kwh) OVER (
            PARTITION BY meter_id
            ORDER BY reading_at, id
        ) AS previous_reading_kwh
    FROM readings
    WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
), intervals AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        reading_id,
        reading_at,
        (julianday(reading_at) - julianday(previous_reading_at)) * 24.0 AS elapsed_hours_raw,
        reading_kwh - previous_reading_kwh AS consumed_kwh_raw
    FROM nonmissing
    WHERE previous_reading_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
    meter_id,
    reading_id,
    reading_at,
    ROUND(elapsed_hours_raw, 2) AS elapsed_hours,
    ROUND(consumed_kwh_raw, 2) AS consumed_kwh,
    CASE
        WHEN elapsed_hours_raw = 0 THEN NULL
        ELSE ROUND(consumed_kwh_raw / elapsed_hours_raw, 3)
    END AS average_kw
FROM intervals
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using readings.id as the requested reading_id; the needed reading values and timestamps are available.

results.question: For each meter, derive consumed kWh between consecutive nonmissing readings, sequencing by reading_at and then reading_id ascending. Omit the first reading because it has no preceding interval. For every remaining interval, calculate the arithmetic mean of its consumption and up to two preceding interval consumptions for that meter; divide by the number of available intervals, without time weighting. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, consumed_kwh, trailing_mean_kwh, with both kWh outputs rounded to two decimals. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH nonmissing AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        id AS reading_id,
        reading_at,
        reading_kwh,
        LAG(reading_kwh) OVER (
            PARTITION BY meter_id
            ORDER BY reading_at, id
        ) AS previous_reading_kwh
    FROM readings
    WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
), intervals AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        reading_id,
        reading_at,
        reading_kwh - previous_reading_kwh AS consumed_kwh
    FROM nonmissing
    WHERE previous_reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
), averaged AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        reading_id,
        reading_at,
        consumed_kwh,
        AVG(consumed_kwh) OVER (
            PARTITION BY meter_id
            ORDER BY reading_at, reading_id
            ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS trailing_mean_kwh
    FROM intervals
)
SELECT
    meter_id,
    reading_id,
    reading_at,
    ROUND(consumed_kwh, 2) AS consumed_kwh,
    ROUND(trailing_mean_kwh, 2) AS trailing_mean_kwh
FROM averaged
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using meter readings. The requested reading_id corresponds to the readings table’s id, and the interval calculations and trailing mean can be derived from the available data.

results.question: Rank meters having at least two nonmissing readings by observed consumption, defined as maximum minus minimum reading, in descending order. Equal unrounded consumption values share a rank, and the next rank skips the number of tied positions. Return meter_id, label, observed_consumption_kwh rounded to two decimals, consumption_rank, ordered by consumption_rank and then meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH meter_consumption AS (
    SELECT
        m.id AS meter_id,
        m.label,
        MAX(r.reading_kwh) - MIN(r.reading_kwh) AS observed_consumption_kwh
    FROM meters AS m
    JOIN readings AS r ON r.meter_id = m.id
    WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY m.id, m.label
    HAVING COUNT(r.reading_kwh) >= 2
), ranked_meters AS (
    SELECT
        meter_id,
        label,
        observed_consumption_kwh,
        RANK() OVER (ORDER BY observed_consumption_kwh DESC) AS consumption_rank
    FROM meter_consumption
)
SELECT
    meter_id,
    label,
    ROUND(observed_consumption_kwh, 2) AS observed_consumption_kwh,
    consumption_rank
FROM ranked_meters
ORDER BY consumption_rank, meter_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the readings and meters tables to calculate and rank observed consumption.

results.question: List active routes. Return route_id, name, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS route_id, name
FROM routes
WHERE active = 1
ORDER BY id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The routes table contains active status, route IDs, and names, so this read-only request is answerable.

results.question: List stops in the Central zone. Return stop_id, name, ordered by stop_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS stop_id, name
FROM stops
WHERE zone = 'Central'
ORDER BY id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The stops table contains zone, stop ID, and name, so this read-only request is answerable.

results.question: Count trips in each status occurring from service date 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-03, both dates inclusive. Return status, trip_count, ordered by status alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS trip_count
FROM trips
WHERE service_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-03'
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: The trips table contains service_date and status, so the requested count by status over the inclusive date range is answerable.

results.question: For every route, report its number of listed stop positions and highest stop sequence. A route with no listed stops has stop_count zero and last_stop_sequence NULL. Return route_id, name, stop_count, last_stop_sequence, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS route_id, r.name, COUNT(rs.stop_sequence) AS stop_count, MAX(rs.stop_sequence) AS last_stop_sequence
FROM routes AS r
LEFT JOIN route_stops AS rs ON rs.route_id = r.id
GROUP BY r.id, r.name
ORDER BY route_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains routes and route_stops, so the requested stop count and highest stop sequence can be reported for every route, including routes with no listed stops.

results.question: For each completed trip with an actual departure recorded, calculate departure delay in minutes as actual departure minus scheduled departure, allowing negative values for early departures. Return trip_id, route_name, delay_minutes rounded to two decimals, ordered by trip_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS trip_id, r.name AS route_name, ROUND((julianday(t.actual_departure) - julianday(t.scheduled_departure)) * 1440, 2) AS delay_minutes
FROM trips AS t
JOIN routes AS r ON r.id = t.route_id
WHERE t.status = 'completed'
  AND t.actual_departure IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY t.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The trips table contains status, scheduled departure, and actual departure, and routes provides the route name. The requested delay calculation and ordering can be derived from these fields.

results.question: For every route, report its number of completed trips and number of listed stop positions, counting each trip and each position once. Use zero for missing counts. Return route_id, name, completed_trip_count, stop_count, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH completed_trips AS (
  SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS completed_trip_count
  FROM trips
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY route_id
), stop_counts AS (
  SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS stop_count
  FROM route_stops
  GROUP BY route_id
)
SELECT r.id AS route_id,
       r.name,
       COALESCE(ct.completed_trip_count, 0) AS completed_trip_count,
       COALESCE(sc.stop_count, 0) AS stop_count
FROM routes AS r
LEFT JOIN completed_trips AS ct ON ct.route_id = r.id
LEFT JOIN stop_counts AS sc ON sc.route_id = r.id
ORDER BY r.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting completed trips and listed stop positions for every route, including routes with zero counts, and ordering the results by route_id.

results.question: Show every pair of adjacent stop positions on the same route, where the destination sequence is exactly one greater than the origin sequence. Return route_id, origin_sequence, origin_stop, destination_stop, segment_minutes using the destination position's travel_minutes_from_previous. Order by route_id and then origin_sequence ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  origin.route_id,
  origin.stop_sequence AS origin_sequence,
  origin_stop.name AS origin_stop,
  destination_stop.name AS destination_stop,
  destination.travel_minutes_from_previous AS segment_minutes
FROM route_stops AS origin
JOIN route_stops AS destination
  ON destination.route_id = origin.route_id
 AND destination.stop_sequence = origin.stop_sequence + 1
JOIN stops AS origin_stop
  ON origin_stop.id = origin.stop_id
JOIN stops AS destination_stop
  ON destination_stop.id = destination.stop_id
ORDER BY origin.route_id ASC, origin.stop_sequence ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the route_stops, routes, and stops data. It asks for adjacent stop positions and their segment travel times, which can be obtained by joining the relevant records.

results.question: For every listed route stop, calculate planned elapsed travel minutes from the first stop through that position, treating a missing segment time as zero. Return route_id, stop_sequence, stop_name, elapsed_minutes, ordered by route_id and then stop_sequence ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ordered_stops AS (
  SELECT
    rs.route_id,
    rs.stop_sequence,
    rs.stop_id,
    rs.travel_minutes_from_previous,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY rs.route_id
      ORDER BY rs.stop_sequence
    ) AS position
  FROM route_stops AS rs
)
SELECT
  os.route_id,
  os.stop_sequence,
  s.name AS stop_name,
  SUM(CASE WHEN os.position = 1 THEN 0 ELSE COALESCE(os.travel_minutes_from_previous, 0) END) OVER (
    PARTITION BY os.route_id
    ORDER BY os.stop_sequence
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS elapsed_minutes
FROM ordered_stops AS os
JOIN stops AS s ON s.id = os.stop_id
ORDER BY os.route_id ASC, os.stop_sequence ASC
results.classification_explanation: The route-stop table includes the segment travel time and stop sequence needed to calculate cumulative planned elapsed minutes, with stop names available by joining stops.

results.question: For every route with a completed trip, return exactly its latest completed trip, choosing by service_date descending, then scheduled_departure descending, then trip_id descending. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked_completed_trips AS (
    SELECT
        t.route_id,
        t.id AS trip_id,
        t.service_date,
        t.actual_departure,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY t.route_id
            ORDER BY t.service_date DESC, t.scheduled_departure DESC, t.id DESC
        ) AS trip_rank
    FROM trips AS t
    WHERE t.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure
FROM ranked_completed_trips
WHERE trip_rank = 1
ORDER BY route_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available trips and routes data supports finding each route’s latest completed trip using the specified ordering and returning the requested fields.

results.question: Within each route, divide completed trips in chronological order into two batches of sizes differing by at most one. Order trips by service_date, scheduled_departure, and trip_id ascending; batch 1 contains the earlier trips and gets the extra trip when the count is odd. A route with one completed trip uses only batch 1. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, batch_number, ordered by route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH completed_trips AS (
    SELECT
        route_id,
        id AS trip_id,
        service_date,
        scheduled_departure,
        NTILE(2) OVER (
            PARTITION BY route_id
            ORDER BY service_date, scheduled_departure, id
        ) AS batch_number
    FROM trips
    WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT route_id, trip_id, service_date, batch_number
FROM completed_trips
ORDER BY route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using trips and routes. The requested trip_id corresponds to trips.id, and the batches can be calculated from completed trips ordered as specified.

results.question: List visitors whose known signup date is at least 2025-01-02 and before 2025-01-05. Return visitor_id, country, signup_date, ordered by signup_date and then visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS visitor_id, country, signup_date
FROM visitors
WHERE signup_date IS NOT NULL
  AND signup_date >= '2025-01-02'
  AND signup_date < '2025-01-05'
ORDER BY signup_date ASC, visitor_id ASC
LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only query using the visitors table and its signup_date, country, and id columns.
critique_issues: The `LIMIT 1000` can omit matching visitors. Remove it to return the full list.

results.question: List purchase events with revenue of at least 20. Return event_id, session_id, event_at, revenue, ordered by event_at and then event_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS event_id, session_id, event_at, revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
  AND revenue >= 20
ORDER BY event_at ASC, id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the events table; it filters purchase events by revenue and specifies the requested fields and ordering.

results.question: Count sessions for each device type that occurs. Return device, session_count, ordered by device alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT device, COUNT(*) AS session_count
FROM sessions
GROUP BY device
ORDER BY device ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the sessions table's device column.

results.question: For every visitor, count their sessions, including visitors with no sessions as zero. Return visitor_id, country, session_count, ordered by visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT v.id AS visitor_id, v.country, COUNT(s.id) AS session_count
FROM visitors AS v
LEFT JOIN sessions AS s ON s.visitor_id = v.id
GROUP BY v.id, v.country
ORDER BY visitor_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the visitors and sessions tables, including visitors with zero sessions.

results.question: For each session referrer, using direct for NULL, report the number of sessions, the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event, and total purchase-event revenue. Count each session once even when it contains multiple events, retain sessions without events, and use zero revenue when there are no purchases. Return referrer, session_count, converting_session_count, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, ordered by referrer alphabetically.
results.sql:
WITH purchase_summary AS (
    SELECT
        session_id,
        SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchase_count,
        SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS purchase_revenue
    FROM events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT
    COALESCE(s.referrer, 'direct') AS referrer,
    COUNT(*) AS session_count,
    SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(p.purchase_count, 0) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converting_session_count,
    ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(p.purchase_revenue), 0), 2) AS purchase_revenue
FROM sessions AS s
LEFT JOIN purchase_summary AS p ON p.session_id = s.id
GROUP BY COALESCE(s.referrer, 'direct')
ORDER BY referrer ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is answerable from the sessions and events tables. It specifies how to group NULL referrers, count sessions with purchase events without double-counting, include sessions without events, and calculate rounded purchase revenue.

results.question: For every session, count its events and calculate the span in whole seconds from its earliest to latest event. Return NULL span for a session with no events and zero for one event. Return session_id, event_count, event_span_seconds, ordered by session_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT s.id AS session_id,
       COUNT(e.id) AS event_count,
       CASE
           WHEN COUNT(e.id) = 0 THEN NULL
           ELSE CAST((MAX(julianday(e.event_at)) - MIN(julianday(e.event_at))) * 86400.0 + 0.0001 AS INTEGER)
       END AS event_span_seconds
FROM sessions AS s
LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.session_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id
ORDER BY s.id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the sessions and events tables; event counts and spans can be calculated for every session, including sessions with no events.

results.question: For each visitor country with at least one session, calculate its session conversion rate: 100 times the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event divided by all sessions from that country. A session with multiple purchase events counts once. Return country, session_count, converting_session_count, conversion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by country alphabetically.
results.sql:
SELECT v.country,
       COUNT(*) AS session_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (
           SELECT 1
           FROM events e
           WHERE e.session_id = s.id
             AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
       ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converting_session_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (
           SELECT 1
           FROM events e
           WHERE e.session_id = s.id
             AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
       ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_percent
FROM sessions s
JOIN visitors v ON v.id = s.visitor_id
GROUP BY v.country
ORDER BY v.country ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the available visitors, sessions, and events tables.

results.question: For every session, show the previous session start for the same visitor and the elapsed hours since it. Sequence each visitor's sessions by started_at and then session_id ascending, including ties in start time. The first session has NULL for the previous start and gap. Return visitor_id, session_id, started_at, previous_started_at, gap_hours rounded to two decimals, ordered by visitor_id, started_at, session_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  visitor_id,
  session_id,
  started_at,
  previous_started_at,
  ROUND((julianday(started_at) - julianday(previous_started_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS gap_hours
FROM (
  SELECT
    visitor_id,
    id AS session_id,
    started_at,
    LAG(started_at) OVER (
      PARTITION BY visitor_id
      ORDER BY started_at ASC, id ASC
    ) AS previous_started_at
  FROM sessions
)
ORDER BY visitor_id ASC, started_at ASC, session_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the sessions table; the requested sequencing, previous start, elapsed-hour calculation, rounding, and ordering can be derived from the available columns.

results.question: For each UTC calendar day from 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-04 inclusive, show purchase-event revenue, cumulative revenue since 2025-01-01, and the arithmetic mean of that day's and the preceding calendar day's revenue within this reporting period. Include days without purchases as zero; the first day's mean uses only that day. Return day formatted YYYY-MM-DD, purchase_revenue, cumulative_revenue, two_day_mean_revenue, with all revenue values rounded to two decimals, ordered by day ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
    SELECT date('2025-01-01')
    UNION ALL
    SELECT date(day, '+1 day')
    FROM days
    WHERE day < '2025-01-04'
), daily AS (
    SELECT
        date(e.event_at) AS day,
        SUM(COALESCE(e.revenue, 0)) AS purchase_revenue
    FROM events AS e
    WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase'
      AND date(e.event_at) >= '2025-01-01'
      AND date(e.event_at) <= '2025-01-04'
    GROUP BY date(e.event_at)
), filled AS (
    SELECT
        days.day,
        COALESCE(daily.purchase_revenue, 0) AS purchase_revenue
    FROM days
    LEFT JOIN daily ON daily.day = days.day
)
SELECT
    day,
    ROUND(purchase_revenue, 2) AS purchase_revenue,
    ROUND(SUM(purchase_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day), 2) AS cumulative_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(purchase_revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ), 2) AS two_day_mean_revenue
FROM filled
ORDER BY day ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the events table. It specifies the date range, purchase events, daily aggregation, cumulative revenue, a two-day mean with zero-purchase days included, and the requested output format.

results.question: For every visitor, total their purchase-event revenue, using zero for visitors without purchases or sessions. Rank visitors by unrounded revenue ascending with equal revenues sharing the first position occupied by that tie group, and calculate percentile_fraction as (rank minus one) divided by (number of visitors minus one); use zero if there is only one visitor. Return visitor_id, country, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, percentile_fraction rounded to four decimals, ordered by unrounded purchase revenue and then visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH visitor_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    v.id AS visitor_id,
    v.country,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'purchase' THEN e.revenue ELSE 0 END), 0) AS purchase_revenue
  FROM visitors AS v
  LEFT JOIN sessions AS s ON s.visitor_id = v.id
  LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.session_id = s.id
  GROUP BY v.id, v.country
), ranked AS (
  SELECT
    visitor_id,
    country,
    purchase_revenue,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY purchase_revenue ASC) AS revenue_rank,
    COUNT(*) OVER () AS visitor_count
  FROM visitor_revenue
)
SELECT
  visitor_id,
  country,
  ROUND(purchase_revenue, 2) AS purchase_revenue,
  ROUND(
    CASE WHEN visitor_count = 1 THEN 0.0
         ELSE CAST(revenue_rank - 1 AS REAL) / (visitor_count - 1)
    END,
    4
  ) AS percentile_fraction
FROM ranked
ORDER BY purchase_revenue ASC, visitor_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available visitors, sessions, and events tables. It asks for aggregated purchase revenue and a visitor ranking with a percentile calculation.

results.question: List open listings without a reserve price. Return listing_id and title, ordered by listing_id.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS listing_id, title
FROM listings
WHERE status = 'open'
  AND reserve_price IS NULL
ORDER BY id;
results.classification_explanation: The listings table has status, reserve_price, id, and title columns, so this read-only request can be answered.

results.question: Count listings in each status. Return status and listing_count, ordered by status.
results.sql:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS listing_count
FROM listings
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only aggregation over the listings table's status column.

results.question: List bids of at least 100. Return bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, and amount, ordered by amount descending and then bid_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, amount
FROM bids
WHERE amount >= 100
ORDER BY amount DESC, bid_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the bids table and its available columns.

results.question: For every listing, show listing_id, title, bid_count, and highest_bid. Count actual bids; highest_bid must be NULL for a listing without bids. Order by listing_id.
results.sql:
SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title, COUNT(b.id) AS bid_count, MAX(b.amount) AS highest_bid
FROM listings AS l
LEFT JOIN bids AS b ON b.listing_id = l.id
GROUP BY l.id, l.title
ORDER BY l.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains listings and bids, so the requested bid count and highest bid can be calculated for every listing, including listings with no bids.

results.question: Return the distinct user_id values of users who have listed an item or placed a bid, considering all listing statuses. Order by user_id.
results.sql:
SELECT seller_id AS user_id FROM listings
UNION
SELECT bidder_id AS user_id FROM bids
ORDER BY user_id
results.classification_explanation: The request can be answered using listing sellers and bid bidders; “user_id” refers to the users’ IDs, and all listing statuses are available.

results.question: Which users have both listed an item and placed a bid, considering all listing statuses? Return distinct user_id values ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS user_id
FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT seller_id FROM listings)
  AND id IN (SELECT bidder_id FROM bids)
ORDER BY user_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying users who appear as both listing sellers and bid placers, regardless of listing status.

results.question: Find open listings whose reserve has been met by at least one bid. A listing with no reserve qualifies only if it has at least one bid. Return listing_id and title, ordered by listing_id.
results.sql:
SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title
FROM listings AS l
WHERE l.status = 'open'
  AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM bids AS b
    WHERE b.listing_id = l.id
      AND (l.reserve_price IS NULL OR b.amount >= l.reserve_price)
  )
ORDER BY l.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains listing status, reserve price, bids, and listing titles, so this can be answered using the available data.

results.question: Find sellers who have at least one open listing and for whom every open listing has received a bid. Return seller_id and name, ordered by seller_id. Closed listings do not affect eligibility.
results.sql:
SELECT u.id AS seller_id, u.name
FROM users AS u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM listings AS l
  WHERE l.seller_id = u.id
    AND l.status = 'open'
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM listings AS l
  WHERE l.seller_id = u.id
    AND l.status = 'open'
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM bids AS b
      WHERE b.listing_id = l.id
    )
)
ORDER BY seller_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes seller IDs, listing statuses, and bids, so sellers with at least one open listing and bids on every open listing can be identified.

results.question: For every listing that has bids, return every bid tied for its highest amount. Return listing_id, title, bidder_id, bid_id, and amount, ordered by listing_id then bid_id. Include open and closed listings.
results.sql:
SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title, b.bidder_id, b.id AS bid_id, b.amount
FROM bids AS b
JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id
WHERE b.amount = (
  SELECT MAX(b2.amount)
  FROM bids AS b2
  WHERE b2.listing_id = b.listing_id
)
ORDER BY l.id, b.id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the available listings and bids tables.

results.question: Find unordered pairs of bidders who have both bid on at least two distinct open listings. Return smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id, and shared_listing_count, ordered by those two IDs. Multiple bids by one bidder on one listing count only once.
results.sql:
WITH bidder_open_listings AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT b.bidder_id, b.listing_id
  FROM bids AS b
  JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id
  WHERE l.status = 'open'
), shared_listings AS (
  SELECT a.bidder_id AS smaller_bidder_id,
         c.bidder_id AS larger_bidder_id,
         COUNT(*) AS shared_listing_count
  FROM bidder_open_listings AS a
  JOIN bidder_open_listings AS c
    ON a.listing_id = c.listing_id
   AND a.bidder_id < c.bidder_id
  GROUP BY a.bidder_id, c.bidder_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
)
SELECT smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id, shared_listing_count
FROM shared_listings
ORDER BY smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes bidders, listing statuses, and bid records, so the shared open listings can be counted for each unordered bidder pair.

results.question: List mandatory questions. Return question_id and prompt, ordered by question_id.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS question_id, prompt
FROM questions
WHERE required = 1
ORDER BY id;
results.classification_explanation: The questions table includes a required field, so mandatory questions can be listed with their IDs and prompts in question_id order.

results.question: List responses with a score of at least 4. Return response_id, participant_id, question_id, and score, ordered by response_id.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS response_id, participant_id, question_id, score
FROM responses
WHERE score >= 4
ORDER BY response_id
results.classification_explanation: The responses table contains the requested fields and score, so this read-only database query is answerable.

results.question: Count registered participants by group, displaying NULL group names as Unassigned. Return group_name and participant_count, ordered by the displayed group_name.
results.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name, COUNT(*) AS participant_count
FROM participants
GROUP BY COALESCE(group_name, 'Unassigned')
ORDER BY group_name;
results.classification_explanation: The participants table contains group_name, so registered participants can be counted by group, with NULL names displayed as Unassigned and results ordered by the displayed group name.

results.question: For every question, return question_id, prompt, answered_count, and average_score rounded to two decimals. Ignore NULL scores in both statistics; average_score must be NULL when nobody answered. Order by question_id.
results.sql:
SELECT q.id AS question_id, q.prompt, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count, ROUND(AVG(r.score), 2) AS average_score
FROM questions AS q
LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.question_id = q.id
GROUP BY q.id, q.prompt
ORDER BY q.id
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using the questions and responses tables, counting and averaging only non-NULL scores and ordering by question_id.

results.question: Which participants answered question 1 but did not answer question 2? A NULL score does not count as an answer. Return participant_id values ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT r1.participant_id
FROM responses AS r1
WHERE r1.question_id = 1
  AND r1.score IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM responses AS r2
    WHERE r2.participant_id = r1.participant_id
      AND r2.question_id = 2
      AND r2.score IS NOT NULL
  )
ORDER BY r1.participant_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The available responses data can identify participants with a non-NULL score for question 1 and no non-NULL score for question 2, then return their participant IDs in ascending order.

results.question: Combine the participant IDs of all non-NULL responses to question 1 with those of all non-NULL responses to question 2. Keep duplicates so a participant who answered both appears twice. Return only participant_id, sorted ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT participant_id
FROM (
  SELECT participant_id FROM responses WHERE question_id = 1 AND score IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT participant_id FROM responses WHERE question_id = 2 AND score IS NOT NULL
)
ORDER BY participant_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the responses table; non-NULL responses to questions 1 and 2 can be combined while preserving duplicates and sorted by participant_id.

results.question: For every registered participant, return participant_id, name, and answered_count (the number of questions answered with a non-NULL score), in that order. Include participants with zero answers. Sort by participant_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count
FROM participants AS p
LEFT JOIN responses AS r
  ON r.participant_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the participants and responses tables.

results.question: Which participants answered every mandatory question with a non-NULL score? Return participant_id and name, ordered by participant_id. Optional questions do not affect eligibility. If there are no mandatory questions, every participant qualifies.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name
FROM participants AS p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM questions AS q
    WHERE q.required = 1
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM responses AS r
          WHERE r.participant_id = p.id
            AND r.question_id = q.id
            AND r.score IS NOT NULL
      )
)
ORDER BY p.id;
results.classification_explanation: This is answerable from the participants, questions, and responses tables; the mandatory-question and non-NULL-score conditions can be evaluated, including the case where no mandatory questions exist.

results.question: Find unordered participant pairs with exactly the same set of mandatory questions answered with non-NULL scores. Require that each participant answered at least one mandatory question. Return smaller_participant_id and larger_participant_id, ordered by both IDs.
results.sql:
WITH answered AS (
  SELECT r.participant_id, r.question_id
  FROM responses AS r
  JOIN questions AS q ON q.id = r.question_id
  WHERE q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
), eligible AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT participant_id
  FROM answered
)
SELECT p1.id AS smaller_participant_id,
       p2.id AS larger_participant_id
FROM eligible AS e1
JOIN participants AS p1 ON p1.id = e1.participant_id
JOIN eligible AS e2 ON e2.participant_id > e1.participant_id
JOIN participants AS p2 ON p2.id = e2.participant_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM answered AS a1
  WHERE a1.participant_id = p1.id
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM answered AS a2
      WHERE a2.participant_id = p2.id
        AND a2.question_id = a1.question_id
    )
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM answered AS a2
  WHERE a2.participant_id = p2.id
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM answered AS a1
      WHERE a1.participant_id = p1.id
        AND a1.question_id = a2.question_id
    )
)
ORDER BY smaller_participant_id, larger_participant_id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the participants, questions, and responses tables.

results.question: For each registered participant group, compute the percentage of mandatory question-participant combinations that have a non-NULL score. The denominator is all registered participants in the group times the total number of mandatory questions; skips and missing responses are incomplete. Return group_name (Unassigned for NULL) and completion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by group_name. Use NULL if there are no mandatory questions.
results.sql:
WITH group_participants AS (
  SELECT group_name, COUNT(*) AS participant_count
  FROM participants
  GROUP BY group_name
), mandatory_questions AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS question_count
  FROM questions
  WHERE required = 1
), completed AS (
  SELECT p.group_name, COUNT(*) AS completed_count
  FROM participants AS p
  JOIN responses AS r ON r.participant_id = p.id
  JOIN questions AS q ON q.id = r.question_id
  WHERE q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY p.group_name
)
SELECT
  COALESCE(gp.group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name,
  CASE
    WHEN mq.question_count = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(c.completed_count, 0) /
               (gp.participant_count * mq.question_count), 2)
  END AS completion_percent
FROM group_participants AS gp
CROSS JOIN mandatory_questions AS mq
LEFT JOIN completed AS c
  ON c.group_name IS gp.group_name
ORDER BY group_name
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains the participant groups, mandatory questions, and response scores needed to calculate completion percentages, including missing responses and unassigned groups.

results.question: List players on team 1. Return player_id, name, and position, ordered by player_id.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS player_id, name, position
FROM players
WHERE team_id = 1
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The players table contains team_id, player name, position, and player ID, so this read-only request is answerable.
critique_issues: The query still includes LIMIT 1000, which can omit players. Remove the LIMIT to return all players on team 1.

results.question: List completed matches that ended in a draw. Return match_id, home_team_id, away_team_id, and the home score as goals_each, ordered by match_id.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS match_id, home_team_id, away_team_id, home_score AS goals_each
FROM matches
WHERE status = 'completed'
  AND home_score = away_score
ORDER BY match_id
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM matches);
results.classification_explanation: The available matches table contains the match status, team IDs, and scores needed to list completed matches that ended in a draw.

results.question: For every team, count players in its current roster. Return team_id, name, and player_count, ordered by team_id. Include teams with zero players.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name, COUNT(p.id) AS player_count
FROM teams AS t
LEFT JOIN players AS p ON p.team_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id, t.name
ORDER BY t.id
results.classification_explanation: The teams and players tables provide the data needed to count each team's roster, including teams with no players.

results.question: For every player, sum goals from their recorded appearances in completed matches only. Return player_id, name, and recorded_goals, using 0 if none. Order by recorded_goals descending, then player_id.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS player_id, p.name, COALESCE(SUM(a.goals), 0) AS recorded_goals
FROM players AS p
LEFT JOIN (appearances AS a JOIN matches AS m ON m.id = a.match_id AND m.status = 'completed')
  ON a.player_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY recorded_goals DESC, player_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes players, appearances, and match status, so this read-only request can sum each player's goals in completed matches, include players with no qualifying appearances as 0, and order the results as requested.

results.question: List distinct team_id values for teams that have played in at least one completed match, whether at home or away. Order by team_id.
results.sql:
SELECT team_id
FROM (
  SELECT home_team_id AS team_id
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  UNION
  SELECT away_team_id AS team_id
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY team_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes match status and home/away team IDs, so teams appearing in at least one completed match can be identified and ordered by team ID.

results.question: Which teams have won at least one completed home match and at least one completed away match? Return distinct team_id values ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT team_id
FROM (
  SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, 'home' AS win_type
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND home_score > away_score
  UNION ALL
  SELECT away_team_id AS team_id, 'away' AS win_type
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND away_score > home_score
)
GROUP BY team_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT win_type) = 2
ORDER BY team_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes match status, home and away teams, and scores, so it can identify teams with at least one completed home win and one completed away win.

results.question: Compute league points for every team from completed matches: 3 per win, 1 per draw, 0 per loss. Return team_id, name, and points, including 0 for teams without completed matches. Order by points descending, then team_id.
results.sql:
WITH team_points AS (
  SELECT home_team_id AS team_id,
         CASE WHEN home_score > away_score THEN 3
              WHEN home_score = away_score THEN 1
              ELSE 0 END AS points
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND home_score IS NOT NULL
    AND away_score IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT away_team_id AS team_id,
         CASE WHEN away_score > home_score THEN 3
              WHEN away_score = home_score THEN 1
              ELSE 0 END AS points
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND home_score IS NOT NULL
    AND away_score IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT t.id AS team_id,
       t.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(tp.points), 0) AS points
FROM teams AS t
LEFT JOIN team_points AS tp ON tp.team_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id, t.name
ORDER BY points DESC, team_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains teams and match statuses and scores, which are sufficient to calculate points from completed matches and include teams with no completed matches.

results.question: Find teams with at least one completed match and no completed losses. Return team_id and name, ordered by team_id. Ignore scheduled matches.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name
FROM teams AS t
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM matches AS m
    WHERE m.status = 'completed'
      AND (m.home_team_id = t.id OR m.away_team_id = t.id)
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM matches AS m
    WHERE m.status = 'completed'
      AND (
          (m.home_team_id = t.id AND m.home_score < m.away_score)
          OR (m.away_team_id = t.id AND m.away_score < m.home_score)
      )
)
ORDER BY t.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains match status, scores, and team identifiers, so this can be answered by considering completed matches, excluding scheduled matches, and checking each team's results.

results.question: Find players with a recorded appearance in every completed match involving their current team. Require that the team has at least one completed match. Return player_id and name, ordered by player_id. A missing appearance does not count as participation.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS player_id, p.name
FROM players AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM matches AS m
    WHERE m.status = 'completed'
      AND (m.home_team_id = p.team_id OR m.away_team_id = p.team_id)
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM matches AS m
    WHERE m.status = 'completed'
      AND (m.home_team_id = p.team_id OR m.away_team_id = p.team_id)
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM appearances AS a
          WHERE a.match_id = m.id
            AND a.player_id = p.id
      )
)
ORDER BY p.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema provides player-team assignments, completed match records, and player appearances, so this can be answered by comparing each player's appearances against all completed matches involving their current team.

results.question: For each team that has won a completed match, identify the strongest opponent it defeated. Strength is that opponent's total league points from all completed matches (3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss). Choose the lowest opponent ID if points tie. Return team_id, opponent_id, and opponent_points, ordered by team_id. Count an opponent once even if defeated repeatedly.
results.sql:
WITH team_points AS (
  SELECT team_id, SUM(points) AS points
  FROM (
    SELECT home_team_id AS team_id,
           CASE WHEN home_score > away_score THEN 3
                WHEN home_score = away_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points
    FROM matches
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT away_team_id AS team_id,
           CASE WHEN away_score > home_score THEN 3
                WHEN away_score = home_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points
    FROM matches
    WHERE status = 'completed'
  )
  GROUP BY team_id
), defeats AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT home_team_id AS team_id, away_team_id AS opponent_id
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed' AND home_score > away_score
  UNION
  SELECT DISTINCT away_team_id AS team_id, home_team_id AS opponent_id
  FROM matches
  WHERE status = 'completed' AND away_score > home_score
), ranked AS (
  SELECT d.team_id, d.opponent_id, tp.points AS opponent_points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY d.team_id
           ORDER BY tp.points DESC, d.opponent_id ASC
         ) AS rn
  FROM defeats d
  JOIN team_points tp ON tp.team_id = d.opponent_id
)
SELECT team_id, opponent_id, opponent_points
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY team_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains completed-match results and team IDs, so wins and each opponent’s total league points can be calculated from the available data.

results.question: List completed runs. Return run_id, experiment_id, and variant, in that order, sorted by run_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS run_id, experiment_id, variant
FROM runs
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The runs table contains run IDs, experiment IDs, variants, and status, so completed runs can be listed in the requested order and sorted by run ID.

results.question: List stored measurements whose reading is NULL. Return measurement_id, run_id, and metric, in that order, sorted by measurement_id ascending. Include all run statuses.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS measurement_id, run_id, metric
FROM measurements
WHERE value IS NULL
ORDER BY measurement_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The measurements table contains the reading value and the requested measurement ID, run ID, and metric; NULL readings can be filtered and sorted as specified, including all run statuses.

results.question: Which defined metrics have never had a measurement row recorded, including rows with NULL readings? Return metric and unit, in that order, sorted by metric ascending. Include all runs.
results.sql:
SELECT m.name AS metric, m.unit AS unit
FROM metrics AS m
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM measurements AS ms
    WHERE ms.metric = m.name
)
ORDER BY m.name ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using metrics and measurements; measurement rows count regardless of whether their readings are NULL, and no run filtering is needed.

results.question: For every experiment, return experiment_id, name, run_count, completed_runs, and failed_runs, in that order. Include experiments without runs with zero counts; running runs count only toward run_count. Sort by experiment_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT
  e.id AS experiment_id,
  e.name AS name,
  COUNT(r.id) AS run_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_runs,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed_runs
FROM experiments AS e
LEFT JOIN runs AS r ON r.experiment_id = e.id
GROUP BY e.id, e.name
ORDER BY e.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available experiments and runs tables support these counts, including experiments with no runs and counts grouped by run status.

results.question: Find runs with at least one non-NULL temperature reading but no non-NULL pressure reading. Include every run status. Return distinct run_id values sorted ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT m.run_id
FROM measurements AS m
WHERE m.metric = 'temperature'
  AND m.value IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM measurements AS p
    WHERE p.run_id = m.run_id
      AND p.metric = 'pressure'
      AND p.value IS NOT NULL
  )
ORDER BY m.run_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying runs with non-NULL temperature measurements and no non-NULL pressure measurements, across all statuses, and returning distinct run IDs in ascending order.

results.question: Combine all non-NULL temperature readings from run 1 with all non-NULL temperature readings from run 2, keeping repeated readings even when values match. Return one column named value, sorted ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT value
FROM measurements
WHERE run_id IN (1, 2)
  AND metric = 'temperature'
  AND value IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY value ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports filtering non-NULL temperature measurements by run and combining the readings while preserving duplicates, then sorting them ascending.

results.question: For every run, return run_id and target_coverage_percent, in that order, sorted by run_id. Coverage is 100 times the number of distinct target metrics with at least one non-NULL reading for that run divided by the number of defined metrics with non-NULL targets. Include all statuses and runs without readings, use zero coverage when no target is measured, return NULL if there are no target metrics, and round percentages to two decimals.
results.sql: SELECT r.id AS run_id, CASE WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM metrics WHERE target IS NOT NULL) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN mt.target IS NOT NULL AND m.value IS NOT NULL THEN mt.name END) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM metrics WHERE target IS NOT NULL), 2) END AS target_coverage_percent FROM runs AS r LEFT JOIN measurements AS m ON m.run_id = r.id LEFT JOIN metrics AS mt ON mt.name = m.metric GROUP BY r.id ORDER BY r.id
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the runs, measurements, and metrics tables. It specifies the calculation, inclusion of runs without readings, NULL and zero cases, rounding, and sort order.

results.question: Find completed runs that have at least one non-NULL reading for every defined metric whose target is non-NULL. If there are no target metrics, all completed runs qualify. Return run_id and experiment_id, in that order, sorted by run_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT r.id AS run_id, r.experiment_id
FROM runs AS r
WHERE r.status = 'completed'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM metrics AS m
    WHERE m.target IS NOT NULL
      AND NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM measurements AS meas
        WHERE meas.run_id = r.id
          AND meas.metric = m.name
          AND meas.value IS NOT NULL
      )
  )
ORDER BY r.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered using the runs, measurements, and metrics tables. The request specifies completed runs, requires a non-NULL reading for each metric with a non-NULL target, and defines the case where there are no target metrics.

results.question: Compare treatment and control yield for each experiment using completed runs only. First average non-NULL yield readings within each run, then average those run means within each variant so runs have equal weight. Ignore runs with no known yield and include only experiments with a known mean for both variants. Return experiment_id, control_mean, treatment_mean, and percent_change, in that order. Percent change is 100 times (treatment minus control) divided by control; return NULL when control is zero. Round all three calculated values to two decimals and sort by experiment_id.
results.sql:
WITH run_means AS (
  SELECT
    r.id AS run_id,
    r.experiment_id,
    r.variant,
    AVG(m.value) AS run_mean
  FROM runs AS r
  JOIN measurements AS m ON m.run_id = r.id
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND m.metric = 'yield'
    AND m.value IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY r.id, r.experiment_id, r.variant
), variant_means AS (
  SELECT
    experiment_id,
    AVG(CASE WHEN variant = 'control' THEN run_mean END) AS control_mean,
    AVG(CASE WHEN variant = 'treatment' THEN run_mean END) AS treatment_mean
  FROM run_means
  GROUP BY experiment_id
)
SELECT
  experiment_id,
  ROUND(control_mean, 2) AS control_mean,
  ROUND(treatment_mean, 2) AS treatment_mean,
  CASE
    WHEN control_mean = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE ROUND(100.0 * (treatment_mean - control_mean) / control_mean, 2)
  END AS percent_change
FROM variant_means
WHERE control_mean IS NOT NULL
  AND treatment_mean IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY experiment_id;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the available experiments, runs, measurements, and metrics tables.

results.question: For each metric with a non-NULL target, find the completed runs whose mean non-NULL reading is closest to that target. Average repeated readings within a run, omit runs without a known reading, compare absolute distances before rounding, and keep all tied runs. Return metric, run_id, mean_value, and distance, in that order. Round mean_value and distance to two decimals and sort by metric ascending, then run_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH run_means AS (
    SELECT m.metric, mt.target, r.id AS run_id, AVG(m.value) AS mean_value
    FROM measurements AS m
    JOIN runs AS r ON r.id = m.run_id
    JOIN metrics AS mt ON mt.name = m.metric
    WHERE mt.target IS NOT NULL
      AND r.status = 'completed'
      AND m.value IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY m.metric, mt.target, r.id
), distances AS (
    SELECT metric, run_id, mean_value, ABS(mean_value - target) AS distance
    FROM run_means
), ranked AS (
    SELECT metric, run_id, mean_value, distance,
           MIN(distance) OVER (PARTITION BY metric) AS closest_distance
    FROM distances
)
SELECT metric,
       run_id,
       ROUND(mean_value, 2) AS mean_value,
       ROUND(distance, 2) AS distance
FROM ranked
WHERE distance = closest_distance
ORDER BY metric ASC, run_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the available metrics, runs, and measurements data.

results.question: List tasks with no assignee, including every status. Return task_id, project_id, title, and due_date, in that order, keeping NULL due dates. Sort by task_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS task_id, project_id, title, due_date
FROM tasks
WHERE assignee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY id ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the tasks table; all requested fields and sorting criteria are available.
critique_issues: LIMIT 1000 can omit matching tasks when more than 1,000 tasks have no assignee. Remove the LIMIT to return every matching task.

results.question: For every person, total the hours they personally logged across all tasks and dates, regardless of task status or assignment. Return person_id, name, and total_hours, in that order; use zero for people with no entries, round hours to two decimals, and sort by person_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS person_id, p.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(te.hours), 0), 2) AS total_hours
FROM people AS p
LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te ON te.person_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This can be answered by aggregating time entries by person and including people with no entries, using the available people and time_entries tables.

results.question: List tasks with no due date, regardless of status. Return task_id, title, and status, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT id AS task_id, title, status
FROM tasks
WHERE due_date IS NULL
ORDER BY id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request using the tasks table and its due_date field.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, name, known_cost, and unpriced_hours, in that order. Include all task statuses and dates. Known cost is the sum of hours times billed_rate for entries with a non-NULL rate; unpriced hours are hours with a NULL rate. Use zero for missing totals and projects with no work, round both totals to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH project_totals AS (
    SELECT
        t.project_id,
        SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NOT NULL THEN te.hours * te.billed_rate ELSE 0 END) AS known_cost,
        SUM(CASE WHEN te.billed_rate IS NULL THEN te.hours ELSE 0 END) AS unpriced_hours
    FROM tasks AS t
    LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te ON te.task_id = t.id
    GROUP BY t.project_id
)
SELECT
    p.id AS project_id,
    p.name,
    ROUND(COALESCE(pt.known_cost, 0), 2) AS known_cost,
    ROUND(COALESCE(pt.unpriced_hours, 0), 2) AS unpriced_hours
FROM projects AS p
LEFT JOIN project_totals AS pt ON pt.project_id = p.id
ORDER BY project_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request. Projects, tasks, and time entries provide the needed data; the requested totals can be calculated while including all task statuses and dates.

results.question: Find tasks whose own status is not done and whose direct prerequisites are all done. Tasks without prerequisites qualify. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending. Consider only direct prerequisites, regardless of the task due date or assignee.
results.sql:
SELECT t.id AS task_id, t.title
FROM tasks AS t
WHERE t.status <> 'done'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM dependencies AS d
      JOIN tasks AS prerequisite ON prerequisite.id = d.depends_on
      WHERE d.task_id = t.id
        AND prerequisite.status <> 'done'
  )
ORDER BY t.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema includes tasks and direct dependencies, so this read-only request can identify not-done tasks whose direct prerequisites are all done, including tasks with no prerequisites.

results.question: Find direct dependency edges for which the dependent task and its prerequisite have the same non-NULL assignee, regardless of task status. Return task_id, depends_on, and assignee_id, in that order. Sort by task_id ascending, then depends_on ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT d.task_id, d.depends_on, t.assignee_id
FROM dependencies AS d
JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = d.task_id
JOIN tasks AS prerequisite ON prerequisite.id = d.depends_on
WHERE t.assignee_id IS NOT NULL
  AND t.assignee_id = prerequisite.assignee_id
ORDER BY d.task_id ASC, d.depends_on ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database request using the dependencies and tasks tables, with the requested assignee comparison and sorting.
