results.question: Which projects contain at least one task but no task with status blocked? Return project_id and name, in that order, sorted by project_id ascending. Projects with no tasks must be excluded.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS project_id, p.name
FROM projects AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM tasks AS t
    WHERE t.project_id = p.id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM tasks AS t
    WHERE t.project_id = p.id
      AND t.status = 'blocked'
)
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only database question using the projects and tasks tables.

results.question: List every direct or indirect prerequisite of task 5. Follow dependency edges recursively, return each prerequisite only once even if reachable through multiple paths, and exclude task 5 itself. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending; include prerequisites of any status.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE prerequisites(task_id) AS (
  SELECT depends_on
  FROM dependencies
  WHERE task_id = 5
  UNION
  SELECT d.depends_on
  FROM dependencies AS d
  JOIN prerequisites AS p ON d.task_id = p.task_id
)
SELECT t.id AS task_id, t.title
FROM prerequisites AS p
JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = p.task_id
WHERE p.task_id <> 5
ORDER BY task_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only request. The dependencies table supports recursively finding direct and indirect prerequisites, and the tasks table provides their titles; the requested deduplication, filtering, and sorting are also supported.

results.question: Find the task with the greatest known cost within each project, keeping all tied tasks and omitting projects with no tasks. Include every task status and date. A task known cost is the sum of hours times non-NULL billed_rate, or zero when it has no priced entries. Compare unrounded costs. Return project_id, task_id, title, and known_cost, in that order, round known_cost to two decimals, and sort by project_id then task_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_costs AS (
    SELECT
        t.project_id,
        t.id AS task_id,
        t.title,
        COALESCE(SUM(te.hours * te.billed_rate), 0) AS known_cost
    FROM tasks AS t
    LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te
        ON te.task_id = t.id
       AND te.billed_rate IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY t.project_id, t.id, t.title
), ranked AS (
    SELECT
        project_id,
        task_id,
        title,
        known_cost,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY project_id ORDER BY known_cost DESC) AS cost_rank
    FROM task_costs
)
SELECT
    project_id,
    task_id,
    title,
    ROUND(known_cost, 2) AS known_cost
FROM ranked
WHERE cost_rank = 1
ORDER BY project_id ASC, task_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports finding each project’s maximum task cost, retaining ties, and including task status and due date. The requested cost can be calculated from time entries, treating unpriced entries as zero.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, task_count, dependency_edge_count, and total_hours, in that order. Count each task once, count each direct dependency edge once for the project owning its dependent task, and sum each time entry once. Include all statuses and dates, preserve projects without tasks with zero totals, round hours to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_counts AS (
    SELECT project_id, COUNT(*) AS task_count
    FROM tasks
    GROUP BY project_id
), dependency_counts AS (
    SELECT t.project_id, COUNT(*) AS dependency_edge_count
    FROM dependencies d
    JOIN tasks t ON t.id = d.task_id
    GROUP BY t.project_id
), hour_totals AS (
    SELECT t.project_id, SUM(te.hours) AS total_hours
    FROM time_entries te
    JOIN tasks t ON t.id = te.task_id
    GROUP BY t.project_id
)
SELECT
    p.id AS project_id,
    COALESCE(tc.task_count, 0) AS task_count,
    COALESCE(dc.dependency_edge_count, 0) AS dependency_edge_count,
    ROUND(COALESCE(ht.total_hours, 0), 2) AS total_hours
FROM projects p
LEFT JOIN task_counts tc ON tc.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN dependency_counts dc ON dc.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN hour_totals ht ON ht.project_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: This is an answerable read-only aggregation using the available projects, tasks, dependencies, and time_entries tables. The requested counts and hours can be grouped by project, including projects with no tasks.

results.question: List product ID, name, and current catalog price for products priced at least 50, ordered by product ID.
results.sql: SELECT id AS product_id, name, price AS catalog_price FROM products WHERE price >= 50 ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The products table contains the ID, name, and catalog price needed to filter products priced at 50 or more and sort them by ID.
critique_issues: LIMIT 100 can omit qualifying products. Remove it to return every product with a catalog price of at least 50, ordered by product ID.

results.question: Count orders in each status. Return status and order count, sorted alphabetically by status.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: The orders table contains the status column, so orders can be counted by status and the results sorted alphabetically.

results.question: Which customer regions are present? Return each distinct region once, alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT DISTINCT region FROM customers ORDER BY region ASC
results.classification_explanation: The customers table has a region column, so the distinct regions can be listed alphabetically with a read-only query.

results.question: Return every customer ID, name, and completed-order revenue rounded to two decimals, including zero for customers without completed sales. Use item quantities and historical unit prices. Sort by customer ID.
results.sql: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0), 2) AS completed_order_revenue FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'completed' LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every customer by ID and name, summing quantity times historical unit price for completed orders, rounding revenue to two decimals, returning zero for customers without completed sales, and sorting by customer ID.

results.question: Which three products sold the most units in completed orders? Return product ID, name, and units. Exclude products without completed item lines; sort units descending, then product ID ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.name, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units FROM products AS p JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.product_id = p.id JOIN orders AS o ON o.id = oi.order_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY units DESC, product_id ASC LIMIT 3
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports summing item quantities by product for completed orders, excluding products without matching item lines, and returning the top three by units descending and product ID ascending.

results.question: Which completed orders have an item total strictly above 100? Return order ID and total rounded to two decimals, sorted by order ID. Calculate totals from quantity times historical unit price.
results.sql: SELECT o.id AS order_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS total FROM orders AS o JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY o.id HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 100 ORDER BY o.id LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed')
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying completed orders and summing each order’s item quantities multiplied by their historical unit prices. The total can be filtered strictly above 100 before rounding to two decimals, and the results can be sorted by order ID.

results.question: Which customers have both a completed order and a cancelled order? Return customer ID and name once each, ordered by ID.
results.sql: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'completed') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'cancelled') ORDER BY c.id LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The customers and orders tables can identify customers with at least one completed order and at least one cancelled order, then return each customer's ID and name once, ordered by ID.
critique_issues: The follow-up explicitly requested removing the limit, but the proposal adds `LIMIT 1000`, which can omit qualifying customers. Delete `LIMIT 1000` and retain `ORDER BY c.id`.

results.question: For each month with completed orders, return YYYY-MM, revenue rounded to two decimals, and percentage change from the previous month present in the result, rounded to two decimals. Revenue uses historical item prices; empty orders contribute zero. Return NULL for the first change or a zero prior revenue. Sort by month.
results.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_at) AS month,
         COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0.0) AS revenue
  FROM orders AS o
  LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_at)
), compared AS (
  SELECT month, revenue,
         LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prior_revenue
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - prior_revenue) / NULLIF(prior_revenue, 0), 2) AS percentage_change
FROM compared
ORDER BY month
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports grouping completed orders by month, calculating revenue from historical item prices and quantities while counting empty orders as zero, and comparing each month with the previous month in the result.

results.question: Find the product or products with the highest completed-order revenue within each category, including ties. Include all catalog products in the comparison with zero revenue when unsold. Return category, product ID, name, and revenue rounded to two decimals; sort category then product ID. Use historical item prices.
results.sql:
WITH completed_revenue AS (
  SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN orders AS o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY oi.product_id
), ranked_products AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.id AS product_id, p.name,
         COALESCE(cr.revenue, 0) AS revenue,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY COALESCE(cr.revenue, 0) DESC) AS revenue_rank
  FROM products AS p
  LEFT JOIN completed_revenue AS cr ON cr.product_id = p.id
)
SELECT category, product_id, name, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue
FROM ranked_products
WHERE revenue_rank = 1
ORDER BY category, product_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports calculating completed-order revenue from item quantities and historical unit prices, including every catalog product with zero revenue when it has no completed sales, and returning all products tied for the highest revenue in each category.

results.question: Which customers have bought every catalog product in the Home category through completed orders? Require the Home category to contain at least one product. Return customer ID and name, ordered by ID.
results.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products WHERE category = 'Home')
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM products AS p
    WHERE p.category = 'Home'
      AND NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM orders AS o
        JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
          AND o.status = 'completed'
          AND oi.product_id = p.id
          AND oi.quantity > 0
      )
  )
ORDER BY c.id
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying customers who bought every Home product through completed orders, excluding the case where Home has no products, and returning customer IDs and names ordered by ID.

results.question: List employee ID and name for employees hired from 2021-01-01 through 2022-12-31 inclusive, ordered by employee ID.
results.sql: SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE hired_at >= '2021-01-01' AND hired_at < '2023-01-01' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The employees table contains the ID, name, and hire date needed to filter by the inclusive date range and sort by employee ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 so the query returns every qualifying employee in employee ID order. Update the explanation to remove the statement about the 1,000-row cap.

results.question: Return each department ID, name, and average salary rounded to two decimals. Include departments without employees with NULL average salary; order by department ID.
results.sql: SELECT d.id AS department_id, d.name AS department_name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS average_salary FROM departments AS d LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name ORDER BY d.id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports a read-only query that lists departments by ID, calculates each department’s average salary rounded to two decimal places, and returns NULL for departments without employees.

results.question: Return every distinct employee job title, sorted alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT DISTINCT title FROM employees ORDER BY title ASC
results.classification_explanation: The employees table contains job titles, which can be listed without duplicates and sorted alphabetically in a read-only query.

results.question: For every employee, return employee ID, employee name, and direct manager name. Return NULL manager name when there is no manager. Order by employee ID.
results.sql: SELECT e.id AS employee_id, e.name AS employee_name, m.name AS manager_name FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.id ORDER BY e.id
results.classification_explanation: The employees table contains the IDs, names, and manager references needed to list every employee in ID order, with a NULL manager name for employees who have no manager.

results.question: Which employees earn strictly more than the average salary in their own department? Exclude unassigned employees. Return employee ID, name, department ID, and salary; sort by employee ID.
results.sql:
WITH department_averages AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS average_salary
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.id AS employee_id, e.name, e.department_id, e.salary
FROM employees AS e
JOIN department_averages AS da ON da.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.salary > da.average_salary
ORDER BY e.id
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees)
results.classification_explanation: The employees table contains all requested fields and supports comparing each assigned employee’s salary with their department’s average, then sorting by employee ID.
critique_issues: The proposal retains the count-based LIMIT despite the explicit request to remove it. Delete `LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees)` and keep `ORDER BY e.id`.

results.question: Return every department ID, name, and total hours logged by its own employees in May 2025, including zero for departments without matching logs. Attribute hours to the employee department regardless of the project department. Sort by department ID.
results.sql: SELECT d.id AS department_id, d.name AS department_name, COALESCE(SUM(w.hours), 0) AS total_hours FROM departments AS d LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.id LEFT JOIN work_logs AS w ON w.employee_id = e.id AND w.worked_at >= '2025-05-01' AND w.worked_at < '2025-06-01' GROUP BY d.id, d.name ORDER BY d.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports totaling May 2025 work logs by each employee’s department, regardless of the project’s department, while including departments with no matching logs as zero and sorting by department ID.

results.question: Which employees have no work logs during May 2025? Return employee ID and name, ordered by ID.
results.sql: SELECT e.id, e.name FROM employees AS e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM work_logs AS w WHERE w.employee_id = e.id AND w.worked_at >= '2025-05-01' AND w.worked_at < '2025-06-01') ORDER BY e.id LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying employees with no work logs in May 2025 and returning their IDs and names in ID order.

results.question: Trace the reporting chain above employee 7. Return manager employee ID, manager name, and distance, where the direct manager is distance 1. Exclude employee 7; sort by distance ascending.
results.sql: WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, manager_id, distance, path) AS (SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0, printf(',%lld,', id) FROM employees WHERE id = 7 UNION ALL SELECT m.id, m.name, m.manager_id, c.distance + 1, c.path || printf('%lld,', m.id) FROM chain AS c JOIN employees AS m ON m.id = c.manager_id WHERE instr(c.path, printf(',%lld,', m.id)) = 0) SELECT id AS manager_employee_id, name AS manager_name, distance FROM chain WHERE distance > 0 ORDER BY distance ASC
results.classification_explanation: The employees table contains the IDs, names, and manager references needed to trace employee 7’s reporting chain, calculate each manager’s distance, and sort the results from nearest to farthest.

results.question: Within each non-NULL department, return employees in the top two distinct salary levels, including everyone tied at either level. Return department ID, employee ID, name, salary, and dense salary rank. Sort by department ID, rank, then employee ID.
results.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT department_id, id AS employee_id, name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, salary, salary_rank FROM ranked WHERE salary_rank <= 2 ORDER BY department_id, salary_rank, employee_id;
results.classification_explanation: The employees table provides all requested fields. The top two distinct salary levels can be determined with a read-only dense rank within each non-NULL department, including all ties and applying the requested sort order.

results.question: For each employee assigned to a department, return department ID, employee ID, name, all-time logged hours, and percentage of that department's logged hours rounded to two decimals. Include employees with zero hours; return 0 percent when a department has no hours. Sort by department ID then employee ID.
results.sql: WITH employee_hours AS (SELECT e.department_id, e.id AS employee_id, e.name, COALESCE(SUM(w.hours), 0) AS logged_hours FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN work_logs AS w ON w.employee_id = e.id WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY e.department_id, e.id, e.name), department_totals AS (SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, logged_hours, SUM(logged_hours) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) AS department_hours FROM employee_hours) SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, logged_hours, COALESCE(ROUND(100.0 * logged_hours / NULLIF(department_hours, 0), 2), 0.0) AS department_hours_pct FROM department_totals ORDER BY department_id, employee_id LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The available employee, department, and work-log data supports this read-only report, including employees with zero logged hours and departments with zero total hours.

results.question: Return ID and name of students majoring in CS or Math whose names contain the letter a, ignoring ASCII case. Order by student ID.
results.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE major IN ('CS', 'Math') AND instr(lower(name), 'a') > 0 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The students table has the ID, name, and major fields needed to apply both filters and sort the results by student ID.
critique_issues: The follow-up explicitly requests removing the limit. LIMIT 1000 can omit qualifying students; delete it and retain ORDER BY id.

results.question: Sort all courses by credits descending, breaking ties by course ID ascending. Return the third and fourth rows of that ordering, with course ID, title, and credits in that order.
results.sql: SELECT id, title, credits FROM courses ORDER BY credits DESC, id ASC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2
results.classification_explanation: The courses table contains the ID, title, and credits needed to sort the courses as specified and return the third and fourth rows.

results.question: Count enrollment records in each status across all terms. Return status and count, ordered by status.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS count FROM enrollments GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;
results.classification_explanation: The enrollments table has a status column, so records can be counted by status across all terms and the results ordered by status.

results.question: For every student, return student ID, name, and credit-weighted average score rounded to two decimals across completed enrollments with a non-NULL score. Count repeat completions separately. Return NULL when no eligible grades exist. Sort by student ID.
results.sql: WITH weighted_scores AS (SELECT e.student_id, ROUND(SUM(e.score * c.credits) / NULLIF(SUM(c.credits), 0), 2) AS weighted_average_score FROM enrollments AS e JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE e.status = 'completed' AND e.score IS NOT NULL GROUP BY e.student_id) SELECT s.id AS student_id, s.name, w.weighted_average_score FROM students AS s LEFT JOIN weighted_scores AS w ON w.student_id = s.id ORDER BY s.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains student IDs and names, enrollment statuses and scores, and course credits. Each term's completion can be counted separately, and students with no eligible grades can be included with a NULL average.

results.question: For every course, return course ID, title, and number of non-withdrawn enrollment records in 2025-Spring, including zero. Sort by course ID.
results.sql: SELECT c.id AS course_id, c.title, COUNT(e.course_id) AS enrollment_count FROM courses AS c LEFT JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.course_id = c.id AND e.term = '2025-Spring' AND e.status <> 'withdrawn' GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY c.id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting non-withdrawn enrollment records for 2025-Spring for every course, including courses with zero matching records, and sorting by course ID.

results.question: Which students have never completed any enrollment? Return student ID and name, sorted by ID.
results.sql: SELECT s.id AS student_id, s.name FROM students AS s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments AS e WHERE e.student_id = s.id AND e.status = 'completed' COLLATE NOCASE) ORDER BY s.id LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The students and enrollments tables contain the student IDs, names, and enrollment statuses needed to identify students with no completed enrollments and sort them by ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The request calls for all qualifying students, and the limit omits any after the first 1,000. Keep ORDER BY s.id to preserve the requested sort order.

results.question: For every instructor, return instructor ID, name, number of assigned catalog courses, and total credits of those courses. Include instructors with no courses using zero counts and zero credits. Count each catalog course once regardless of enrollments; sort by instructor ID.
results.sql: SELECT i.id AS instructor_id, i.name, COUNT(c.id) AS course_count, COALESCE(SUM(c.credits), 0) AS total_credits FROM instructors AS i LEFT JOIN courses AS c ON c.instructor_id = i.id GROUP BY i.id, i.name ORDER BY i.id
results.classification_explanation: The instructors and courses tables contain all the data needed to count assigned catalog courses and sum their credits for each instructor, including instructors with no courses. Enrollment data is not needed.

results.question: Which students have completed every required course in their own major in any term? Exclude majors with no required courses. Return student ID and name, sorted by ID.
results.sql: SELECT s.id AS student_id, s.name FROM students AS s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM courses AS c WHERE c.major = s.major AND c.is_required = 1) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM courses AS c WHERE c.major = s.major AND c.is_required = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments AS e WHERE e.student_id = s.id AND e.course_id = c.id AND e.status = 'completed')) ORDER BY s.id LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports checking enrollment status across all terms for every required course in each student's major, excluding majors with no required courses, and returning student IDs and names sorted by ID.

results.question: For each term, find the course or courses with the highest average score among completed enrollments with non-NULL scores, retaining ties before rounding. Return term, course ID, title, and average score rounded to two decimals; sort by term then course ID.
results.sql:
WITH course_averages AS (
  SELECT e.term, c.id AS course_id, c.title, AVG(e.score) AS avg_score
  FROM enrollments AS e
  JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id
  WHERE e.status = 'completed' AND e.score IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY e.term, c.id, c.title
), ranked AS (
  SELECT term, course_id, title, avg_score,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY term ORDER BY avg_score DESC) AS score_rank
  FROM course_averages
)
SELECT term, course_id, title, ROUND(avg_score, 2) AS average_score
FROM ranked
WHERE score_rank = 1
ORDER BY term, course_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports filtering completed enrollments with non-NULL scores, comparing unrounded course averages within each term to retain ties, and joining courses for titles before rounding and sorting the results.

results.question: Among distinct students with a non-withdrawn enrollment in 2024-Fall, how many also have a non-withdrawn enrollment in 2025-Spring? Return one row with cohort student count, retained student count, and retention percent rounded to two decimals. A student counts once per group; return NULL percent for an empty cohort.
results.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT DISTINCT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE term = '2024-Fall' AND LOWER(status) <> 'withdrawn' AND student_id IS NOT NULL), spring AS (SELECT DISTINCT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE term = '2025-Spring' AND LOWER(status) <> 'withdrawn' AND student_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT COUNT(*) AS cohort_student_count, COUNT(spring.student_id) AS retained_student_count, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(spring.student_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS retention_percent FROM cohort LEFT JOIN spring USING (student_id)
results.classification_explanation: The enrollments table provides the student IDs, terms, and statuses needed to count distinct cohort and retained students and calculate retention rounded to two decimals, with NULL for an empty cohort.

results.question: List book ID, title, and publication year for all books, ordered by publication year descending then book ID ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS book_id, title, published_year FROM books ORDER BY published_year DESC, id ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The books table contains the ID, title, and publication year needed to list all books in the requested order.

results.question: Which loans were active at the end of 2025-06-30? A loan is active if loaned on or before that date and not returned by that date. Return loan ID and book ID, ordered by loan ID.
results.sql: SELECT id AS loan_id, book_id FROM loans WHERE date(loaned_at) <= '2025-06-30' AND (returned_at IS NULL OR date(returned_at) > '2025-06-30') ORDER BY id LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The loans table contains the loan ID, book ID, loan date, and return date needed to identify loans active at the end of June 30, 2025, and list them in loan ID order.

results.question: Return author ID, author name, and number of catalog book titles for every author, including authors with zero titles. Order by author ID.
results.sql: SELECT a.id AS author_id, a.name AS author_name, COUNT(b.id) AS title_count FROM authors AS a LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id GROUP BY a.id, a.name ORDER BY a.id
results.classification_explanation: The authors and books tables support counting catalog titles for each author, including authors with no books, and ordering the results by author ID.

results.question: For loans active at the end of 2025-06-30 whose due date is strictly earlier than that date, return loan ID, member name, book title, and integer days overdue as of 2025-06-30. A return after that date still counts as active. Sort by loan ID.
results.sql: SELECT l.id AS loan_id, m.name AS member_name, b.title AS book_title, CAST(julianday('2025-06-30') - julianday(date(l.due_at)) AS INTEGER) AS days_overdue FROM loans AS l LEFT JOIN members AS m ON m.id = l.member_id LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.id = l.book_id WHERE date(l.loaned_at) <= '2025-06-30' AND date(l.due_at) < '2025-06-30' AND (l.returned_at IS NULL OR date(l.returned_at) > '2025-06-30') ORDER BY l.id LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying loans that were active and overdue on 2025-06-30, including loans returned later, and provides the member names, book titles, due dates, and loan IDs needed for the requested output and sorting.

results.question: For every member, return member ID, name, returned-loan count, and average loan duration in days rounded to two decimals. Use all loans with a recorded return, including July returns. Return zero count and NULL average when none are returned; sort by member ID.
results.sql: SELECT m.id AS member_id, m.name, COUNT(l.id) AS returned_loan_count, ROUND(AVG(julianday(l.returned_at) - julianday(l.loaned_at)), 2) AS average_loan_duration_days FROM members AS m LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id AND l.returned_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY m.id
results.classification_explanation: The members and loans tables contain all the data needed to count returned loans and calculate average loan duration for every member, including July returns and members with no returned loans.

results.question: Find all book titles tied for the highest number of loan records across all dates. Exclude titles never borrowed. Return book ID, title, and loan count; order by book ID.
results.sql: WITH book_loan_counts AS (SELECT b.id AS book_id, b.title, COUNT(*) AS loan_count FROM books AS b JOIN loans AS l ON l.book_id = b.id GROUP BY b.id, b.title) SELECT book_id, title, loan_count FROM book_loan_counts WHERE loan_count = (SELECT MAX(loan_count) FROM book_loan_counts) ORDER BY book_id;
results.classification_explanation: The books and loans tables contain the data needed to count loan records per book across all dates, exclude books with no loans, and return every book tied for the highest count, ordered by book ID.

results.question: Which members have borrowed titles from at least two different authors across all dates? Return member ID and name, ordered by member ID.
results.sql: SELECT m.id AS member_id, m.name FROM members AS m JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id JOIN books AS b ON b.id = l.book_id JOIN authors AS a ON a.id = b.author_id GROUP BY m.id, m.name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) >= 2 ORDER BY m.id
results.classification_explanation: The members, loans, and books tables provide the data needed to count distinct authors borrowed by each member across all dates and return qualifying members’ IDs and names in member ID order.

results.question: For each loan, return member ID, loan ID, loan date, and integer days since that member's previous loan date. Order a member's loans by loan date then loan ID, and use NULL for the first loan. Sort the result by member ID, loan date, then loan ID.
results.sql: WITH dated_loans AS (SELECT member_id, id AS loan_id, date(loaned_at) AS loan_date FROM loans), loan_history AS (SELECT member_id, loan_id, loan_date, LAG(loan_date) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loan_date, loan_id) AS previous_loan_date FROM dated_loans) SELECT member_id, loan_id, loan_date, CAST(julianday(loan_date) - julianday(previous_loan_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_previous_loan FROM loan_history ORDER BY member_id, loan_date, loan_id LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans)
results.classification_explanation: The loans table has the member IDs, loan IDs, and loan dates needed to calculate integer days since each member’s previous loan, with NULL for their first loan and the requested ordering.
critique_issues: The follow-up explicitly asks to remove LIMIT. Delete `LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans)` and retain `ORDER BY member_id, loan_date, loan_id`. SQLite does not require a LIMIT for detail listings.

results.question: For each book, return book ID, title, and copies available at the end of 2025-06-30. Subtract loans started on or before that date and not returned by that date from total copies. Include titles with no active loans; order by book ID.
results.sql: SELECT b.id AS book_id, b.title, b.total_copies - COUNT(l.id) AS copies_available FROM books AS b LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.book_id = b.id AND l.loaned_at < '2025-07-01' AND (l.returned_at IS NULL OR l.returned_at >= '2025-07-01') GROUP BY b.id, b.title, b.total_copies ORDER BY b.id
results.classification_explanation: The books and loans tables contain the IDs, titles, copy totals, and loan and return dates needed to calculate availability at the end of June 30, 2025, including books with no active loans, and sort by book ID.

results.question: Which members have borrowed every catalog title by author 1 at least once across all dates? Require author 1 to have at least one title. Return member ID and name, ordered by ID.
results.sql: SELECT m.id AS member_id, m.name FROM members AS m WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books AS b WHERE b.author_id = 1) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books AS b WHERE b.author_id = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l WHERE l.book_id = b.id AND l.member_id = m.id)) ORDER BY m.id
results.classification_explanation: The books, loans, and members tables provide all the data needed to verify that author 1 has at least one catalog title and return the ID and name of each member who borrowed every such title at least once, ordered by member ID.

results.question: Return shipment ID and weight for in-transit shipments weighing at least 5 kilograms, ordered by shipment ID.
results.sql: SELECT id AS shipment_id, weight_kg FROM shipments WHERE status = 'in_transit' AND weight_kg >= 5 ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The shipments table contains the ID, weight in kilograms, and status needed to filter for in-transit shipments weighing at least 5 kilograms and sort them by shipment ID.

results.question: Return every carrier ID, name, and total assigned shipment count across all statuses, including zero. Order by carrier ID.
results.sql: SELECT c.id AS carrier_id, c.name, COUNT(s.id) AS total_assigned_shipments FROM carriers AS c LEFT JOIN shipments AS s ON s.carrier_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every carrier by ID and name, counting its assigned shipments across all statuses (including zero), and sorting by carrier ID.

results.question: Return each distinct tracking-event type in uppercase with underscores replaced by spaces, sorted alphabetically by the formatted value.
results.sql: SELECT DISTINCT UPPER(REPLACE(event_type, '_', ' ')) AS formatted_event_type FROM tracking_events ORDER BY formatted_event_type ASC
results.classification_explanation: The tracking_events table contains event_type, so a read-only query can format the values, remove duplicates, and sort them alphabetically.

results.question: Which delivered shipments arrived strictly after their promised timestamp? Return shipment ID, customer name, and hours late rounded to two decimals; sort by shipment ID.

results.question: For every carrier, return carrier ID, name, and total cost divided by total weight of its non-cancelled shipments, rounded to two decimals. Return NULL when total weight is zero or no eligible shipments exist. Sort by carrier ID.

results.question: For shipments with both picked_up and delivered tracking events, return shipment ID and hours from the first picked_up event to the first delivered event rounded to two decimals. Use event timestamps, not shipment timestamps; sort by shipment ID.
results.sql:
WITH event_times AS (
  SELECT shipment_id,
         MIN(CASE WHEN event_type = 'picked_up' THEN julianday(occurred_at) END) AS first_pickup,
         MIN(CASE WHEN event_type = 'delivered' THEN julianday(occurred_at) END) AS first_delivery
  FROM tracking_events
  WHERE event_type IN ('picked_up', 'delivered')
  GROUP BY shipment_id
)
SELECT s.id AS shipment_id,
       ROUND((e.first_delivery - e.first_pickup) * 24, 2) AS hours_to_delivery
FROM shipments AS s
JOIN event_times AS e ON e.shipment_id = s.id
WHERE e.first_pickup IS NOT NULL AND e.first_delivery IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY s.id
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The tracking_events table provides shipment IDs, event types, and timestamps, so the app can find the first event of each type, calculate the elapsed hours, and sort by shipment ID without modifying data.

results.question: For each non-NULL carrier and each shipping date with non-cancelled shipments, return carrier ID, shipping date as YYYY-MM-DD, daily shipped weight, and cumulative shipped weight through that date for the carrier. Do not add missing dates. Sort by carrier ID then date.

results.question: List patients with a known city. Return patient_id, name, and city, ordered by name and then patient_id.

results.question: Find clinicians with at least two completed appointments. Return clinician_id, name, completed_count, and average completed-appointment fee rounded to two decimals. Order by clinician_id.
results.sql: SELECT c.clinician_id, c.name, COUNT(*) AS completed_count, ROUND(AVG(a.fee), 2) AS average_completed_fee FROM clinicians AS c JOIN appointments AS a ON a.clinician_id = c.clinician_id WHERE a.status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.clinician_id, c.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY c.clinician_id

results.question: For every completed appointment, return appointment_id, patient name, fee, total payments, and balance_due. Balance is fee minus payments; keep negative balances for overpayments and use zero payments when none exist. Round payments and balance to two decimals and order by appointment_id.
results.sql: WITH payment_totals AS (SELECT appointment_id, SUM(amount) AS total_paid FROM payments GROUP BY appointment_id) SELECT a.appointment_id, p.name AS patient_name, a.fee, ROUND(COALESCE(t.total_paid, 0), 2) AS total_payments, ROUND(a.fee - COALESCE(t.total_paid, 0), 2) AS balance_due FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id LEFT JOIN payment_totals AS t ON t.appointment_id = a.appointment_id WHERE a.status = 'completed' ORDER BY a.appointment_id LIMIT 1000

critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 and retain ORDER BY a.appointment_id. The user requested every completed appointment, and the cap omits rows when more than 1,000 qualify.

results.question: Show every clinician, including clinicians without completed appointments, with clinician_id, name, and completed_count. Count only completed appointments and order by clinician_id.

results.question: Produce a reconciliation list containing every appointment and every payment, matching payments to appointments when possible. Keep one row per matched payment, appointments with no payment, and unallocated payments. Return appointment_id, payment_id, and amount; leave missing values NULL. Order by appointment_id with NULLs last, then payment_id.
results.sql:
SELECT appointment_id, payment_id, amount
FROM (
    SELECT a.appointment_id, p.payment_id, p.amount
    FROM appointments AS a
    LEFT JOIN payments AS p ON p.appointment_id = a.appointment_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT NULL AS appointment_id, p.payment_id, p.amount
    FROM payments AS p
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM appointments AS a
        WHERE a.appointment_id = p.appointment_id
    )
)
ORDER BY appointment_id IS NULL, appointment_id, payment_id
LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports matching payments to appointments by appointment_id, retaining unmatched rows from both tables, and sorting the requested columns as specified.

results.question: Within each specialty, find the completed appointment or appointments with the highest fee, including ties. Return specialty, appointment_id, and fee, ordered by specialty and then appointment_id.
results.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT c.specialty, a.appointment_id, a.fee, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.specialty ORDER BY a.fee DESC) AS fee_rank FROM appointments AS a JOIN clinicians AS c ON c.clinician_id = a.clinician_id WHERE a.status = 'completed') SELECT specialty, appointment_id, fee FROM ranked WHERE fee_rank = 1 ORDER BY specialty, appointment_id

results.question: Which patients have at least one completed appointment and have fully paid every completed appointment? An appointment is fully paid when its summed payments are at least its fee; missing payments count as zero. Ignore appointments of other statuses. Return patient_id and name, ordered by patient_id.
results.sql: WITH completed AS (SELECT a.patient_id, a.fee, COALESCE((SELECT SUM(pay.amount) FROM payments AS pay WHERE pay.appointment_id = a.appointment_id), 0) AS paid FROM appointments AS a WHERE a.status = 'completed'), fully_paid_patients AS (SELECT patient_id FROM completed GROUP BY patient_id HAVING MIN(paid >= fee) = 1) SELECT p.patient_id, p.name FROM patients AS p JOIN fully_paid_patients AS f ON f.patient_id = p.patient_id ORDER BY p.patient_id LIMIT -1

results.question: List withdrawal entries posted during March 2025. Return entry_id, account_id, posted_at, and the signed amount, ordered by posted_at and then entry_id.
results.sql: SELECT entry_id, account_id, posted_at, -ABS(amount) AS signed_amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE entry_type = 'withdrawal' AND posted_at >= '2025-03-01' AND posted_at < '2025-04-01' ORDER BY posted_at, entry_id LIMIT 1000

results.question: Across all ledger entries, show each entry_type, its entry count, and the sum of signed amounts rounded to two decimals. Order by entry_type.

results.question: For every customer, return customer_id, name, and the combined current balance of all their accounts, including closed accounts. Current balance is opening_balance plus all ledger entries. Customers without accounts should show zero. Round the combined balance to two decimals and order by customer_id.
results.sql:
WITH ledger_totals AS (
  SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS net_amount
  FROM ledger_entries
  GROUP BY account_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(a.opening_balance + COALESCE(l.net_amount, 0)), 0), 2) AS combined_balance
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN accounts AS a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN ledger_totals AS l ON l.account_id = a.account_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id

results.question: Find accounts with at least two negative ledger entries, including fees as well as withdrawals. Return account_number, negative_entry_count, and the positive total of money removed, rounded to two decimals. Use all posting dates and order by account_number.

SELECT a.account_number, COUNT(*) AS negative_entry_count, ROUND(-SUM(l.amount), 2) AS total_money_removed
FROM accounts AS a

results.question: For every account, count ledger entries posted on or before March 31, 2025, and sum their signed amounts. Include accounts without qualifying entries with count zero and net change zero. Return account_number, entry_count, and net_change rounded to two decimals, ordered by account_number.
results.sql: SELECT a.account_number, COUNT(l.entry_id) AS entry_count, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0), 2) AS net_change FROM accounts AS a LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS l ON l.account_id = a.account_id AND date(l.posted_at) <= '2025-03-31' GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_number ORDER BY a.account_number

results.question: Compare each account with its March 31, 2025 statement when the statement ending balance is known. Show only mismatches after rounding both balances to two decimals. The book balance is opening_balance plus postings through March 31. Return account_number, book_balance, statement_balance, and the rounded book balance minus the rounded statement balance as difference. Round every monetary output to two decimals. Order by account_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH balances AS (
    SELECT a.account_number,
           ROUND(a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0), 2) AS book_balance,
           ROUND(s.ending_balance, 2) AS statement_balance
    FROM accounts AS a
    JOIN statements AS s ON s.account_number = a.account_number
    LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS l ON l.account_id = a.account_id
        AND DATE(l.posted_at) <= '2025-03-31'
    WHERE DATE(s.statement_date) = '2025-03-31'
      AND s.ending_balance IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY a.account_number, a.opening_balance, s.ending_balance
)
SELECT account_number, book_balance, statement_balance,
       ROUND(book_balance - statement_balance, 2) AS difference
FROM balances
WHERE book_balance <> statement_balance
ORDER BY account_number ASC
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM balances WHERE book_balance <> statement_balance)
results.classification_explanation: The available tables support calculating book balances through March 31, 2025, comparing them with known statement balances after rounding, and returning only mismatches in account-number order.
critique_issues: The follow-up explicitly asks to remove LIMIT, but the proposal retains the count-based LIMIT. Delete the entire LIMIT clause and end the query with ORDER BY account_number ASC.

results.question: Reconcile all local accounts with all imported statements dated March 31, 2025, retaining unmatched records on either side. Return account_number, book_balance, statement_balance, and the rounded book balance minus the rounded statement balance as difference. Book balance uses opening_balance plus postings through March 31. Round monetary outputs to two decimals; use NULL for a missing book balance, a missing or unknown statement balance, and any difference involving NULL. Order by account_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH postings AS (
  SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
  FROM ledger_entries
  WHERE date(posted_at) <= '2025-03-31'
  GROUP BY account_id
), books AS (
  SELECT a.account_number,
         ROUND(a.opening_balance + COALESCE(p.total_amount, 0), 2) AS book_balance
  FROM accounts AS a
  LEFT JOIN postings AS p ON p.account_id = a.account_id
), march_statements AS (
  SELECT account_number, ROUND(ending_balance, 2) AS statement_balance
  FROM statements
  WHERE date(statement_date) = '2025-03-31'
), reconciled AS (
  SELECT b.account_number, b.book_balance, s.statement_balance
  FROM books AS b
  LEFT JOIN march_statements AS s ON s.account_number = b.account_number
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.account_number, NULL AS book_balance, s.statement_balance
  FROM march_statements AS s
  LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.account_number = s.account_number
  WHERE b.account_number IS NULL
)
SELECT account_number, book_balance, statement_balance,
       ROUND(book_balance - statement_balance, 2) AS difference
FROM reconciled
ORDER BY account_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports this read-only reconciliation: it provides account opening balances, dated ledger postings, and dated statement balances, with account numbers available to match records and retain unmatched rows on either side.

results.question: Show every ledger entry with its account running balance, starting from the account opening balance. Within an account, apply entries in posted_at then entry_id order, including all dates. Return account_number, entry_id, posted_at, and running_balance rounded to two decimals. Order the output by account_number, posted_at, and entry_id.
results.sql: SELECT a.account_number, e.entry_id, e.posted_at, ROUND(a.opening_balance + SUM(e.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY e.account_id ORDER BY e.posted_at, e.entry_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_balance FROM ledger_entries AS e JOIN accounts AS a ON a.account_id = e.account_id ORDER BY a.account_number, e.posted_at, e.entry_id LIMIT -1

results.question: Find open accounts whose current balance is strictly below the average current balance of open accounts of the same kind. Current balance includes opening_balance and all postings; include accounts with no entries in the comparison. Compare unrounded balances. Return account_number, kind, and current_balance rounded to two decimals, ordered by account_number.
results.sql: WITH balances AS (SELECT a.account_number, a.kind, a.opening_balance + COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0) AS current_balance FROM accounts AS a LEFT JOIN ledger_entries AS l ON l.account_id = a.account_id WHERE a.status = 'open' GROUP BY a.account_id, a.account_number, a.kind, a.opening_balance), compared AS (SELECT account_number, kind, current_balance, AVG(current_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY kind) AS kind_average FROM balances) SELECT account_number, kind, ROUND(current_balance, 2) AS current_balance FROM compared WHERE current_balance < kind_average ORDER BY account_number LIMIT -1

results.question: Show paid invoice revenue by billing month, using the historical invoice amounts. Return month as YYYY-MM and revenue rounded to two decimals. Include only months with paid invoices and order chronologically.

results.question: For every customer, return customer_id, name, and total paid invoice amount across all their subscriptions, regardless of subscription status. Include customers with no paid invoices as zero, round the total to two decimals, and order by customer_id.
results.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(i.amount), 0), 2) AS total_paid_invoice_amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id LEFT JOIN invoices AS i ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id AND i.status = 'paid' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY c.customer_id;

results.question: For every plan, including plans with no active subscriptions, return plan_id, name, and active_subscription_count. Count status active only and order by plan_id.

results.question: Which subscriptions exceeded their plan included_units allowance during January 2025? Ignore subscription status. Return subscription_id, plan name, January units used, and units above the allowance. Include only positive overages and order by subscription_id.
results.sql: SELECT s.subscription_id, p.name AS plan_name, SUM(u.units) AS january_units_used, SUM(u.units) - p.included_units AS units_above_allowance FROM subscriptions AS s JOIN plans AS p ON p.plan_id = s.plan_id JOIN usage_events AS u ON u.subscription_id = s.subscription_id WHERE u.used_on >= '2025-01-01' AND u.used_on < '2025-02-01' GROUP BY s.subscription_id, p.name, p.included_units HAVING SUM(u.units) > p.included_units ORDER BY s.subscription_id

results.question: Find customers whose open invoices total at least 50 across all subscriptions. Return customer_id, name, open_invoice_count, and open_amount rounded to two decimals, ordered by customer_id. Exclude paid and void invoices.
results.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(*) AS open_invoice_count, ROUND(SUM(i.amount), 2) AS open_amount FROM customers AS c JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN invoices AS i ON i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id WHERE LOWER(i.status) NOT IN ('paid', 'void') GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name HAVING SUM(i.amount) >= 50 ORDER BY c.customer_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports joining customers to invoices through subscriptions, excluding paid and void invoices, and counting and summing the remaining invoices per customer. The results can be filtered to totals of at least 50, rounded to two decimal places for display, and ordered by customer_id.

results.question: Find subscriptions that have at least one usage event but have never had an invoice of any status. Return subscription_id, customer name, and plan name, ordered by subscription_id.
results.sql: SELECT s.subscription_id, c.name AS customer_name, p.name AS plan_name FROM subscriptions AS s JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id JOIN plans AS p ON p.plan_id = s.plan_id WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM usage_events AS u WHERE u.subscription_id = s.subscription_id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoices AS i WHERE i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id) ORDER BY s.subscription_id LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports finding subscriptions with at least one usage event and no invoices of any status, joining to customers and plans for their names, and ordering by subscription_id.
