results.question: Show each paid invoice together with the running paid revenue for its customer across all subscriptions. Apply invoices in billed_on then invoice_id order within each customer. Return customer_id, invoice_id, billed_on, and running_paid_amount rounded to two decimals. Order by customer_id, billed_on, and invoice_id.
results.sql: SELECT s.customer_id, i.invoice_id, i.billed_on, ROUND(SUM(i.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY s.customer_id ORDER BY i.billed_on, i.invoice_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_paid_amount FROM invoices AS i JOIN subscriptions AS s ON s.subscription_id = i.subscription_id WHERE i.status = 'paid' ORDER BY s.customer_id, i.billed_on, i.invoice_id LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports linking paid invoices to customers through subscriptions and calculating each customer's running paid total in billed_on and invoice_id order.

results.question: Which customers have at least one subscription and have at least one paid invoice for every subscription they have ever held, including cancelled or paused subscriptions? Return customer_id and name, ordered by customer_id.
results.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM subscriptions AS s
    WHERE s.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM subscriptions AS s
    WHERE s.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND NOT EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM invoices AS i
          WHERE i.subscription_id = s.subscription_id
            AND i.status = 'paid'
      )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id
LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The schema links customers to subscriptions and subscriptions to invoices. Invoice status identifies paid invoices, and all subscriptions can be checked without filtering out cancelled or paused ones.

results.question: Which high-priority tickets currently have status open? Return ticket_id, opened_at, and assigned_agent_id, retaining NULL for unassigned tickets. Sort by opened_at ascending, then ticket_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT ticket_id, opened_at, assigned_agent_id FROM tickets WHERE priority = 'high' AND status = 'open' ORDER BY opened_at ASC, ticket_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The tickets table contains all fields needed to filter for open, high-priority tickets, retain NULL for unassigned agents, and sort by opened_at and then ticket_id in ascending order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 so the query returns all open, high-priority tickets in the requested order, even when more than 100 match.

results.question: Count closed tickets for each priority that has at least one closed ticket. Return priority and closed_ticket_count, sorted by priority alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT priority, COUNT(*) AS closed_ticket_count FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed' GROUP BY priority ORDER BY priority COLLATE NOCASE ASC, priority ASC
results.classification_explanation: The tickets table contains status and priority, so closed tickets can be counted by priority and the results sorted alphabetically.

results.question: List the agents in team 1. Return agent_id and name, sorted by name alphabetically, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT agent_id, name FROM agents WHERE team_id = 1 ORDER BY name COLLATE NOCASE ASC, agent_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM agents WHERE team_id = 1);
results.classification_explanation: The agents table contains all the fields needed to filter by team 1 and return agent_id and name, sorted first by name and then by agent_id.

results.question: For every team, count its unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending, including tickets without an assigned agent. Include teams with zero unresolved tickets. Return team_id, team_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT t.team_id, t.name AS team_name, COUNT(k.ticket_id) AS unresolved_ticket_count FROM teams AS t LEFT JOIN tickets AS k ON k.team_id = t.team_id AND k.status IN ('open', 'pending') GROUP BY t.team_id, t.name ORDER BY t.team_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The teams and tickets tables can provide a count of open or pending tickets for every team, including unassigned tickets and teams with zero unresolved tickets, sorted by team ID.

results.question: For every customer, report the number of tickets of any status and the number of those tickets with no assigned agent. Include customers without tickets with both counts zero. Return customer_id, customer_name, ticket_count, and unassigned_ticket_count, sorted by customer_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name AS customer_name, COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS ticket_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN t.assigned_agent_id IS NULL THEN t.ticket_id END) AS unassigned_ticket_count FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN tickets AS t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The customers and tickets tables provide all the data needed to count total and unassigned tickets per customer, include customers with no tickets, and sort by customer_id.

results.question: For each ticket that has received an agent_reply event, find its earliest agent reply and the elapsed hours from opening to that reply. Ignore other event types. Return ticket_id, first_reply_at, and response_hours rounded to two decimal places, sorted by ticket_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH first_replies AS (
  SELECT ticket_id, created_at AS first_reply_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ticket_id ORDER BY julianday(created_at), event_id) AS reply_rank
  FROM ticket_events
  WHERE event_type = 'agent_reply'
)
SELECT t.ticket_id, r.first_reply_at,
       ROUND((julianday(r.first_reply_at) - julianday(t.opened_at)) * 24, 2) AS response_hours
FROM tickets AS t
JOIN first_replies AS r ON r.ticket_id = t.ticket_id AND r.reply_rank = 1
ORDER BY t.ticket_id ASC
LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The tickets and ticket_events tables provide the opening and event timestamps needed to find each ticket’s earliest agent_reply, calculate elapsed hours rounded to two decimal places, and sort by ticket_id.

results.question: Which agents are assigned at least two tickets with status closed? Return agent_id, agent_name, and closed_ticket_count. Sort by closed_ticket_count descending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, COUNT(*) AS closed_ticket_count FROM agents AS a JOIN tickets AS t ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id WHERE t.status = 'closed' GROUP BY a.agent_id, a.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY closed_ticket_count DESC, a.agent_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available tables support counting closed tickets by assigned agent, filtering to agents with at least two, and sorting by count descending and agent ID ascending.

results.question: Find the oldest unresolved ticket, meaning status open or pending, for each team that has one. Exclude tickets without a team. If a team has several tickets opened at the same time, choose the lowest ticket_id. Return team_id, team_name, ticket_id, and opened_at, sorted by team_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked_tickets AS (
  SELECT team_id, ticket_id, opened_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY opened_at ASC, ticket_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM tickets
  WHERE team_id IS NOT NULL AND status IN ('open', 'pending')
)
SELECT t.team_id, t.name AS team_name, r.ticket_id, r.opened_at
FROM ranked_tickets AS r
JOIN teams AS t ON t.team_id = r.team_id
WHERE r.rn = 1
ORDER BY t.team_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The tickets and teams tables contain all the fields needed to select the oldest open or pending ticket for each team, exclude unassigned teams’ tickets, and break timestamp ties by the lowest ticket_id.

results.question: Build a complete assignment roster showing every ticket of any status with its assigned agent, every unassigned ticket with NULL agent fields, and every agent with no tickets with NULL ticket fields. Return agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, and status. Sort by agent_id ascending with NULL agents last, then ticket_id ascending with NULL tickets last.
results.sql: SELECT agent_id, agent_name, ticket_id, status FROM (SELECT a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, t.ticket_id, t.status FROM tickets AS t LEFT JOIN agents AS a ON a.agent_id = t.assigned_agent_id UNION ALL SELECT a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, NULL AS ticket_id, NULL AS status FROM agents AS a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tickets AS t WHERE t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id)) AS roster ORDER BY agent_id ASC NULLS LAST, ticket_id ASC NULLS LAST LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The tickets and agents tables contain all the fields needed to include assigned tickets, unassigned tickets, and agents with no tickets, with NULLs for missing fields and the requested sort order.

results.question: For each team, identify all agents tied for the largest number of assigned unresolved tickets, meaning status open or pending. Exclude teams where every agent has zero assigned unresolved tickets. Count workload by the agent's team, and ignore unassigned tickets. Return team_id, team_name, agent_id, agent_name, and unresolved_ticket_count, sorted by team_id ascending, then agent_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH workloads AS (
    SELECT a.team_id, a.agent_id, a.name AS agent_name, COUNT(*) AS unresolved_ticket_count
    FROM agents AS a
    JOIN tickets AS t ON t.assigned_agent_id = a.agent_id
    WHERE t.status IN ('open', 'pending')
    GROUP BY a.team_id, a.agent_id, a.name
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY unresolved_ticket_count DESC) AS workload_rank
    FROM workloads
)
SELECT r.team_id, tm.name AS team_name, r.agent_id, r.agent_name, r.unresolved_ticket_count
FROM ranked AS r
JOIN teams AS tm ON tm.team_id = r.team_id
WHERE r.workload_rank = 1
ORDER BY r.team_id ASC, r.agent_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting assigned open or pending tickets by agent, grouping agents by their team, and returning every agent tied for the highest positive count in each team in the requested order.

results.question: Which rooms have a current nightly_rate of 160 or less? Return room_number, room_type, and nightly_rate. Sort by nightly_rate descending, then room_number ascending.
results.sql: SELECT room_number, room_type, nightly_rate FROM rooms WHERE nightly_rate <= 160 ORDER BY nightly_rate DESC, room_number ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The rooms table contains all requested columns and supports filtering for nightly rates of 160 or less and sorting as requested.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The user asked for all qualifying rooms, and the limit omits results if more than 100 rooms have a nightly_rate of 160 or less.

results.question: List confirmed bookings whose check-in date falls in February or March 2025. Return booking_id, check_in, and check_out, sorted by check_in ascending, then booking_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT booking_id, check_in, check_out FROM bookings WHERE status = 'confirmed' AND check_in >= '2025-02-01' AND check_in < '2025-04-01' ORDER BY check_in ASC, booking_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The bookings table has all the fields needed to filter confirmed bookings by check-in date, return the requested columns, and apply the requested sort order.
critique_issues: Remove `LIMIT 1000`. The user requested all matching bookings, so the limit would omit valid results if more than 1,000 bookings match.

results.question: For each checked_out booking, calculate its number of nights and booking value using booked_nightly_rate. Checkout day is excluded. Return booking_id, nights as an integer, and booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH stays AS (SELECT booking_id, CAST(julianday(date(check_out)) - julianday(date(check_in)) AS INTEGER) AS nights, booked_nightly_rate FROM bookings WHERE status = 'checked_out') SELECT booking_id, nights, ROUND(nights * booked_nightly_rate, 2) AS booking_value FROM stays ORDER BY booking_id ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The bookings table contains all the fields needed to filter checked-out bookings, count nights excluding the checkout day, and calculate and sort the requested results.

results.question: For every room, count checked_out bookings and their total nights, excluding checkout days. Include rooms without checked_out bookings with both totals zero. Return room_id, room_number, completed_booking_count, and total_nights as an integer, sorted by room_number ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.room_id, r.room_number, COUNT(b.booking_id) AS completed_booking_count, CAST(COALESCE(SUM(julianday(date(b.check_out)) - julianday(date(b.check_in))), 0) AS INTEGER) AS total_nights FROM rooms AS r LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.room_id = r.room_id AND b.status = 'checked_out' GROUP BY r.room_id, r.room_number ORDER BY r.room_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: The rooms and bookings tables provide all the data needed to count checked-out bookings and sum their nights from check-in up to, but not including, checkout. Rooms with no checked-out bookings can be included with both totals set to zero.

results.question: For every guest, total the booking value of their checked_out stays, using each booking's historical booked_nightly_rate multiplied by nights and excluding checkout days. Include guests with no checked_out stays with a zero total. Return guest_id, guest_name, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT g.guest_id, g.name AS guest_name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM((julianday(date(b.check_out)) - julianday(date(b.check_in))) * b.booked_nightly_rate), 0), 2) AS completed_booking_value FROM guests AS g LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.guest_id = g.guest_id AND b.status = 'checked_out' GROUP BY g.guest_id, g.name ORDER BY g.guest_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The guests and bookings tables contain all the data needed to calculate each guest’s checked-out booking value using historical rates and nights excluding checkout day, with a zero total for guests who have no checked-out stays.

results.question: How much net cash has been received for checked_out bookings in each room type? Sum signed payments so refunds reduce the total; exclude payments for other booking statuses and unallocated payments. Only include room types with at least one qualifying payment. Return room_type and net_payments rounded to two decimal places, sorted by room_type alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT r.room_type, ROUND(SUM(p.amount), 2) AS net_payments FROM payments AS p JOIN bookings AS b ON b.booking_id = p.booking_id JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = b.room_id WHERE b.status = 'checked_out' GROUP BY r.room_type ORDER BY r.room_type ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports linking payments to checked-out bookings and their rooms, excluding unallocated payments, and summing signed amounts by room type with the requested rounding and sorting.

results.question: Which checked_out bookings still have a positive outstanding balance? Balance equals nights excluding checkout day times booked_nightly_rate, minus all signed payments for that booking; treat no payments as zero. Return booking_id, guest_name, room_number, and outstanding_balance rounded to two decimal places, sorted by booking_id ascending. Test positivity before rounding.
results.sql: WITH payment_totals AS (SELECT booking_id, SUM(amount) AS total_paid FROM payments GROUP BY booking_id), balances AS (SELECT b.booking_id, g.name AS guest_name, r.room_number, (JULIANDAY(DATE(b.check_out)) - JULIANDAY(DATE(b.check_in))) * b.booked_nightly_rate - COALESCE(p.total_paid, 0) AS balance FROM bookings AS b JOIN guests AS g ON g.guest_id = b.guest_id JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = b.room_id LEFT JOIN payment_totals AS p ON p.booking_id = b.booking_id WHERE b.status = 'checked_out') SELECT booking_id, guest_name, room_number, ROUND(balance, 2) AS outstanding_balance FROM balances WHERE balance > 0 ORDER BY booking_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports joining bookings to guests and rooms, totaling signed payments per booking, and calculating the outstanding balance for checked-out bookings. The balance can be tested for positivity before rounding, with results sorted by booking ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The user explicitly asked to remove the cap, which omits qualifying bookings after the first 1,000. Keep ORDER BY booking_id ASC.

results.question: Find overlapping pairs of bookings for the same room, considering only confirmed and checked_out bookings. A booking occupies [check_in, check_out), so a checkout on another booking's check-in date is not an overlap. Return each pair once, with the lower booking_id first. Return room_number, first_booking_id, and second_booking_id, sorted by room_number, first_booking_id, then second_booking_id, all ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.room_number, a.booking_id AS first_booking_id, b.booking_id AS second_booking_id FROM bookings AS a JOIN bookings AS b ON a.room_id = b.room_id AND a.booking_id < b.booking_id AND a.check_in < b.check_out AND b.check_in < a.check_out JOIN rooms AS r ON r.room_id = a.room_id WHERE a.status IN ('confirmed', 'checked_out') AND b.status IN ('confirmed', 'checked_out') AND a.check_in < a.check_out AND b.check_in < b.check_out ORDER BY r.room_number ASC, first_booking_id ASC, second_booking_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema contains the booking statuses, dates, IDs, and room numbers needed to find and sort unique pairs of overlapping bookings without modifying any data.
critique_issues: Remove `LIMIT 1000`. The user requested every qualifying pair and explicitly asked to remove the cap; it omits valid pairs whenever more than 1,000 qualify.

results.question: Within each room type, find every room tied for the highest total booking value from checked_out stays. Use historical booked_nightly_rate times nights excluding checkout days, and assign zero to rooms without checked_out stays; if every room in a type has zero, return all of them. Return room_type, room_number, and completed_booking_value rounded to two decimal places. Rank using unrounded totals and sort by room_type alphabetically, then room_number ascending.
results.sql:
WITH room_totals AS (
  SELECT r.room_id, r.room_type, r.room_number,
         COALESCE(SUM(b.booked_nightly_rate * (julianday(date(b.check_out)) - julianday(date(b.check_in)))), 0) AS total_value
  FROM rooms AS r
  LEFT JOIN bookings AS b ON b.room_id = r.room_id AND b.status = 'checked_out'
  GROUP BY r.room_id, r.room_type, r.room_number
), ranked AS (
  SELECT room_type, room_number, total_value,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY room_type ORDER BY total_value DESC) AS value_rank
  FROM room_totals
)
SELECT room_type, room_number, ROUND(total_value, 2) AS completed_booking_value
FROM ranked
WHERE value_rank = 1
ORDER BY room_type ASC, room_number ASC
results.classification_explanation: The rooms and bookings tables contain the data needed to calculate completed booking values, include rooms with no checked-out stays, and return all rooms tied for the highest unrounded total within each room type.

results.question: Which guests have at least two checked_out stays and an average stay length strictly above the average length across all checked_out bookings? Compute nights excluding checkout day, and compare the unrounded averages; the overall average is per booking, not per guest. Return guest_id, guest_name, and average_nights rounded to two decimal places, sorted by guest_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH checked_out_stays AS (
  SELECT guest_id, julianday(date(check_out)) - julianday(date(check_in)) AS nights
  FROM bookings
  WHERE status = 'checked_out'
)
SELECT g.guest_id, g.name AS guest_name, ROUND(AVG(s.nights), 2) AS average_nights
FROM guests AS g
JOIN checked_out_stays AS s ON s.guest_id = g.guest_id
GROUP BY g.guest_id, g.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
   AND AVG(s.nights) > (SELECT AVG(nights) FROM checked_out_stays)
ORDER BY g.guest_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The bookings and guests tables contain the fields needed to filter checked-out stays, calculate nights from the check-in and check-out dates, and compare each qualifying guest’s unrounded average with the overall per-booking average.

results.question: List raw parts with a unit cost of at least 3. Return part_id, name, unit_cost, ordered by unit_cost descending and then part_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS part_id, name, unit_cost FROM parts WHERE kind = 'raw' AND unit_cost >= 3 ORDER BY unit_cost DESC, part_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The parts table supports filtering by kind and unit cost, returning id as part_id alongside name and unit_cost, and sorting as requested.
critique_issues: LIMIT 100 can omit qualifying raw parts and was explicitly requested to be removed. Remove LIMIT 100 and retain ORDER BY unit_cost DESC, part_id ASC.

results.question: List work orders whose status is planned or in_progress and whose due date is before 2025-02-15. Return work_order_id, part_id, quantity, due_date, ordered by due_date and then work_order_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS work_order_id, part_id, quantity, due_date FROM work_orders WHERE status IN ('planned', 'in_progress') AND due_date < '2025-02-15' ORDER BY due_date ASC, work_order_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The work_orders table contains all fields needed to filter by status and due date, return id as work_order_id, and sort by due_date and work_order_id in ascending order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 as explicitly requested. It can omit qualifying work orders; return all matches in the specified order.

results.question: Count work orders in each status that occurs. Return status, work_order_count, ordered by status alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS work_order_count FROM work_orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: The work_orders table has a status column, so the app can count work orders for each status that occurs and sort the results alphabetically by status.

results.question: For every part, report the total quantity on work orders with status planned or in_progress, using zero when there are none. Return part_id, name, active_quantity, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS part_id, p.name, COALESCE(SUM(w.quantity), 0) AS active_quantity FROM parts AS p LEFT JOIN work_orders AS w ON w.part_id = p.id AND w.status IN ('planned', 'in_progress') GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The parts and work_orders tables support summing planned and in-progress quantities for each part, including parts with no matching work orders as zero, and sorting by part ID.

results.question: Show completed work orders that finished after their due date. Return work_order_id, part_name, days_late as an integer calendar-day difference, quantity, ordered by work_order_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT w.id AS work_order_id, p.name AS part_name, CAST(julianday(date(w.completed_date)) - julianday(date(w.due_date)) AS INTEGER) AS days_late, w.quantity FROM work_orders AS w JOIN parts AS p ON p.id = w.part_id WHERE lower(w.status) = 'completed' AND date(w.completed_date) > date(w.due_date) ORDER BY w.id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports joining work orders to parts, identifying completed orders that finished after their due date, calculating integer calendar days late, and returning the requested fields in ascending work order ID order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 so the query returns every qualifying work order. Keep ORDER BY w.id ASC and update the explanation to reflect that the results are not capped.

results.question: For every part classified as assembly, count its distinct direct component parts and sum their direct quantities per one assembly unit. Use zero for both values when the assembly has no components. Return part_id, name, component_count, component_quantity, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS part_id, p.name, COUNT(DISTINCT b.component_part_id) AS component_count, COALESCE(SUM(b.quantity), 0) AS component_quantity FROM parts AS p LEFT JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = p.id WHERE p.kind = 'assembly' GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY part_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The parts and bom tables support counting distinct direct components and summing their quantities per assembly unit, including assemblies with no components.

results.question: For each part with at least one completed work order, show the total completed quantity and the number of distinct direct component parts in its bill of materials. The completed quantity must count each work order once; a part without direct components has a component count of zero. Return part_id, name, completed_quantity, component_count, ordered by part_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH completed AS (SELECT part_id, SUM(quantity) AS completed_quantity FROM work_orders WHERE completed_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY part_id), components AS (SELECT parent_part_id, COUNT(DISTINCT component_part_id) AS component_count FROM bom GROUP BY parent_part_id) SELECT p.id AS part_id, p.name, c.completed_quantity, COALESCE(b.component_count, 0) AS component_count FROM completed AS c JOIN parts AS p ON p.id = c.part_id LEFT JOIN components AS b ON b.parent_part_id = p.id ORDER BY part_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports summing completed work-order quantities once per order and separately counting distinct direct components, with zero for parts that have none.

results.question: For each completed work order, show the previous completed work order date for the same part and the integer calendar-day gap from it. Within each part, sequence completed orders by completed_date and then work_order_id ascending; the first order has NULL for the previous date and gap. Return part_id, work_order_id, completed_date, previous_completed_date, gap_days, ordered by part_id, completed_date, work_order_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH sequenced AS (SELECT part_id, id AS work_order_id, completed_date, LAG(completed_date) OVER (PARTITION BY part_id ORDER BY completed_date ASC, id ASC) AS previous_completed_date FROM work_orders WHERE completed_date IS NOT NULL) SELECT part_id, work_order_id, completed_date, previous_completed_date, CAST(JULIANDAY(DATE(completed_date)) - JULIANDAY(DATE(previous_completed_date)) AS INTEGER) AS gap_days FROM sequenced ORDER BY part_id ASC, completed_date ASC, work_order_id ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The work_orders table has the fields needed to identify completed orders, sequence them by part and completion date using id as work_order_id, and calculate the calendar-day gap from the preceding order.

results.question: Calculate the leaf-material requirements for building three Desk lamps (part_id 1). A leaf material is a descendant with no components of its own. Multiply quantities along each path, add quantities when a leaf appears along multiple paths, and price the resulting quantity at the leaf part's unit_cost. Return leaf_part_id, name, required_quantity, material_cost rounded to two decimal places, ordered by leaf_part_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH RECURSIVE expanded(part_id, required_quantity, path) AS (SELECT b.component_part_id, 3.0 * b.quantity, printf('/1/%d/', b.component_part_id) FROM bom AS b WHERE b.parent_part_id = 1 AND b.component_part_id <> 1 UNION ALL SELECT b.component_part_id, e.required_quantity * b.quantity, e.path || printf('%d/', b.component_part_id) FROM expanded AS e JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = e.part_id WHERE instr(e.path, printf('/%d/', b.component_part_id)) = 0), leaf_totals AS (SELECT e.part_id, SUM(e.required_quantity) AS required_quantity FROM expanded AS e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bom AS b WHERE b.parent_part_id = e.part_id) GROUP BY e.part_id) SELECT p.id AS leaf_part_id, p.name, l.required_quantity, ROUND(l.required_quantity * p.unit_cost, 2) AS material_cost FROM leaf_totals AS l JOIN parts AS p ON p.id = l.part_id ORDER BY leaf_part_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The bom and parts tables support a read-only calculation that traverses the bill of materials, sums each leaf's required quantity across all paths for three Desk lamps, and prices it using the leaf's unit cost.

results.question: For every ancestor part that has components, list all its direct and indirect descendant parts. For one unit of the ancestor, multiply quantities along each path and add the quantities across all paths to the same descendant. Exclude the ancestor itself. Return ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, required_quantity, ordered by ancestor_part_id and then descendant_part_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE paths(ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, path_quantity, visited) AS (
  SELECT parent_part_id, component_part_id, quantity,
         printf(',%lld,%lld,', parent_part_id, component_part_id)
  FROM bom
  WHERE parent_part_id <> component_part_id
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.ancestor_part_id, b.component_part_id,
         p.path_quantity * b.quantity,
         p.visited || printf('%lld,', b.component_part_id)
  FROM paths AS p
  JOIN bom AS b ON b.parent_part_id = p.descendant_part_id
  WHERE instr(p.visited, printf(',%lld,', b.component_part_id)) = 0
)
SELECT ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id, SUM(path_quantity) AS required_quantity
FROM paths
GROUP BY ancestor_part_id, descendant_part_id
ORDER BY ancestor_part_id ASC, descendant_part_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The bom table contains the parent–component relationships and quantities needed to trace direct and indirect descendants, multiply quantities along each path, and sum the results for each ancestor–descendant pair.

results.question: List products with a reorder level of at least five units. Return product_id, sku, name, reorder_level, ordered by reorder_level descending and then product_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS product_id, sku, name, reorder_level FROM products WHERE reorder_level >= 5 ORDER BY reorder_level DESC, product_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The products table contains all requested fields. Its id column can be returned as product_id, and the requested filtering and sorting are read-only.

results.question: List recorded movements with a negative quantity change during January 2025, regardless of reason. Return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, ordered by movement_date and then movement_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change FROM movements WHERE quantity_change < 0 AND movement_date >= '2025-01-01' AND movement_date < '2025-02-01' ORDER BY movement_date ASC, movement_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The movements table contains all requested fields, with id serving as movement_id. The January 2025 date filter, negative quantity filter, and requested ordering are supported without filtering by reason.

results.question: For each warehouse with at least one stock record, total its on-hand units across those records. Return warehouse_id, total_on_hand, ordered by warehouse_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT warehouse_id, SUM(on_hand) AS total_on_hand FROM stock GROUP BY warehouse_id ORDER BY warehouse_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The stock table contains warehouse_id and on_hand, so the request can be answered by summing on-hand units for each warehouse with stock records and sorting by warehouse_id.

results.question: For every warehouse, show its total on-hand units and number of stock records. Count a stock record even when on_hand is zero; report zero for both metrics when the warehouse has no records. Return warehouse_id, name, total_on_hand, stock_record_count, ordered by warehouse_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT w.id AS warehouse_id, w.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.on_hand), 0) AS total_on_hand, COUNT(s.product_id) AS stock_record_count FROM warehouses AS w LEFT JOIN stock AS s ON s.warehouse_id = w.id GROUP BY w.id, w.name ORDER BY w.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The warehouses and stock tables support both totals for every warehouse, including counting stock records with zero units and reporting zero for both metrics when a warehouse has no stock records.

results.question: List every warehouse/product combination, treating a missing stock record as zero units on hand. Return warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, ordered by warehouse_id and then product_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT w.id AS warehouse_id, p.id AS product_id, COALESCE(s.on_hand, 0) AS on_hand FROM warehouses AS w CROSS JOIN products AS p LEFT JOIN stock AS s ON s.warehouse_id = w.id AND s.product_id = p.id ORDER BY w.id ASC, p.id ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The warehouses and products tables provide every combination, and the stock table supplies on-hand quantities. Missing stock records can be treated as zero, and the results can be sorted by warehouse_id and then product_id.

results.question: For every product, show total current on-hand units across warehouses and the net sum of all quantity changes recorded during January 2025. Compute the two totals independently, using zero when a product has no stock or no January movements. Return product_id, name, total_on_hand, january_net_change, ordered by product_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH stock_totals AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(on_hand) AS total_on_hand FROM stock GROUP BY product_id), january_totals AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity_change) AS january_net_change FROM movements WHERE movement_date >= '2025-01-01' AND movement_date < '2025-02-01' GROUP BY product_id) SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.name, COALESCE(s.total_on_hand, 0) AS total_on_hand, COALESCE(j.january_net_change, 0) AS january_net_change FROM products AS p LEFT JOIN stock_totals AS s ON s.product_id = p.id LEFT JOIN january_totals AS j ON j.product_id = p.id ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The products, stock, and movements tables support this read-only request. The two totals can be computed independently for every product, with zero used when there are no matching stock rows or January 2025 movements.

results.question: Find existing stock records whose last count was before 2025-01-10 or whose last-count date is unknown. Return warehouse_id, warehouse_name, product_id, product_name, on_hand, last_counted, ordered by warehouse_id and then product_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT s.warehouse_id, w.name AS warehouse_name, s.product_id, p.name AS product_name, s.on_hand, s.last_counted FROM stock AS s JOIN warehouses AS w ON w.id = s.warehouse_id JOIN products AS p ON p.id = s.product_id WHERE s.last_counted < '2025-01-10' OR s.last_counted IS NULL ORDER BY s.warehouse_id ASC, s.product_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: This read-only request can be answered by filtering stock records for last-count dates before 2025-01-10 or missing dates, joining warehouses and products for their names, and sorting by warehouse ID and product ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. It can omit qualifying stock records, and the user requested that the cap be removed. Keep the ascending order by warehouse_id and product_id.

results.question: For every movement at warehouse 1, calculate the running net quantity change for that product, beginning at zero before its first recorded movement. Sequence each product's movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, running_net_change, ordered by product_id, movement_date, movement_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS movement_id, product_id, movement_date, quantity_change, SUM(quantity_change) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY movement_date ASC, id ASC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_net_change FROM movements WHERE warehouse_id = 1 ORDER BY product_id ASC, movement_date ASC, movement_id ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The movements table contains all the data needed to calculate the running net quantity change for each product at warehouse 1, using id as movement_id.

results.question: Rank existing stock records within each warehouse by on_hand descending. Equal quantities share a rank and the next different quantity receives the next consecutive rank with no gaps. Return warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, stock_rank, ordered by warehouse_id, stock_rank, product_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT warehouse_id, product_id, on_hand, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse_id ORDER BY on_hand DESC) AS stock_rank FROM stock ORDER BY warehouse_id ASC, stock_rank ASC, product_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The stock table contains all the required columns. A read-only calculation can assign ranks without gaps within each warehouse and return the results in the requested order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The request calls for all existing stock records, and the limit omits rows when stock contains more than 1,000 records. The dense ranking and ordering are correct.

results.question: For each movement whose reason is outbound, show the date of the immediately following recorded movement for the same warehouse and product, considering all reasons when finding that following movement. Sequence movements by movement_date and then movement_id ascending. Return movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, next_movement_date, gap_days as an integer calendar-day difference; use NULL for the final two columns if there is no later movement. Order by movement_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH sequenced AS (SELECT id AS movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, reason, LEAD(movement_date) OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse_id, product_id ORDER BY movement_date ASC, id ASC) AS next_movement_date FROM movements) SELECT movement_id, warehouse_id, product_id, movement_date, next_movement_date, CAST(julianday(date(next_movement_date)) - julianday(date(movement_date)) AS INTEGER) AS gap_days FROM sequenced WHERE reason = 'outbound' ORDER BY movement_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The movements table supports this read-only request. Its id column can be returned as movement_id and used to break ties when finding the next movement across all reasons. The movement dates support calculating the calendar-day gap.

results.question: List meters with no retirement date. Return meter_id, label, site_id, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS meter_id, label, site_id FROM meters WHERE retired_on IS NULL ORDER BY meter_id ASC LIMIT 1000;
results.classification_explanation: The meters table supports filtering for a missing retirement date and returning id as meter_id, label, and site_id in ascending meter ID order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The user requested all meters with no retirement date, and the cap omits matching rows when more than 1,000 meters qualify.

results.question: List nonmissing energy readings recorded on 2025-01-02 UTC. Return reading_id, meter_id, reading_at, reading_kwh, ordered by reading_at and then reading_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS reading_id, meter_id, reading_at, reading_kwh FROM readings WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL AND date(reading_at) = '2025-01-02' ORDER BY reading_at ASC, reading_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The readings table contains all the fields needed to list nonmissing readings for the specified UTC date. Its id column can be returned as reading_id, and the results can be sorted as requested.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The request asks for all matching readings, but the limit omits rows whenever more than 1,000 qualify.

results.question: For every meter represented in the readings table, count its nonmissing readings and show their minimum and maximum kWh values. A meter with only missing readings has count zero and NULL minimum and maximum. Return meter_id, valid_reading_count, minimum_kwh, maximum_kwh, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT meter_id, COUNT(reading_kwh) AS valid_reading_count, MIN(reading_kwh) AS minimum_kwh, MAX(reading_kwh) AS maximum_kwh FROM readings GROUP BY meter_id ORDER BY meter_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The readings table contains meter_id and reading_kwh, so the requested counts, minimums, and maximums can be computed per meter and sorted by meter_id. Meters with only NULL readings will have a count of zero and NULL minimum and maximum values.

results.question: For every site, report its total number of meters and the number with no retirement date. Sites without meters should have zero for both counts. Return site_id, name, meter_count, active_meter_count, ordered by site_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT s.id AS site_id, s.name, COUNT(m.id) AS meter_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN m.retired_on IS NULL THEN m.id END) AS active_meter_count FROM sites AS s LEFT JOIN meters AS m ON m.site_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name ORDER BY site_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The sites and meters tables support counting all meters and meters with no retirement date for every site, including zero counts for sites without meters, ordered by site ID.

results.question: List meters that have no nonmissing energy reading, including meters with no reading records and meters whose records are all missing. Return meter_id, label, site_name, ordered by meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT m.id AS meter_id, m.label, s.name AS site_name
FROM meters AS m
JOIN sites AS s ON s.id = m.site_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM readings AS r
    WHERE r.meter_id = m.id AND r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
)
ORDER BY m.id ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing meters with no non-NULL energy readings, including meters with no reading records, along with their labels and site names, ordered by meter ID.
critique_issues: Remove `LIMIT 1000`: the user requested all qualifying meters, and the limit omits any matches after the first 1,000. Keep `ORDER BY m.id ASC`.

results.question: For every meter with at least two nonmissing readings, report the minimum reading, maximum reading, and observed kWh range defined as maximum minus minimum. Return site_id, meter_id, label, minimum_kwh, maximum_kwh, observed_range_kwh rounded to two decimal places, ordered by site_id and then meter_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT m.site_id, m.id AS meter_id, m.label, MIN(r.reading_kwh) AS minimum_kwh, MAX(r.reading_kwh) AS maximum_kwh, ROUND(MAX(r.reading_kwh) - MIN(r.reading_kwh), 2) AS observed_range_kwh FROM meters AS m JOIN readings AS r ON r.meter_id = m.id GROUP BY m.site_id, m.id, m.label HAVING COUNT(r.reading_kwh) >= 2 ORDER BY m.site_id ASC, m.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The meters and readings tables provide all the data needed to filter for meters with at least two nonmissing readings and report their minimum, maximum, and observed kWh range in the requested order.

results.question: For each nonmissing reading with a matching regional tariff, show the tariff effective on that reading's UTC calendar date. The valid_from date is inclusive, valid_to is exclusive, and NULL valid_to has no upper limit. Return reading_id, meter_id, reading_date formatted YYYY-MM-DD, price_per_kwh, ordered by reading_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.id AS reading_id, r.meter_id, date(r.reading_at) AS reading_date, t.price_per_kwh FROM readings AS r JOIN meters AS m ON m.id = r.meter_id JOIN sites AS s ON s.id = m.site_id JOIN tariffs AS t ON t.region = s.region AND date(r.reading_at) >= t.valid_from AND (t.valid_to IS NULL OR date(r.reading_at) < t.valid_to) WHERE r.reading_kwh IS NOT NULL ORDER BY r.id ASC, t.id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports matching nonmissing readings to tariffs through each meter’s site region, using the reading’s UTC calendar date and the specified tariff validity bounds.
critique_issues: Remove `LIMIT 1000` entirely. It truncates the result when more than 1,000 rows match, but the user requested every qualifying reading and explicitly asked for no limit.

results.question: Within each meter, sequence nonmissing readings by reading_at and then reading_id ascending and form intervals between consecutive nonmissing readings. Omit the first reading. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, elapsed_hours rounded to two decimals, consumed_kwh as current minus previous reading rounded to two decimals, average_kw as consumed_kwh divided by elapsed hours rounded to three decimals. Use NULL average_kw for zero elapsed hours. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH sequenced AS (
  SELECT meter_id, id AS reading_id, reading_at, reading_kwh,
         LAG(reading_at) OVER w AS previous_at,
         LAG(reading_kwh) OVER w AS previous_kwh
  FROM readings
  WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY reading_at, id)
), intervals AS (
  SELECT meter_id, reading_id, reading_at,
         (julianday(reading_at) - julianday(previous_at)) * 24.0 AS hours,
         reading_kwh - previous_kwh AS kwh
  FROM sequenced
  WHERE previous_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT meter_id, reading_id, reading_at,
       ROUND(hours, 2) AS elapsed_hours,
       ROUND(kwh, 2) AS consumed_kwh,
       ROUND(kwh / NULLIF(hours, 0.0), 3) AS average_kw
FROM intervals
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The readings table contains all the data needed to sequence nonmissing readings within each meter and compute the requested interval metrics. The requested reading_id corresponds to readings.id.
critique_issues: The query retains LIMIT 1000, which can omit qualifying intervals and directly contradicts the follow-up request. Delete the LIMIT clause and keep ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id.

results.question: For each meter, derive consumed kWh between consecutive nonmissing readings, sequencing by reading_at and then reading_id ascending. Omit the first reading because it has no preceding interval. For every remaining interval, calculate the arithmetic mean of its consumption and up to two preceding interval consumptions for that meter; divide by the number of available intervals, without time weighting. Return meter_id, reading_id, reading_at, consumed_kwh, trailing_mean_kwh, with both kWh outputs rounded to two decimals. Order by meter_id, reading_at, reading_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH sequenced AS (
  SELECT meter_id, id AS reading_id, reading_at, reading_kwh,
         LAG(reading_kwh) OVER (
           PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY reading_at, id
         ) AS previous_kwh
  FROM readings
  WHERE reading_kwh IS NOT NULL
), intervals AS (
  SELECT meter_id, reading_id, reading_at,
         reading_kwh - previous_kwh AS consumed_kwh
  FROM sequenced
  WHERE previous_kwh IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT meter_id, reading_id, reading_at,
       ROUND(consumed_kwh, 2) AS consumed_kwh,
       ROUND(AVG(consumed_kwh) OVER (
         PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY reading_at, reading_id
         ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 2) AS trailing_mean_kwh
FROM intervals
ORDER BY meter_id, reading_at, reading_id
LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The readings table contains all the required data, with id serving as reading_id. The requested consumption differences and trailing averages can be calculated without modifying the database.

results.question: Rank meters having at least two nonmissing readings by observed consumption, defined as maximum minus minimum reading, in descending order. Equal unrounded consumption values share a rank, and the next rank skips the number of tied positions. Return meter_id, label, observed_consumption_kwh rounded to two decimals, consumption_rank, ordered by consumption_rank and then meter_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH consumption AS (
  SELECT meter_id, MAX(reading_kwh) - MIN(reading_kwh) AS unrounded_consumption
  FROM readings
  GROUP BY meter_id
  HAVING COUNT(reading_kwh) >= 2
), ranked AS (
  SELECT meter_id, unrounded_consumption,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY unrounded_consumption DESC) AS consumption_rank
  FROM consumption
)
SELECT r.meter_id, m.label,
       ROUND(r.unrounded_consumption, 2) AS observed_consumption_kwh,
       r.consumption_rank
FROM ranked AS r
JOIN meters AS m ON m.id = r.meter_id
ORDER BY r.consumption_rank ASC, r.meter_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The meters and readings tables contain all the data needed to filter for meters with at least two nonmissing readings, calculate observed consumption, rank by unrounded values with gaps after ties, and return the requested columns in order.

results.question: List active routes. Return route_id, name, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS route_id, name FROM routes WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY route_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The routes table contains the active flag, ID, and name. The ID can be returned as route_id and sorted in ascending order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 as explicitly requested; it can omit active routes. Keep ORDER BY route_id ASC.

results.question: List stops in the Central zone. Return stop_id, name, ordered by stop_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS stop_id, name FROM stops WHERE zone = 'Central' ORDER BY stop_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stops WHERE zone = 'Central');
results.classification_explanation: The stops table can be filtered to the Central zone and return each stop's id as stop_id and its name, sorted by stop_id ascending.

results.question: Count trips in each status occurring from service date 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-03, both dates inclusive. Return status, trip_count, ordered by status alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS trip_count FROM trips WHERE service_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-03' GROUP BY status ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: The trips table contains service_date and status, so trips can be counted by status for the inclusive date range and sorted alphabetically by status.

results.question: For every route, report its number of listed stop positions and highest stop sequence. A route with no listed stops has stop_count zero and last_stop_sequence NULL. Return route_id, name, stop_count, last_stop_sequence, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.id AS route_id, r.name, COUNT(rs.stop_sequence) AS stop_count, MAX(rs.stop_sequence) AS last_stop_sequence FROM routes AS r LEFT JOIN route_stops AS rs ON rs.route_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id, r.name ORDER BY r.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The routes and route_stops tables provide all the data needed to count listed stop positions and find the highest stop sequence for every route, including routes with no listed stops.

results.question: For each completed trip with an actual departure recorded, calculate departure delay in minutes as actual departure minus scheduled departure, allowing negative values for early departures. Return trip_id, route_name, delay_minutes rounded to two decimals, ordered by trip_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT t.id AS trip_id, r.name AS route_name, ROUND((julianday(t.actual_departure) - julianday(t.scheduled_departure)) * 1440.0, 2) AS delay_minutes FROM trips AS t JOIN routes AS r ON r.id = t.route_id WHERE t.status = 'completed' AND t.actual_departure IS NOT NULL ORDER BY t.id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The trips table provides the trip ID, status, and departure times needed to calculate the signed delay. Joining it to routes provides the route name.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. The user asked for every qualifying trip, but the query omits all qualifying trips after the first 1,000. Suggesting pagination does not make the submitted query return all rows.

results.question: For every route, report its number of completed trips and number of listed stop positions, counting each trip and each position once. Use zero for missing counts. Return route_id, name, completed_trip_count, stop_count, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH completed_trips AS (SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS trip_count FROM trips WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY route_id), listed_stops AS (SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS position_count FROM route_stops GROUP BY route_id) SELECT r.id AS route_id, r.name, COALESCE(t.trip_count, 0) AS completed_trip_count, COALESCE(s.position_count, 0) AS stop_count FROM routes AS r LEFT JOIN completed_trips AS t ON t.route_id = r.id LEFT JOIN listed_stops AS s ON s.route_id = r.id ORDER BY r.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting completed trips by status and listed stop positions by sequence for each route. The counts can be calculated separately to avoid double-counting, with zeros for missing counts and results ordered by route ID.

results.question: Show every pair of adjacent stop positions on the same route, where the destination sequence is exactly one greater than the origin sequence. Return route_id, origin_sequence, origin_stop, destination_stop, segment_minutes using the destination position's travel_minutes_from_previous. Order by route_id and then origin_sequence ascending.
results.sql: SELECT o.route_id, o.stop_sequence AS origin_sequence, os.name AS origin_stop, ds.name AS destination_stop, d.travel_minutes_from_previous AS segment_minutes FROM route_stops AS o JOIN route_stops AS d ON d.route_id = o.route_id AND d.stop_sequence = o.stop_sequence + 1 JOIN stops AS os ON os.id = o.stop_id JOIN stops AS ds ON ds.id = d.stop_id ORDER BY o.route_id ASC, o.stop_sequence ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM route_stops)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports a read-only query that pairs consecutive stop positions on each route, looks up both stop names, and uses the destination position’s travel time as the segment duration.

results.question: For every listed route stop, calculate planned elapsed travel minutes from the first stop through that position, treating a missing segment time as zero. Return route_id, stop_sequence, stop_name, elapsed_minutes, ordered by route_id and then stop_sequence ascending.
results.sql: WITH ordered_stops AS (SELECT route_id, stop_id, stop_sequence, travel_minutes_from_previous, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY stop_sequence) AS stop_position FROM route_stops) SELECT rs.route_id, rs.stop_sequence, s.name AS stop_name, SUM(CASE WHEN rs.stop_position = 1 THEN 0 ELSE COALESCE(rs.travel_minutes_from_previous, 0) END) OVER (PARTITION BY rs.route_id ORDER BY rs.stop_sequence ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS elapsed_minutes FROM ordered_stops AS rs LEFT JOIN stops AS s ON s.id = rs.stop_id ORDER BY rs.route_id ASC, rs.stop_sequence ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM route_stops)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports joining route stops to stop names and calculating a running total of planned segment times for each route in stop order, treating missing times as zero.

results.question: For every route with a completed trip, return exactly its latest completed trip, choosing by service_date descending, then scheduled_departure descending, then trip_id descending. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure, ordered by route_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH ranked_trips AS (SELECT route_id, id AS trip_id, service_date, actual_departure, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY service_date DESC, scheduled_departure DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM trips WHERE status = 'completed') SELECT route_id, trip_id, service_date, actual_departure FROM ranked_trips WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY route_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The trips table contains all the fields needed to select the latest completed trip for each route using the requested tie-breakers. The trips.id column can be returned as trip_id.

results.question: Within each route, divide completed trips in chronological order into two batches of sizes differing by at most one. Order trips by service_date, scheduled_departure, and trip_id ascending; batch 1 contains the earlier trips and gets the extra trip when the count is odd. A route with one completed trip uses only batch 1. Return route_id, trip_id, service_date, batch_number, ordered by route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT route_id, id AS trip_id, service_date, scheduled_departure,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY route_id ORDER BY service_date, scheduled_departure, id) AS trip_position,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY route_id) AS trip_count
  FROM trips
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT route_id, trip_id, service_date,
       CASE WHEN trip_position <= (trip_count + 1) / 2 THEN 1 ELSE 2 END AS batch_number
FROM ranked
ORDER BY route_id, service_date, scheduled_departure, trip_id
LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The trips table contains all the fields needed to filter completed trips, split each route’s trips into chronological batches with batch 1 receiving any extra trip, and return the requested columns in order. The requested trip_id corresponds to trips.id.

results.question: List visitors whose known signup date is at least 2025-01-02 and before 2025-01-05. Return visitor_id, country, signup_date, ordered by signup_date and then visitor_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS visitor_id, country, signup_date FROM visitors WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-02' AND signup_date < '2025-01-05' ORDER BY signup_date ASC, visitor_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The visitors table supports this read-only request. Its id column can be returned as visitor_id, and its signup_date column supports the requested date filter and ordering.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The user requested all matching visitors, so the limit would omit qualifying rows if more than 100 visitors match.

results.question: List purchase events with revenue of at least 20. Return event_id, session_id, event_at, revenue, ordered by event_at and then event_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS event_id, session_id, event_at, revenue FROM events WHERE event_type = 'purchase' AND revenue >= 20 ORDER BY event_at ASC, event_id ASC LIMIT 100
results.classification_explanation: The events table supports filtering purchase events to revenue of at least 20 and sorting by event_at and then id, which can be returned as event_id.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 as requested. It truncates the results when more than 100 purchase events have revenue of at least 20.

results.question: Count sessions for each device type that occurs. Return device, session_count, ordered by device alphabetically.
results.sql: SELECT device, COUNT(*) AS session_count FROM sessions GROUP BY device ORDER BY device ASC
results.classification_explanation: The sessions table contains the device for each session, so the app can count sessions for each device that appears and list the results alphabetically by device.

results.question: For every visitor, count their sessions, including visitors with no sessions as zero. Return visitor_id, country, session_count, ordered by visitor_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT v.id AS visitor_id, v.country, COUNT(s.id) AS session_count FROM visitors AS v LEFT JOIN sessions AS s ON s.visitor_id = v.id GROUP BY v.id, v.country ORDER BY v.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The visitors and sessions tables can be used to count sessions for every visitor, including zero for visitors with no sessions, and return the requested fields in ascending visitor ID order.

results.question: For each session referrer, using direct for NULL, report the number of sessions, the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event, and total purchase-event revenue. Count each session once even when it contains multiple events, retain sessions without events, and use zero revenue when there are no purchases. Return referrer, session_count, converting_session_count, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, ordered by referrer alphabetically.
results.sql:
WITH purchases AS (
    SELECT session_id, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
    FROM events
    WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT COALESCE(s.referrer, 'direct') AS referrer,
       COUNT(*) AS session_count,
       COUNT(p.session_id) AS converting_session_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(p.revenue), 0), 2) AS purchase_revenue
FROM sessions AS s
LEFT JOIN purchases AS p ON p.session_id = s.id
GROUP BY COALESCE(s.referrer, 'direct')
ORDER BY referrer;
results.classification_explanation: The sessions and events tables provide all the data needed to count sessions and converting sessions by referrer and sum purchase revenue, including sessions without events.

results.question: For every session, count its events and calculate the span in whole seconds from its earliest to latest event. Return NULL span for a session with no events and zero for one event. Return session_id, event_count, event_span_seconds, ordered by session_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT s.id AS session_id, COUNT(e.id) AS event_count, CASE COUNT(e.id) WHEN 0 THEN NULL WHEN 1 THEN 0 ELSE CAST(ROUND((MAX(julianday(e.event_at)) - MIN(julianday(e.event_at))) * 86400, 3) AS INTEGER) END AS event_span_seconds FROM sessions AS s LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.session_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id ORDER BY s.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The sessions and events tables provide the session IDs and event timestamps needed to count events and calculate each session’s span in whole seconds, including sessions with no events or just one event.

results.question: For each visitor country with at least one session, calculate its session conversion rate: 100 times the number of sessions containing at least one purchase event divided by all sessions from that country. A session with multiple purchase events counts once. Return country, session_count, converting_session_count, conversion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by country alphabetically.
results.sql:
WITH session_flags AS (
  SELECT v.country,
         EXISTS (
           SELECT 1
           FROM events AS e
           WHERE e.session_id = s.id AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
         ) AS converted
  FROM sessions AS s
  JOIN visitors AS v ON v.id = s.visitor_id
)
SELECT country,
       COUNT(*) AS session_count,
       SUM(converted) AS converting_session_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(converted) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_percent
FROM session_flags
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports grouping sessions by visitor country and counting each session with at least one purchase event once. The requested counts, rounded conversion percentages, and alphabetical ordering can all be produced with a read-only query.

results.question: For every session, show the previous session start for the same visitor and the elapsed hours since it. Sequence each visitor's sessions by started_at and then session_id ascending, including ties in start time. The first session has NULL for the previous start and gap. Return visitor_id, session_id, started_at, previous_started_at, gap_hours rounded to two decimals, ordered by visitor_id, started_at, session_id ascending.
results.sql: WITH sequenced AS (SELECT visitor_id, id AS session_id, started_at, LAG(started_at) OVER (PARTITION BY visitor_id ORDER BY started_at ASC, id ASC) AS previous_started_at FROM sessions) SELECT visitor_id, session_id, started_at, previous_started_at, ROUND((julianday(started_at) - julianday(previous_started_at)) * 24.0, 2) AS gap_hours FROM sequenced ORDER BY visitor_id ASC, started_at ASC, session_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions)
results.classification_explanation: The sessions table contains the visitor ID, session ID, and start time needed to find each visitor’s previous session and calculate the elapsed hours. The session ID breaks ties in start time, and the first session for each visitor can return NULL for both the previous start and the gap.

results.question: For each UTC calendar day from 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-04 inclusive, show purchase-event revenue, cumulative revenue since 2025-01-01, and the arithmetic mean of that day's and the preceding calendar day's revenue within this reporting period. Include days without purchases as zero; the first day's mean uses only that day. Return day formatted YYYY-MM-DD, purchase_revenue, cumulative_revenue, two_day_mean_revenue, with all revenue values rounded to two decimals, ordered by day ascending.
results.sql: WITH days(day) AS (VALUES ('2025-01-01'), ('2025-01-02'), ('2025-01-03'), ('2025-01-04')), daily AS (SELECT d.day, COALESCE(SUM(e.revenue), 0.0) AS revenue FROM days AS d LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.event_type = 'purchase' AND date(e.event_at) = d.day GROUP BY d.day) SELECT day, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS purchase_revenue, ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS cumulative_revenue, ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS two_day_mean_revenue FROM daily ORDER BY day ASC
results.classification_explanation: The events table provides the timestamps, event types, and revenue needed to calculate daily purchase revenue, cumulative revenue, and the two-day mean. The fixed date range allows days without purchases to be included as zero.

results.question: For every visitor, total their purchase-event revenue, using zero for visitors without purchases or sessions. Rank visitors by unrounded revenue ascending with equal revenues sharing the first position occupied by that tie group, and calculate percentile_fraction as (rank minus one) divided by (number of visitors minus one); use zero if there is only one visitor. Return visitor_id, country, purchase_revenue rounded to two decimals, percentile_fraction rounded to four decimals, ordered by unrounded purchase revenue and then visitor_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH visitor_totals AS (
  SELECT v.id AS visitor_id, v.country,
         COALESCE(SUM(e.revenue), 0.0) AS total_revenue
  FROM visitors AS v
  LEFT JOIN sessions AS s ON s.visitor_id = v.id
  LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.session_id = s.id AND e.event_type = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY v.id, v.country
), ranked AS (
  SELECT visitor_id, country, total_revenue,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue ASC) AS revenue_rank,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS visitor_count
  FROM visitor_totals
)
SELECT visitor_id, country,
       ROUND(total_revenue, 2) AS purchase_revenue,
       ROUND(CASE WHEN visitor_count = 1 THEN 0.0
                  ELSE 1.0 * (revenue_rank - 1) / (visitor_count - 1)
             END, 4) AS percentile_fraction
FROM ranked
ORDER BY total_revenue ASC, visitor_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available tables can be joined to total purchase revenue for every visitor, including those without sessions or purchases, and calculate the requested tie-aware ranks, percentile fractions, rounding, and ordering.

results.question: List open listings without a reserve price. Return listing_id and title, ordered by listing_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS listing_id, title FROM listings WHERE status = 'open' AND reserve_price IS NULL ORDER BY listing_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The listings table has the status and reserve price needed to filter the results, and its id can be returned as listing_id alongside the title and used for sorting.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The user requested all open listings without a reserve price, ordered by listing_id. The cap would omit qualifying rows after the first 100.

results.question: Count listings in each status. Return status and listing_count, ordered by status.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS listing_count FROM listings GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;
results.classification_explanation: The listings table contains a status column, so listings can be counted by status and the results sorted by status in a read-only query.

results.question: List bids of at least 100. Return bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, and amount, ordered by amount descending and then bid_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, amount FROM bids WHERE amount >= 100 ORDER BY amount DESC, bid_id ASC LIMIT 100
results.classification_explanation: The bids table contains all requested fields, with id returned as bid_id. The amount filter and both sort keys are supported by a read-only query.
critique_issues: The query still uses LIMIT 100, which omits qualifying bids when more than 100 exist. Remove LIMIT 100 to return every bid with amount >= 100 in the requested order.

results.question: For every listing, show listing_id, title, bid_count, and highest_bid. Count actual bids; highest_bid must be NULL for a listing without bids. Order by listing_id.
results.sql: SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title, COUNT(b.id) AS bid_count, MAX(b.amount) AS highest_bid FROM listings AS l LEFT JOIN bids AS b ON b.listing_id = l.id GROUP BY l.id, l.title ORDER BY l.id
results.classification_explanation: The listings and bids tables contain all the data needed to show every listing in listing ID order, count its actual bids, and return NULL for the highest bid when there are no bids.

results.question: Return the distinct user_id values of users who have listed an item or placed a bid, considering all listing statuses. Order by user_id.
results.sql: SELECT seller_id AS user_id FROM listings UNION SELECT bidder_id AS user_id FROM bids ORDER BY user_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports returning distinct user IDs from listings.seller_id and bids.bidder_id, ordered by user ID, without filtering by listing status.

results.question: Which users have both listed an item and placed a bid, considering all listing statuses? Return distinct user_id values ascending.
results.sql: SELECT u.id AS user_id FROM users AS u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM listings AS l WHERE l.seller_id = u.id) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bids AS b WHERE b.bidder_id = u.id) ORDER BY user_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports finding users who appear as both sellers and bidders, without filtering by listing status, and returning their distinct IDs in ascending order.

results.question: Find open listings whose reserve has been met by at least one bid. A listing with no reserve qualifies only if it has at least one bid. Return listing_id and title, ordered by listing_id.
results.sql: SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title FROM listings AS l WHERE l.status = 'open' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bids AS b WHERE b.listing_id = l.id AND (l.reserve_price IS NULL OR b.amount >= l.reserve_price)) ORDER BY l.id LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports identifying open listings with at least one bid that meets or exceeds the reserve, or any bid if the reserve is null, and returning their IDs and titles ordered by listing ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 so the query returns all qualifying listings, not just the first 100. Keep ORDER BY l.id.

results.question: Find sellers who have at least one open listing and for whom every open listing has received a bid. Return seller_id and name, ordered by seller_id. Closed listings do not affect eligibility.
results.sql: SELECT u.id AS seller_id, u.name FROM users AS u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM listings AS l WHERE l.seller_id = u.id AND l.status = 'open') AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM listings AS l WHERE l.seller_id = u.id AND l.status = 'open' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bids AS b WHERE b.listing_id = l.id)) ORDER BY seller_id
results.classification_explanation: The listings, bids, and users tables provide all the data needed to identify sellers who have at least one open listing and whose open listings all have bids, then return their IDs and names in seller ID order.

results.question: For every listing that has bids, return every bid tied for its highest amount. Return listing_id, title, bidder_id, bid_id, and amount, ordered by listing_id then bid_id. Include open and closed listings.
results.sql: WITH highest_bids AS (SELECT listing_id, MAX(amount) AS max_amount FROM bids GROUP BY listing_id) SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title, b.bidder_id, b.id AS bid_id, b.amount FROM highest_bids AS h JOIN bids AS b ON b.listing_id = h.listing_id AND b.amount = h.max_amount JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id ORDER BY l.id, b.id
results.classification_explanation: The bids and listings tables contain all the requested fields and support returning every bid tied for the highest amount on each listing, regardless of listing status, ordered by listing_id and then bid_id.

results.question: Find unordered pairs of bidders who have both bid on at least two distinct open listings. Return smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id, and shared_listing_count, ordered by those two IDs. Multiple bids by one bidder on one listing count only once.
results.sql:
WITH open_listing_bidders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT b.listing_id, b.bidder_id
  FROM bids AS b
  JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id
  WHERE l.status = 'open'
)
SELECT a.bidder_id AS smaller_bidder_id,
       b.bidder_id AS larger_bidder_id,
       COUNT(*) AS shared_listing_count
FROM open_listing_bidders AS a
JOIN open_listing_bidders AS b
  ON a.listing_id = b.listing_id AND a.bidder_id < b.bidder_id
GROUP BY a.bidder_id, b.bidder_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id;
results.classification_explanation: The bids and listings tables contain the information needed to count distinct shared open listings for each unordered bidder pair, without counting repeat bids.

results.question: List mandatory questions. Return question_id and prompt, ordered by question_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS question_id, prompt FROM questions WHERE required = 1 ORDER BY question_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: Mandatory questions are identified by the required field. Their IDs can be returned as question_id alongside their prompts and sorted by ID.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 as explicitly requested. It omits mandatory questions when more than 100 exist. Keep ORDER BY question_id ASC.

results.question: List responses with a score of at least 4. Return response_id, participant_id, question_id, and score, ordered by response_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS response_id, participant_id, question_id, score FROM responses WHERE score >= 4 ORDER BY response_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The responses table has all the requested fields. Its id can be returned as response_id, and the results can be filtered to scores of at least 4 and ordered by response_id.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The request is to return all responses with score >= 4, ordered by response_id; the cap omits qualifying rows when there are more than 100.

results.question: Count registered participants by group, displaying NULL group names as Unassigned. Return group_name and participant_count, ordered by the displayed group_name.
results.sql: SELECT COALESCE(group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name, COUNT(*) AS participant_count FROM participants GROUP BY COALESCE(group_name, 'Unassigned') ORDER BY group_name
results.classification_explanation: The participants table supports counting participants by group, displaying NULL group names as Unassigned, and sorting by the displayed group name.

results.question: For every question, return question_id, prompt, answered_count, and average_score rounded to two decimals. Ignore NULL scores in both statistics; average_score must be NULL when nobody answered. Order by question_id.
results.sql: SELECT q.id AS question_id, q.prompt, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count, ROUND(AVG(r.score), 2) AS average_score FROM questions AS q LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.question_id = q.id GROUP BY q.id, q.prompt ORDER BY q.id;
results.classification_explanation: The questions and responses tables support a read-only summary for every question, counting only non-NULL scores and averaging those scores to two decimal places. Questions with no non-NULL scores can be included with a count of zero and a NULL average, ordered by question ID.

results.question: Which participants answered question 1 but did not answer question 2? A NULL score does not count as an answer. Return participant_id values ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.participant_id FROM responses AS r WHERE r.question_id = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM responses AS r2 WHERE r2.participant_id = r.participant_id AND r2.question_id = 2 AND r2.score IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY r.participant_id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The responses table can identify participants with a non-NULL score for question 1 and no non-NULL score for question 2, and return their participant IDs in ascending order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 because it can omit qualifying participant IDs. Keep ORDER BY r.participant_id ASC and update the explanation to state that all qualifying IDs are returned in ascending order.

results.question: Combine the participant IDs of all non-NULL responses to question 1 with those of all non-NULL responses to question 2. Keep duplicates so a participant who answered both appears twice. Return only participant_id, sorted ascending.
results.sql: SELECT participant_id FROM responses WHERE question_id IN (1, 2) AND score IS NOT NULL ORDER BY participant_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM responses WHERE question_id IN (1, 2) AND score IS NOT NULL)
results.classification_explanation: The responses table contains the fields needed to return participant IDs for questions 1 and 2 with non-NULL scores, preserve duplicates, and sort the IDs in ascending order.

results.question: For every registered participant, return participant_id, name, and answered_count (the number of questions answered with a non-NULL score), in that order. Include participants with zero answers. Sort by participant_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count FROM participants AS p LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.participant_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available tables support counting responses with non-NULL scores for each participant, including those with zero qualifying responses, and sorting by participant ID.

results.question: Which participants answered every mandatory question with a non-NULL score? Return participant_id and name, ordered by participant_id. Optional questions do not affect eligibility. If there are no mandatory questions, every participant qualifies.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name FROM participants AS p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM questions AS q WHERE q.required = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM responses AS r WHERE r.participant_id = p.id AND r.question_id = q.id AND r.score IS NOT NULL)) ORDER BY p.id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports checking whether each participant has a non-NULL score for every required question and returning eligible participants’ IDs and names in ID order. If there are no required questions, all participants qualify.
