critique_issues: Remove `LIMIT 100`. It omits qualifying listings when more than 100 match. Keep `ORDER BY listing_id ASC` so all matches are returned in the requested order.

results.question: Count listings in each status. Return status and listing_count, ordered by status.
results.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS listing_count FROM listings GROUP BY status ORDER BY status ASC
results.classification_explanation: The listings table contains status, so listings can be counted by status and the results ordered by status.

results.question: List bids of at least 100. Return bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, and amount, ordered by amount descending and then bid_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS bid_id, listing_id, bidder_id, amount FROM bids WHERE amount >= 100 ORDER BY amount DESC, bid_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The bids table contains all requested fields, with id serving as bid_id. Filtering for amounts of at least 100 and applying the requested sort order are read-only operations.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The threshold of 100 applies to bid amount, not row count; the limit omits qualifying bids if more than 100 match.

results.question: For every listing, show listing_id, title, bid_count, and highest_bid. Count actual bids; highest_bid must be NULL for a listing without bids. Order by listing_id.
results.sql: SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title, COUNT(b.id) AS bid_count, MAX(b.amount) AS highest_bid FROM listings AS l LEFT JOIN bids AS b ON b.listing_id = l.id GROUP BY l.id, l.title ORDER BY listing_id
results.classification_explanation: The listings and bids tables support the requested report in listing ID order, including listings with no bids, which have a bid count of 0 and a NULL highest bid.

results.question: Return the distinct user_id values of users who have listed an item or placed a bid, considering all listing statuses. Order by user_id.
results.sql: SELECT seller_id AS user_id FROM listings UNION SELECT bidder_id AS user_id FROM bids ORDER BY user_id
results.classification_explanation: The seller_id in listings and bidder_id in bids both identify users. Their values can be combined across all listing statuses, deduplicated, and sorted as user_id.

results.question: Which users have both listed an item and placed a bid, considering all listing statuses? Return distinct user_id values ascending.
results.sql: SELECT seller_id AS user_id FROM listings INTERSECT SELECT bidder_id AS user_id FROM bids ORDER BY user_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT seller_id) FROM listings)
results.classification_explanation: The database can match seller IDs across all listing statuses with bidder IDs and return the distinct matching user IDs in ascending order.

results.question: Find open listings whose reserve has been met by at least one bid. A listing with no reserve qualifies only if it has at least one bid. Return listing_id and title, ordered by listing_id.
results.sql: SELECT l.id AS listing_id, l.title FROM listings AS l WHERE l.status = 'open' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bids AS b WHERE b.listing_id = l.id AND (l.reserve_price IS NULL OR b.amount >= l.reserve_price)) ORDER BY listing_id LIMIT 100
results.classification_explanation: The listings and bids tables support finding open listings with at least one bid that meets the reserve, or any bid if no reserve is set, and returning listing IDs and titles in ID order.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 and keep ORDER BY listing_id. The limit omits qualifying listings if more than 100 match.

results.question: Find sellers who have at least one open listing and for whom every open listing has received a bid. Return seller_id and name, ordered by seller_id. Closed listings do not affect eligibility.
results.sql: SELECT u.id AS seller_id, u.name FROM users AS u JOIN listings AS l ON l.seller_id = u.id WHERE l.status = 'open' GROUP BY u.id, u.name HAVING MIN(EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bids AS b WHERE b.listing_id = l.id)) = 1 ORDER BY seller_id;
results.classification_explanation: The schema provides seller IDs and names, listing statuses, and bids linked to listings. It supports checking that each seller has at least one open listing and that every open listing has a bid, while ignoring closed listings and ordering by seller_id.

results.question: For every listing that has bids, return every bid tied for its highest amount. Return listing_id, title, bidder_id, bid_id, and amount, ordered by listing_id then bid_id. Include open and closed listings.
results.sql: WITH highest AS (SELECT listing_id, MAX(amount) AS max_amount FROM bids GROUP BY listing_id) SELECT b.listing_id, l.title, b.bidder_id, b.id AS bid_id, b.amount FROM highest AS h JOIN bids AS b ON b.listing_id = h.listing_id AND b.amount = h.max_amount JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id ORDER BY b.listing_id, b.id LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The bids and listings tables provide all requested fields and support returning every bid tied for its listing’s highest amount, including bids on open and closed listings, ordered by listing_id and then bid_id.

results.question: Find unordered pairs of bidders who have both bid on at least two distinct open listings. Return smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id, and shared_listing_count, ordered by those two IDs. Multiple bids by one bidder on one listing count only once.
results.sql: WITH open_bidders AS (SELECT DISTINCT b.listing_id, b.bidder_id FROM bids AS b JOIN listings AS l ON l.id = b.listing_id WHERE l.status = 'open') SELECT a.bidder_id AS smaller_bidder_id, b.bidder_id AS larger_bidder_id, COUNT(*) AS shared_listing_count FROM open_bidders AS a JOIN open_bidders AS b ON a.listing_id = b.listing_id AND a.bidder_id < b.bidder_id GROUP BY a.bidder_id, b.bidder_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY smaller_bidder_id, larger_bidder_id
results.classification_explanation: The bids and listings tables identify which open listings each bidder bid on. Counting distinct shared listings avoids double-counting repeat bids, and ordering the bidder IDs within each pair prevents duplicate pairs.

results.question: List mandatory questions. Return question_id and prompt, ordered by question_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS question_id, prompt FROM questions WHERE required = 1 ORDER BY question_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The questions table identifies mandatory questions with the required flag and provides the id and prompt. Its id can be returned as question_id and used for sorting.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The request is for all mandatory questions in question_id order, and the limit would omit any after the first 100.

results.question: List responses with a score of at least 4. Return response_id, participant_id, question_id, and score, ordered by response_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS response_id, participant_id, question_id, score FROM responses WHERE score >= 4 ORDER BY response_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The responses table contains all requested fields. Its id column serves as response_id for both output and ordering, and its score column supports the inclusive threshold of 4.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. It omits qualifying responses after the first 100, but the user requested all responses with score >= 4, ordered by response_id.

results.question: Count registered participants by group, displaying NULL group names as Unassigned. Return group_name and participant_count, ordered by the displayed group_name.
results.sql: SELECT COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name, COUNT(*) AS participant_count FROM participants AS p GROUP BY p.group_name ORDER BY COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned');
results.classification_explanation: The participants table supports counting participants by group, displaying NULL group names as Unassigned, and sorting by the displayed group name.

results.question: For every question, return question_id, prompt, answered_count, and average_score rounded to two decimals. Ignore NULL scores in both statistics; average_score must be NULL when nobody answered. Order by question_id.
results.sql: SELECT q.id AS question_id, q.prompt, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count, ROUND(AVG(r.score), 2) AS average_score FROM questions AS q LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.question_id = q.id GROUP BY q.id, q.prompt ORDER BY question_id
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every question by ID and prompt, counting only non-NULL scores, and averaging those scores to two decimal places. Questions with no non-NULL scores can be included with a count of zero and a NULL average, and the results can be ordered by question ID.

results.question: Which participants answered question 1 but did not answer question 2? A NULL score does not count as an answer. Return participant_id values ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r1.participant_id FROM responses AS r1 WHERE r1.question_id = 1 AND r1.score IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM responses AS r2 WHERE r2.participant_id = r1.participant_id AND r2.question_id = 2 AND r2.score IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY r1.participant_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM responses WHERE question_id = 1 AND score IS NOT NULL)
results.classification_explanation: The responses table can identify participants with a non-NULL score for question 1 and no non-NULL score for question 2. Their participant_id values can be returned in ascending order.

results.question: Combine the participant IDs of all non-NULL responses to question 1 with those of all non-NULL responses to question 2. Keep duplicates so a participant who answered both appears twice. Return only participant_id, sorted ascending.
results.sql: SELECT participant_id FROM responses WHERE question_id IN (1, 2) AND score IS NOT NULL ORDER BY participant_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM responses WHERE question_id IN (1, 2) AND score IS NOT NULL)
results.classification_explanation: The responses table supports selecting participant IDs for questions 1 and 2 with non-NULL scores, preserving duplicates across questions, and sorting the IDs in ascending order.

results.question: For every registered participant, return participant_id, name, and answered_count (the number of questions answered with a non-NULL score), in that order. Include participants with zero answers. Sort by participant_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name, COUNT(r.score) AS answered_count FROM participants AS p LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.participant_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY participant_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports listing every participant’s ID and name, counting only responses with non-NULL scores, including participants with a count of zero, and sorting by participant ID ascending.

results.question: Which participants answered every mandatory question with a non-NULL score? Return participant_id and name, ordered by participant_id. Optional questions do not affect eligibility. If there are no mandatory questions, every participant qualifies.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS participant_id, p.name FROM participants AS p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM questions AS q WHERE q.required = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM responses AS r WHERE r.participant_id = p.id AND r.question_id = q.id AND r.score IS NOT NULL)) ORDER BY participant_id LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM participants)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports checking whether each participant has a non-NULL score for every required question and returning their ID and name in ID order. Optional questions are ignored, and all participants qualify if none are required.

results.question: Find unordered participant pairs with exactly the same set of mandatory questions answered with non-NULL scores. Require that each participant answered at least one mandatory question. Return smaller_participant_id and larger_participant_id, ordered by both IDs.
results.sql:
WITH answered AS (
  SELECT r.participant_id, r.question_id
  FROM responses AS r
  JOIN questions AS q ON q.id = r.question_id
  WHERE q.required = 1 AND r.score IS NOT NULL
), eligible AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT participant_id FROM answered
)
SELECT a.participant_id AS smaller_participant_id,
       b.participant_id AS larger_participant_id
FROM eligible AS a
JOIN eligible AS b ON a.participant_id < b.participant_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT question_id FROM answered WHERE participant_id = a.participant_id
  EXCEPT
  SELECT question_id FROM answered WHERE participant_id = b.participant_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT question_id FROM answered WHERE participant_id = b.participant_id
  EXCEPT
  SELECT question_id FROM answered WHERE participant_id = a.participant_id
)
ORDER BY smaller_participant_id, larger_participant_id
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) * (COUNT(*) - 1) / 2 FROM eligible)
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports comparing each participant’s set of mandatory questions answered with non-NULL scores, excluding empty sets, and returning each matching pair once in the requested ID order.

results.question: For each registered participant group, compute the percentage of mandatory question-participant combinations that have a non-NULL score. The denominator is all registered participants in the group times the total number of mandatory questions; skips and missing responses are incomplete. Return group_name (Unassigned for NULL) and completion_percent rounded to two decimals, ordered by group_name. Use NULL if there are no mandatory questions.
results.sql: SELECT COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned') AS group_name, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(r.score) / NULLIF(COUNT(q.id), 0), 2) AS completion_percent FROM participants AS p LEFT JOIN questions AS q ON q.required = 1 LEFT JOIN responses AS r ON r.participant_id = p.id AND r.question_id = q.id GROUP BY p.group_name ORDER BY COALESCE(p.group_name, 'Unassigned')
results.classification_explanation: The schema provides participant groups, mandatory-question flags, and response scores. These support the requested read-only percentage calculation, including counting missing responses and NULL scores as incomplete.

results.question: List players on team 1. Return player_id, name, and position, ordered by player_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS player_id, name, position FROM players WHERE team_id = 1 ORDER BY player_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM players WHERE team_id = 1);
results.classification_explanation: The players table can be filtered to team 1 and sorted by id. Its id column can be returned as player_id alongside name and position.

results.question: List completed matches that ended in a draw. Return match_id, home_team_id, away_team_id, and the home score as goals_each, ordered by match_id.
results.sql: SELECT id AS match_id, home_team_id, away_team_id, home_score AS goals_each FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' AND home_score = away_score ORDER BY match_id LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The matches table contains the status and scores needed to identify completed draws. Its id, home_team_id, away_team_id, and home_score provide the requested output, with id used as match_id for ordering and home_score labeled goals_each.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. It omits qualifying draws after the first 100, but the user requested all completed draws ordered by match_id.

results.question: For every team, count players in its current roster. Return team_id, name, and player_count, ordered by team_id. Include teams with zero players.
results.sql: SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name, COUNT(p.id) AS player_count FROM teams AS t LEFT JOIN players AS p ON p.team_id = t.id GROUP BY t.id, t.name ORDER BY team_id;
results.classification_explanation: Each player’s team_id identifies their current team. Roster counts can be reported by team ID and name, ordered by team ID, with zero for teams that have no players.

results.question: For every player, sum goals from their recorded appearances in completed matches only. Return player_id, name, and recorded_goals, using 0 if none. Order by recorded_goals descending, then player_id.
results.sql: WITH completed_goals AS (SELECT a.player_id, SUM(a.goals) AS recorded_goals FROM appearances AS a JOIN matches AS m ON m.id = a.match_id WHERE m.status = 'completed' GROUP BY a.player_id) SELECT p.id AS player_id, p.name, COALESCE(g.recorded_goals, 0) AS recorded_goals FROM players AS p LEFT JOIN completed_goals AS g ON g.player_id = p.id ORDER BY recorded_goals DESC, player_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports totaling each player’s appearance goals in completed matches, including players with no qualifying appearances as zero, and sorting by recorded_goals descending, then player_id.

results.question: List distinct team_id values for teams that have played in at least one completed match, whether at home or away. Order by team_id.
results.sql: SELECT home_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' UNION SELECT away_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' ORDER BY team_id
results.classification_explanation: The matches table contains the match status and both home and away team IDs, so distinct team IDs from completed matches can be listed in ascending order.

results.question: Which teams have won at least one completed home match and at least one completed away match? Return distinct team_id values ascending.
results.sql: SELECT home_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' AND home_score > away_score INTERSECT SELECT away_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' AND away_score > home_score ORDER BY team_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: Match status, scores, and home and away team IDs are available to identify teams with at least one completed win in each role and return their distinct IDs in ascending order.

results.question: Compute league points for every team from completed matches: 3 per win, 1 per draw, 0 per loss. Return team_id, name, and points, including 0 for teams without completed matches. Order by points descending, then team_id.
results.sql: WITH completed AS (SELECT home_team_id, away_team_id, home_score, away_score FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed'), earned AS (SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, CASE WHEN home_score > away_score THEN 3 WHEN home_score = away_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points FROM completed UNION ALL SELECT away_team_id AS team_id, CASE WHEN away_score > home_score THEN 3 WHEN away_score = home_score THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS points FROM completed) SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name, COALESCE(SUM(e.points), 0) AS points FROM teams AS t LEFT JOIN earned AS e ON e.team_id = t.id GROUP BY t.id, t.name ORDER BY points DESC, t.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The teams table identifies every team, and match status and scores allow points to be calculated from completed matches. Teams without completed matches can be included with zero points, and the results can be sorted as requested.

results.question: Find teams with at least one completed match and no completed losses. Return team_id and name, ordered by team_id. Ignore scheduled matches.
results.sql: SELECT t.id AS team_id, t.name FROM teams AS t JOIN matches AS m ON (t.id = m.home_team_id OR t.id = m.away_team_id) WHERE m.status = 'completed' GROUP BY t.id, t.name HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN (t.id = m.home_team_id AND m.home_score < m.away_score) OR (t.id = m.away_team_id AND m.away_score < m.home_score) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 ORDER BY team_id
results.classification_explanation: The match status identifies completed matches, and the home and away scores determine whether each team lost. The teams table provides the requested ID and name, and the results can be ordered by team ID.

results.question: Find players with a recorded appearance in every completed match involving their current team. Require that the team has at least one completed match. Return player_id and name, ordered by player_id. A missing appearance does not count as participation.
results.sql:
WITH completed_team_matches AS (
  SELECT id AS match_id, home_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT id AS match_id, away_team_id AS team_id FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT p.id AS player_id, p.name
FROM players AS p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completed_team_matches AS m WHERE m.team_id = p.team_id
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completed_team_matches AS m
  WHERE m.team_id = p.team_id
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM appearances AS a
      WHERE a.player_id = p.id AND a.match_id = m.match_id
    )
)
ORDER BY player_id
LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM players)
results.classification_explanation: The schema identifies each player’s current team, its completed home and away matches, and the player’s recorded appearances. It supports checking that the team had at least one completed match and that the player appeared in every such match, then returning player IDs and names in ID order.

results.question: For each team that has won a completed match, identify the strongest opponent it defeated. Strength is that opponent's total league points from all completed matches (3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss). Choose the lowest opponent ID if points tie. Return team_id, opponent_id, and opponent_points, ordered by team_id. Count an opponent once even if defeated repeatedly.
results.sql: WITH results AS (SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, away_team_id AS opponent_id, home_score AS scored, away_score AS conceded FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed' UNION ALL SELECT away_team_id, home_team_id, away_score, home_score FROM matches WHERE status = 'completed'), points AS (SELECT team_id, SUM(CASE WHEN scored > conceded THEN 3 WHEN scored = conceded THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS league_points FROM results GROUP BY team_id), defeated AS (SELECT DISTINCT team_id, opponent_id FROM results WHERE scored > conceded), ranked AS (SELECT d.team_id, d.opponent_id, p.league_points AS opponent_points, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY d.team_id ORDER BY p.league_points DESC, d.opponent_id ASC) AS rn FROM defeated AS d JOIN points AS p ON p.team_id = d.opponent_id) SELECT team_id, opponent_id, opponent_points FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY team_id
results.classification_explanation: The matches table contains the team IDs, status, and scores needed to calculate league points and identify each team’s distinct defeated opponents. The lowest opponent ID resolves ties for strongest opponent.

results.question: List completed runs. Return run_id, experiment_id, and variant, in that order, sorted by run_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS run_id, experiment_id, variant FROM runs WHERE status = 'completed' ORDER BY run_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The runs table supports filtering by completed status and returning id as run_id, followed by experiment_id and variant, sorted by run_id ascending.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. It omits completed runs after the first 100, but the request asks for all completed runs in ascending run_id order.

results.question: List stored measurements whose reading is NULL. Return measurement_id, run_id, and metric, in that order, sorted by measurement_id ascending. Include all run statuses.
results.sql: SELECT id AS measurement_id, run_id, metric FROM measurements WHERE value IS NULL ORDER BY measurement_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM measurements WHERE value IS NULL)
results.classification_explanation: The measurements table contains the requested fields: id is the measurement_id, and value is the reading to check for NULL. The results can be sorted by id ascending without filtering by run status.

results.question: Which defined metrics have never had a measurement row recorded, including rows with NULL readings? Return metric and unit, in that order, sorted by metric ascending. Include all runs.
results.sql: SELECT m.name AS metric, m.unit FROM metrics AS m WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM measurements AS r WHERE r.metric = m.name) ORDER BY metric ASC
results.classification_explanation: The database can list the name and unit of each defined metric with no measurement rows across any run, sorted by metric name ascending. A row with a NULL reading counts as recorded.

results.question: For every experiment, return experiment_id, name, run_count, completed_runs, and failed_runs, in that order. Include experiments without runs with zero counts; running runs count only toward run_count. Sort by experiment_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT e.id AS experiment_id, e.name, COUNT(r.id) AS run_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN r.status = 'completed' THEN 1 END) AS completed_runs, COUNT(CASE WHEN r.status = 'failed' THEN 1 END) AS failed_runs FROM experiments AS e LEFT JOIN runs AS r ON r.experiment_id = e.id GROUP BY e.id, e.name ORDER BY e.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The experiments table provides each experiment’s ID and name. Linked runs can be counted overall and by status, with zero counts for experiments without runs. The requested column order and ascending ID sort are supported.

results.question: Find runs with at least one non-NULL temperature reading but no non-NULL pressure reading. Include every run status. Return distinct run_id values sorted ascending.
results.sql: SELECT run_id FROM measurements WHERE value IS NOT NULL AND metric IN ('temperature', 'pressure') GROUP BY run_id HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN metric = 'temperature' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN metric = 'pressure' THEN 1 END) = 0 ORDER BY run_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The measurements table provides the run IDs, metric names, and values needed to find runs with a non-NULL temperature reading and no non-NULL pressure reading. The matching IDs can be returned once each in ascending order without filtering by run status.

results.question: Combine all non-NULL temperature readings from run 1 with all non-NULL temperature readings from run 2, keeping repeated readings even when values match. Return one column named value, sorted ascending.
results.sql: SELECT value FROM measurements WHERE run_id IN (1, 2) AND metric = 'temperature' AND value IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value ASC LIMIT -1
results.classification_explanation: The measurements table supports returning a single value column of non-NULL temperature readings from runs 1 and 2, sorted in ascending order with duplicates preserved.

results.question: For every run, return run_id and target_coverage_percent, in that order, sorted by run_id. Coverage is 100 times the number of distinct target metrics with at least one non-NULL reading for that run divided by the number of defined metrics with non-NULL targets. Include all statuses and runs without readings, use zero coverage when no target is measured, return NULL if there are no target metrics, and round percentages to two decimals.
results.sql: WITH target_metrics AS (SELECT name FROM metrics WHERE target IS NOT NULL), measured AS (SELECT m.run_id, COUNT(DISTINCT m.metric) AS n FROM measurements AS m JOIN target_metrics AS t ON t.name = m.metric WHERE m.value IS NOT NULL GROUP BY m.run_id) SELECT r.id AS run_id, ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(measured.n, 0) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM target_metrics), 0), 2) AS target_coverage_percent FROM runs AS r LEFT JOIN measured ON measured.run_id = r.id ORDER BY r.id
results.classification_explanation: The runs, metrics, and measurements tables provide all required data. The requested coverage can be calculated for every run, including runs without readings, with the specified zero, NULL, rounding, and ordering rules.

results.question: Find completed runs that have at least one non-NULL reading for every defined metric whose target is non-NULL. If there are no target metrics, all completed runs qualify. Return run_id and experiment_id, in that order, sorted by run_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT r.id AS run_id, r.experiment_id FROM runs AS r WHERE r.status = 'completed' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM metrics AS m WHERE m.target IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM measurements AS x WHERE x.run_id = r.id AND x.metric = m.name AND x.value IS NOT NULL)) ORDER BY r.id ASC LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports filtering completed runs and checking for a non-NULL measurement for each metric with a non-NULL target. If no metrics have targets, all completed runs qualify. The requested IDs and sort order are available.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000 and retain ORDER BY r.id ASC. The request asks for all qualifying runs, but the limit omits any matches after the first 1,000.

results.question: Compare treatment and control yield for each experiment using completed runs only. First average non-NULL yield readings within each run, then average those run means within each variant so runs have equal weight. Ignore runs with no known yield and include only experiments with a known mean for both variants. Return experiment_id, control_mean, treatment_mean, and percent_change, in that order. Percent change is 100 times (treatment minus control) divided by control; return NULL when control is zero. Round all three calculated values to two decimals and sort by experiment_id.
results.sql:
WITH run_means AS (
  SELECT r.experiment_id, r.variant, r.id, AVG(m.value) AS run_mean
  FROM runs AS r
  JOIN measurements AS m ON m.run_id = r.id
  WHERE r.status = 'completed'
    AND r.variant IN ('control', 'treatment')
    AND m.metric = 'yield'
    AND m.value IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY r.experiment_id, r.variant, r.id
), experiment_means AS (
  SELECT experiment_id,
         AVG(CASE WHEN variant = 'control' THEN run_mean END) AS control_mean,
         AVG(CASE WHEN variant = 'treatment' THEN run_mean END) AS treatment_mean
  FROM run_means
  GROUP BY experiment_id
)
SELECT experiment_id,
       ROUND(control_mean, 2) AS control_mean,
       ROUND(treatment_mean, 2) AS treatment_mean,
       ROUND(100.0 * (treatment_mean - control_mean) / NULLIF(control_mean, 0), 2) AS percent_change
FROM experiment_means
WHERE control_mean IS NOT NULL AND treatment_mean IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY experiment_id
results.classification_explanation: The measurements and runs tables contain the yield readings, run status, variant, and experiment ID needed for the comparison. The equal-weight averages, eligibility filters, percent change, rounding, and sorting are all read-only calculations.

results.question: For each metric with a non-NULL target, find the completed runs whose mean non-NULL reading is closest to that target. Average repeated readings within a run, omit runs without a known reading, compare absolute distances before rounding, and keep all tied runs. Return metric, run_id, mean_value, and distance, in that order. Round mean_value and distance to two decimals and sort by metric ascending, then run_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH run_means AS (
  SELECT m.name AS metric, r.id AS run_id, AVG(v.value) AS mean_value, m.target
  FROM metrics AS m
  JOIN measurements AS v ON v.metric = m.name
  JOIN runs AS r ON r.id = v.run_id
  WHERE m.target IS NOT NULL AND v.value IS NOT NULL AND r.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY m.name, r.id, m.target
), distances AS (
  SELECT metric, run_id, mean_value, ABS(mean_value - target) AS distance
  FROM run_means
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY metric ORDER BY distance) AS distance_rank
  FROM distances
)
SELECT metric, run_id, ROUND(mean_value, 2) AS mean_value, ROUND(distance, 2) AS distance
FROM ranked
WHERE distance_rank = 1
ORDER BY metric ASC, run_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema provides run status, metric targets, and readings. A read-only query can average the known readings for each completed run and metric, keep all runs tied for the smallest unrounded absolute distance to the target, and round and sort the results as requested.

results.question: List tasks with no assignee, including every status. Return task_id, project_id, title, and due_date, in that order, keeping NULL due dates. Sort by task_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS task_id, project_id, title, due_date FROM tasks WHERE assignee_id IS NULL ORDER BY task_id ASC LIMIT 100;
results.classification_explanation: The tasks table contains all requested fields, with id serving as task_id. Unassigned tasks can be identified by a NULL assignee_id, retaining every status and NULL due dates, with the requested column order and ascending task_id sort.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100. The request calls for all unassigned tasks, but the limit omits qualifying tasks after the first 100.

results.question: For every person, total the hours they personally logged across all tasks and dates, regardless of task status or assignment. Return person_id, name, and total_hours, in that order; use zero for people with no entries, round hours to two decimals, and sort by person_id ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT p.id AS person_id, p.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(te.hours), 0), 2) AS total_hours
FROM people AS p
LEFT JOIN time_entries AS te ON te.person_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY person_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The people and time_entries tables can provide each person’s ID, name, and total hours using the person who logged each entry, regardless of task status or assignment. People with no entries can be included with zero hours, and the requested column order, rounding, and sorting are supported.

results.question: List tasks with no due date, regardless of status. Return task_id, title, and status, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT id AS task_id, title, status FROM tasks WHERE due_date IS NULL ORDER BY task_id ASC LIMIT 100
results.classification_explanation: The tasks table supports listing tasks with no due date across all statuses, returning id as task_id, then title and status, sorted by task_id ascending.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 100 so the query returns all tasks with a NULL due_date, not just the first 100.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, name, known_cost, and unpriced_hours, in that order. Include all task statuses and dates. Known cost is the sum of hours times billed_rate for entries with a non-NULL rate; unpriced hours are hours with a NULL rate. Use zero for missing totals and projects with no work, round both totals to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS project_id, p.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.billed_rate IS NOT NULL THEN e.hours * e.billed_rate END), 0), 2) AS known_cost, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.billed_rate IS NULL THEN e.hours END), 0), 2) AS unpriced_hours FROM projects AS p LEFT JOIN tasks AS t ON t.project_id = p.id LEFT JOIN time_entries AS e ON e.task_id = t.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY project_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The available tables link projects to tasks and time entries, so both totals can be calculated across all statuses and dates. The request is read-only and can include projects with no work, use zero for missing totals, and apply the requested rounding and ordering.

results.question: Find tasks whose own status is not done and whose direct prerequisites are all done. Tasks without prerequisites qualify. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending. Consider only direct prerequisites, regardless of the task due date or assignee.
results.sql: SELECT t.id AS task_id, t.title FROM tasks AS t WHERE t.status <> 'done' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dependencies AS d JOIN tasks AS p ON p.id = d.depends_on WHERE d.task_id = t.id AND p.status <> 'done') ORDER BY task_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tasks);
results.classification_explanation: The tasks and dependencies tables can identify non-done tasks with no unfinished direct prerequisite, including tasks with no prerequisites. The results can return task_id and title in that order, sorted by task_id ascending.

results.question: Find direct dependency edges for which the dependent task and its prerequisite have the same non-NULL assignee, regardless of task status. Return task_id, depends_on, and assignee_id, in that order. Sort by task_id ascending, then depends_on ascending.
results.sql:
SELECT d.task_id, d.depends_on, t.assignee_id
FROM dependencies AS d
JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = d.task_id
JOIN tasks AS p ON p.id = d.depends_on
WHERE t.assignee_id = p.assignee_id
ORDER BY d.task_id ASC, d.depends_on ASC
LIMIT 1000
results.classification_explanation: The dependencies table identifies each direct edge, and the tasks table provides the assignee for each endpoint. Edges with matching non-NULL assignees can be returned in the requested column and sort order without filtering by status.
critique_issues: Remove LIMIT 1000. It omits qualifying edges after the first 1,000, but the user requested all matching edges.

results.question: Which projects contain at least one task but no task with status blocked? Return project_id and name, in that order, sorted by project_id ascending. Projects with no tasks must be excluded.
results.sql: SELECT p.id AS project_id, p.name FROM projects AS p JOIN tasks AS t ON t.project_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status = 'blocked' THEN 1 END) = 0 ORDER BY project_id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The projects and tasks tables can identify projects with at least one task and no blocked tasks. Project ID and name can be returned in that order, sorted by project ID ascending.

results.question: List every direct or indirect prerequisite of task 5. Follow dependency edges recursively, return each prerequisite only once even if reachable through multiple paths, and exclude task 5 itself. Return task_id and title, in that order, sorted by task_id ascending; include prerequisites of any status.
results.sql: WITH RECURSIVE reachable(id) AS (VALUES (5) UNION SELECT d.depends_on FROM reachable AS r JOIN dependencies AS d ON d.task_id = r.id) SELECT t.id AS task_id, t.title FROM reachable AS r JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = r.id WHERE t.id <> 5 ORDER BY task_id ASC LIMIT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tasks)
results.classification_explanation: The dependencies table can be followed recursively to find each distinct prerequisite of task 5, excluding task 5 itself. The tasks table supplies the titles, and the results can include all statuses and be sorted by task_id ascending.

results.question: Find the task with the greatest known cost within each project, keeping all tied tasks and omitting projects with no tasks. Include every task status and date. A task known cost is the sum of hours times non-NULL billed_rate, or zero when it has no priced entries. Compare unrounded costs. Return project_id, task_id, title, and known_cost, in that order, round known_cost to two decimals, and sort by project_id then task_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_costs AS (
  SELECT t.project_id, t.id AS task_id, t.title,
         COALESCE(SUM(e.hours * e.billed_rate), 0.0) AS raw_cost
  FROM tasks AS t
  LEFT JOIN time_entries AS e ON e.task_id = t.id
  GROUP BY t.project_id, t.id, t.title
), ranked AS (
  SELECT task_costs.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY project_id ORDER BY raw_cost DESC) AS cost_rank
  FROM task_costs
)
SELECT project_id, task_id, title, ROUND(raw_cost, 2) AS known_cost
FROM ranked
WHERE cost_rank = 1
ORDER BY project_id ASC, task_id ASC;
results.classification_explanation: The tasks and time entries provide all required data. Known costs can be compared before rounding, retaining all ties within each project without filtering by status or date.

results.question: For every project, return project_id, task_count, dependency_edge_count, and total_hours, in that order. Count each task once, count each direct dependency edge once for the project owning its dependent task, and sum each time entry once. Include all statuses and dates, preserve projects without tasks with zero totals, round hours to two decimals, and sort by project_id ascending.
results.sql:
WITH task_counts AS (
  SELECT project_id, COUNT(*) AS task_count
  FROM tasks
  GROUP BY project_id
), edge_counts AS (
  SELECT t.project_id, COUNT(*) AS dependency_edge_count
  FROM dependencies AS d
  JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = d.task_id
  GROUP BY t.project_id
), project_hours AS (
  SELECT t.project_id, SUM(e.hours) AS total_hours
  FROM time_entries AS e
  JOIN tasks AS t ON t.id = e.task_id
  GROUP BY t.project_id
)
SELECT p.id AS project_id,
       COALESCE(tc.task_count, 0) AS task_count,
       COALESCE(ec.dependency_edge_count, 0) AS dependency_edge_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(ph.total_hours, 0.0), 2) AS total_hours
FROM projects AS p
LEFT JOIN task_counts AS tc ON tc.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN edge_counts AS ec ON ec.project_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN project_hours AS ph ON ph.project_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.id ASC
results.classification_explanation: The schema supports counting each task and direct dependency edge once for the specified project and summing each time entry once. The requested read-only report can include all statuses and dates, retain empty projects with zero totals, and apply the specified rounding and ordering.
